title: Republican senator blocks Trump cyber nominee over January 6 denial
author: Robert Mackey
text:
Thom Tillis move comes after Michael LoSapio, nominated for Cisa role, told hearing ‘I don’t believe it was an attack’

Senator Thom Tillis, the outgoing North Carolina Republican who is due to be replaced by a Democrat, has reportedly blocked a confirmation vote on Donald Trump’s nominee to lead a key US cybersecurity agency, Michael LoSapio, after he denied during a hearing that the Capitol was attacked on January 6 2021.

Tillis, who declined to run for re-election and after repeated clashes with Trump’s, confirmed to HuffPost on Friday that he has placed a hold on LoSapio’s nomination to serve as a director of the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency (Cisa). His block on the nomination will prevent it from being included in a package of nominees to be voted on next month, before the Republicans lose their majority in the Senate.

At his Senate confirmation hearing on Thursday, LoSapio, the chief information security officer for Palantir, a technology firm founded by JD Vance’s mentor, Peter Thiel, was asked by senator Richard Blumenthal, a Connecticut Democrat: “Was there an attack on the Capitol of January 6 2021?”

After initially replying, “I don’t know,” LoSapio said: “No, I don’t believe it was an attack.”

Tillis told the Hill that the question of whether a mob of Trump supporters attacked the US Capitol in an attempt to overturn Joe Biden’s 2020 victory was not open for debate.

“It’s binary,” Tillis told the outlet. “The minute you pretend like it didn’t exist or you can’t even acknowledge it, I don’t have any time because it’s not a very thoughtful person.”

The agency LoSapio was nominated by Trump to lead, Cisa, plays a role in protecting US elections infrastructure from hacking.

The week after the 2020 election, as Trump falsely claimed that count had been rigged, Cisa was one of a number of federal agencies with oversight of election infrastructure to issue a statement calling the election “the most secure in American history” and noting that there was “no evidence that any voting system deleted or lost votes, changed votes, or was in any way compromised.”

After he returned to the White House last year, Trump signed an April 2025 presidential memorandum directing executive offices to take steps to address supposed “risks from Chris Krebs”, who led Cisa in 2020.

“Krebs, through CISA, falsely and baselessly denied that the 2020 election was rigged and stolen, including by inappropriately and categorically dismissing widespread election malfeasance and serious vulnerabilities with voting machines,” Trump’s memorandum claimed.

title: Judge approves $7.25bn Bayer payout to settle claims that Roundup causes cancer
author: Reuters
text:
German company faced 65,000 claims from people who said they developed cancer after using weedkiller

A Missouri judge on Friday approved Bayer ’s $7.25bn settlement of lawsuits ⁠alleging that its weedkiller ​Roundup causes cancer, potentially resolving litigation that has weighed on the German company for close to a decade.

Judge Timothy Boyer of a state court in St Louis ⁠found the settlement “fair, reasonable and adequate”.

He overruled objections that payouts to individual cancer victims would be too low because claimants who previously settled were paid more.

The judge also said delaying payouts could ⁠force victims, including those whose cancer is terminal, to wait “an indeterminate number of years” to be paid.

Bayer had faced approximately ​65,000 claims in US state and federal courts from ‌people who said they developed cancer ‌after using Roundup at home or on the job.

The settlement announced in February aimed to resolve nearly all current ‌and future Roundup claims in the US.

“The court’s final approval is a decisive milestone in the company’s strategy to mitigate the risks of both pending and future Roundup litigation,” Bayer’s CEO, Bill Anderson, said in a statement.

Bayer has faced extensive litigation over Roundup, and had seen its share price fall 46% since it bought Monsanto , which produces the weedkiller, for $63bn in 2018.

The company settled much of the Roundup litigation for $10.9bn in 2020, ‌but was unable to win court approval of a $1.25bn settlement to resolve future Roundup claims.

Bayer has long maintained that Roundup and its active ingredient glyphosate were safe, and that decades ​of studies had shown that glyphosate did not cause cancer.

The settlement was approved five months after the US supreme court overturned a $1.25m jury award for a Missouri man, John Durnell, who blamed years of exposure to glyphosate in Roundup for his non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

In a 7-2 decision, the court agreed with Bayer that a federal law regulating pesticides barred failure-to-warn claims brought under ⁠state law, undercutting a central pillar of many lawsuits.

Christopher Seeger, a lawyer for ​many of the plaintiffs, said the Durnell ​decision narrowed the ability of Roundup victims ​to pursue claims in court.

“We look forward to getting this relief into the hands of all ​Roundup victims as quickly ‌as possible,” he ​said in a statement.

Lawyers for ​some of the Roundup victims who objected to the settlement did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The settlement excludes some lawsuits that remain pending in federal court. Bayer has said that about 200 of those cases were still being litigated, and that the supreme court decision gave it strong defenses.

title: Every Wahoo Bike Computer Is Up to 35% Off for Black Friday—Here’s Which One to Buy
author: Josh Ross
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Welcome to Velo Deals. We sift through the retail landscape to bring you deals worth paying attention to. It might be a discount or it might just be a product so good you should grab it. Either way, if it’s worth your time, you’ll see it here. If you’d like to see the rest of the category, check all our Velo Deals coverage.

When it comes to bike computers, the biggest players are Garmin and Wahoo, and each takes a fundamentally different approach to solving the same puzzle. If you want simple, Wahoo is the one for you, and all three size options are being offered at a massive discount right now.

Across the entire lineup, Wahoo makes the easiest-to-use bike computers on the market. They are the ultimate “it just works” devices: add your accounts, connect to Wi-Fi, and you’re ready to ride. You aren’t giving up serious metrics for that simplicity, either. Instead of painstakingly assigning data to individual boxes, you just list your fields in order of importance in the app and use the side buttons to zoom in or out on the fly. Even if you normally like a lot of data, it’s great to zoom in to just power and speed when it’s late in a ride, everything hurts, and you just need to pedal.

The main trade-off in the past was always that Wahoo doesn’t offer an all-encompassing 24/7 wearable ecosystem, but even that’s been fixed recently. Wahoo has a partnership with Coros, and if you want a full picture of both training and recovery, you can use the Coros backend system and a Coros watch seamlessly with your Wahoo computer.

At the top of the lineup sits the Elemnt Ace, which is Wahoo’s answer for riders who want maximum screen real estate and every feature the brand makes. It has a large 3.8-inch color touchscreen, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, a built-in speaker for voice turn-by-turn navigation, and up to 30 hours of claimed battery life. Its headline differentiator is an integrated wind sensor that measures live airspeed to quantify headwinds, tailwinds, and drafting. All of that hardware comes with a clear trade-off in size and weight—at 208 grams, it is noticeably larger and heavier than a standard head unit, which is why Wahoo includes an aluminum out-front mount in the box.

This is probably the one you really want. It keeps almost everything that makes the Ace appealing—including the 16-million-color touchscreen interface, 64GB of storage, dual-band GPS, and the built-in speaker for audible turn-by-turn prompts—while dropping the wind sensor and massive size. Instead of a 3.8-inch display, it steps down to a still very usable 2.8-inch screen and cuts the weight nearly in half to 109 grams, with a claimed battery life of up to 25 hours.

If you want something smaller and lighter for racing or just prefer a cleaner cockpit, the Elemnt Bolt 3 strips the formula down to the essentials. This is also the best budget play, but it’s still a very capable computer. Weighing in at 84 grams with a 2.3-inch color display, it drops both the touchscreen and the audio speaker, relying strictly on physical buttons for control. Storage drops to 32GB and claimed battery life dips to 20 hours, but you still get the same dual-band GPS, high-contrast color screen tech, and updated Ready-To-Ride interface found on its bigger siblings.

title: These E-Bikes Make City Riding a Joy
author: Alison Jaksen
text:
The Aventon Solterra 3. (Photo: Aventon)

Riding a bike, at its heart, is amazing because it’s so simple. Two wheels, a frame, and suddenly you’re zooming around and discovering that going places can be fun . That’s why fixed-gear and single-speed bikes have such passionate fans: They prioritize the freedom that comes from embracing simplicity. With less weight and extraneous features, biking reenters the realm of play, and a daily commute or jaunt to grab groceries can feel a lot like flying.

Enter Aventon’s Soltera 2.5 and Soltera 3 ADV, which capture that fixie magic. The brand launched its legendary fixed gear Mataró model back in 2013, and that minimalist spirit infuses this new pair of e-bikes. They both marry a light-is-right sensibility with powerful but barely-there motors, all of it in a stealth design that will change the way you think about e-bikes.

The Class 1 Soltera 3 ADV Ebike ($1,499) will delight purists. Powered by a 250-watt (500-watt peak) motor, it offers 40 Nm of torque and a 70-mile range in a featherweight 37-pound package. It swaps a clanky chain for a carbon reinforced polymer belt that’s way easier to maintain and can last two to three times longer than any chain. Its single-speed configuration keeps you nimble and agile in the stop-start flow and narrow corridors you’ll encounter in urban traffic.

The Soltera 3’s updated geometry sings in the concrete maze, too—and everywhere. A longer wheelbase and lower bottom bracket keep it planted and predictable at speed, while a taller stack puts you in a more upright position that’s easier on your back, wrists, and neck on longer rides. A lower standover makes it easy to hop on and off at every light. With its ease of use and maintenance, there’s no simpler way to get some electric oomph into your daily ride.

Want to go down the zen road of simplicity but retain a bit more flex and options? You want the Soltera 2.5 Ebike ($1,199). For a scant 9 more pounds, you get a Shimano 7-speed drivetrain, on-demand throttle, wired features, and a 46-mile range. It brings a more traditional city e-bike feel while paring away the fluff to maintain fixie-forward geometry and feel.

Swapping your trusty-rusty analog commuting horse for an e-bike can feel like settling for an underpowered motorcycle. But both Soltera models deliver electric power while reaching back to a style of riding with less weight, complication, and stress—and more of what you need to make city streets fun to ride.

Aventon Bikes is here to inspire adventures, both big and small, in all terrains of life. No matter what we look like now, a year from now, or a decade from now, this is what keeps us moving forward. Redefine adventure and learn more at aventon.com .

title: Cost of Man Utd hiring and firing managers nears £100m
text:
Manchester United borrowed another £10m three days after confirming Mauricio Pochettino as their new head coach.

In an extended Stock Market filing to go with their first-quarter financial results that were released on Thursday, United said they would be liable to pay £7.5m in compensation to US Soccer to hire the Argentine.

United announced Pochettino had agreed a two-and-a-half-year deal on 13 November. They borrowed £10m on 16 November.

The loan is one of three confirmed after the 30 September first-quarter reporting date, which takes the overall amount owed on their rolling credit limit to £240m.

The amount paid to release Pochettino from his USA deal takes the sums paid hiring and firing managers since Sir Alex Ferguson retired in 2013 to £95m. However, that figure is likely to top £100m once the cost of hiring Pochettino's staff and sacking Michael Carrick is added.

Carrick was sacked last week with the club in the relegation zone and enduring their worst start to a season in 40 years. The former midfielder only signed a two-year contract in the summer after a successful six-month spell in caretaker charge last season.

Pochettino is the ninth full-time manager to be appointed since Ferguson, including Ralf Rangnick in November 2021. United have changed their manager in the middle of the last three campaigns.

The club also confirmed they had spent £5.7m to either acquire or extend registrations of "certain players and members of coaching staff".

The filing also revealed they owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £181m of which is due after one year. United said on Thursday their substantial $750m debt was £577.4m when converted to sterling on 30 September.

title: NSW passes Mount Pleasant coalmine law as Greens claim change an attempt to head off One Nation
author: Penry Buckley and Lisa Cox
text:
Labor says allowing mine to increase production reflects ‘gravity of situation facing hundreds of workers’ – but critics call it ‘unprecedented and dangerous’

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales government has passed special legislation to allow a coalmine in the Hunter Valley to increase production by 32% in its final act of parliament before the March state election, in which the region will be a key battleground for One Nation.

After a marathon session in the legislative council on Friday, the Minns government and the Coalition voted at 1.36am on Saturday morning to allow the Mount Pleasant mine to increase its annual extraction rate from 12.5MT to 16.5MT until 2032.

At the start of debate, the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, told the upper house “this is a unique bill applying to unique circumstances”.

“Taking the decision to intervene in the way we have is not an easy one, but it is an important one,” she said. “And it does reflect the gravity of the situation facing hundreds of workers and their families in the Hunter.”

The legislation has drawn outcry from legal and anti-corruption experts, climate groups, crossbenchers and civil liberties organisations, after the high court ruled last month that an approval for an expansion that would increase the mine’s annual output to 21MT until 2048 was invalid.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to properly consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burned overseas.

Despite saying he would not bypass the court’s decision, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, subsequently announced the legislation , claiming it would save 400 jobs ahead of Christmas.

On Friday, the government and Coalition used their numbers to block almost 200 amendments to the bill sought by the Greens, who called the legislation “exceptional and unprecedented and dangerous”. Animal Justice party MLC Emma Hurst also opposed the bill.

“Labor describes the circumstances as exceptional, says this case is unique, and assures the public that other companies shouldn’t expect the same treatment,” the Greens climate spokesperson, Sue Higginson, told the parliament.

“But a political assurance offers no protection against the precedent being set.”

She accused the premier of being motivated by a desire to withstand a threat from One Nation to Labor seats in the Hunter.

“It’s very clear to us why Chris Minns has gone here, and that is because we’re really on the eve of an election, and One Nation is right now his threat,” she said at a press conference on Thursday.

The Hunter region, the centre of NSW’s coalmining industry, is emerging as a key battleground at the March 2027 state election. The One Nation NSW upper house candidate and former coalminer Stuart Bonds contested the Labor-held federal seat of Hunter in 2025, winning 41% of the two-candidate preferred vote. The party’s NSW leader, Mike Newman, is running in the Labor-held lower house seat of Cessnock .

Higginson told the upper house that in bringing the bill, the government had turned its back on the advice of the state’s Net Zero Commission, which has said further coalmine expansions are incompatible with meeting legislated emissions reduction targets.

“But who seems to care any more? What does the rule of law matter when [the premier] visits the Hunter and decides he needs to do something for someone so that he can remain somewhat popular in his own mind?” she said.

The Coalition, which supported the bill, said it was “about people”.

“It’s about the hundreds of workers at MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant mine who, since the high court handed down its decision in October, have been left wondering whether they will still have a job in the new year,” Nationals MLC Sarah Mitchell said.

She said “losing hundreds of jobs in one go would completely devastate the Hunter region”.

The legislation ties consent for the mine expansion to a jobs guarantee protecting workers at the mine. Data provided to the government by the mine for the jobs guarantee, which covers more than 720 workers, is subject to an independent audit.

At a press conference on Wednesday, Minns said the legal proceedings would return to the land and environment court for consideration, but it would be “a tragedy if, in the meantime, that community effectively shut down as a result of this decision”.

“Most of the workers from Mount Pleasant live in Muswellbrook, and if the mine closed, the unemployment rate would jump by 5% just in that small town,” he said, speaking alongside workers at the mine and the Mining and Energy Union, which has welcomed the legislation.

In a report published on Tuesday, the parliament’s legislation review committee found the Mount Pleasant bill would “effectively undermine” proceedings that were still before the land and environment court and “would undermine procedural fairness” by removing avenues for legal challenge.

That report also highlighted concerns with a so-called Henry VIII clause that the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson warned this week posed a “serious corruption risk” to the state.

The clause, allowing the resources minister of the day to override state laws as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development, was amended by the government in the lower house. Following the amendments, it cannot be used to prevent development from being subject to Icac investigations or to change the permitted coal production limit.

The Nature Conservation Council of NSW said the government had been “embarrassed into amending its own coalmining bill”, while the Greens said the amendments did not go far enough to constrain the power any resources minister might hold under the clause.…

title: Yankees non-tender Fernando Cruz, Luis Gil
author: Peter Brody
text:
Cruz and Gil become free agents while the Yankees’ other seven arbitration-eligible players were tendered contracts.

The deadline to tender contracts to arbitration-eligible players arrived at 5pm ET on November 20th, and the Yankees have decided to non-tender Fernando Cruz and Luis Gil. The pair of right-handed pitchers become free agents, while Luis García Jr., Anthony Volpe, Ryan Weathers, Clarke Schmidt, Austin Wells, José Caballero, and Heliot Ramos have the next few months to decide whether to accept the Yankees’ offer or submit their own offers as the initial step in negotiating a salary for 2027.

Should both parties fail to agree on a number, the case would be submitted to an arbitration hearing. These hearings typically occur in February — subject to change due to the looming expiry of the CBA and expected owner lockout of the players — with the arbitration panel resolving the case by awarding the figure tendered by either the club or the player as opposed to a midpoint of those two figures.

The decision to non-tender Cruz and Gil does not come as much of a surprise. Both players were tabbed to earn $2.3 million in 2027 according to MLB Trade Rumors’ arbitration projections — an affordable amount that the Yankees nonetheless decided was better spent elsewhere given the question marks surrounding both players’ health and effectiveness going forward. It is the second year in the row that the Yankees have used the non-tender as a way to clear roster space on the pitching side. In 2025, they non-tendered five pitchers — Mark Leiter Jr., Ian Hamilton, Scott Effross, Jake Cousins, and Michael Arias — out of their 14 arbitration-eligible players.

Our own Andrés Chávez identified Gil as a non-tender candidate at the beginning of the month. It has been a precipitous fall from the stratospheric seven-start stretch that ultimately won Gil the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year Award. He has battled lat and shoulder injuries over the past two seasons, limiting him to 20 appearances (15 starts) with a 3.74 ERA, 5.44 FIP, and 58 strikeouts in 84.1 innings. An alarming loss of velocity on his fastball and worsening command has seen his strikeout rate crater from 27.3-percent between 2021-2024 to just 15.8-percent in the last two years, creating an untenable 1.9-percent strikeout-minus-walk ratio. There were question whether Gil might rediscover some effectiveness in a max-effort bullpen role, but ultimately the Yankees decided that the experiment wasn’t worth the effort. In five big league seasons with the Yankees, Gil went 21-11 in 56 appearances (51 starts), posting a 3.61 ERA, 4.54 FIP, 272 strikeouts, and 2.8 fWAR in 269.1 innings.

As for Cruz, the righty reliever became something of a cult hero thanks to his devastating splitter and enthusiastic celebrations. Arriving via trade from the Reds in the 2024-25 offseason, Cruz carved out a late-inning high leverage role by posting a 32-percent strikeout rate thanks to the splitter that allowed him to sit at the very top of the league whiff rate leaderboard. However, his appearances waned across his final two months of action in 2026, and it was subsequently revealed that he had suffered a partial tear of his UCL. The injury ended his campaign despite Cruz opting not to undergo surgery in the hope of making a late-season comeback. He was recently able to begin a throwing program, and GM Brian Cashman expressed optimism about his availability in 2027, but it appears the medicals on his elbow were scary enough to not be worth the risk at that price. In two seasons with the Yankees, Cruz made 110 relief appearances, pitching to a 3.33 ERA and 3.71 FIP with 139 strikeouts and 1.2 fWAR in 102.2 innings.

It is no surprise that the Yankees tendered contracts to the remaining seven arbitration-eligible players. The only other plausible candidate for non-tender was Schmidt, who is projected to earn $4.5 million in his third and final year of arbitration eligibility. The 30-year-old righty has missed significant parts of the last three seasons to injury — a lat strain in 2024, Tommy John surgery in 2025, and a biceps injury shortly after his return from Tommy John rehab in 2026. In total, he has made just 30 starts since the start of 2024, pitching just 164.2 innings after tossing a career-high 159 in 2023. However, Cashman confirmed that Schmidt is fully healthy entering this offseason, and the righty offers a much high floor and ceiling than Gil as starting rotation depth while also representing an intriguing multi-inning relief option.

With Cruz and Gil’s non-tenders, the Yankees have now subtracted two more arms from their already depleted relief corps. David Bednar did choose to return on the qualifying offer while the team has also reunited with Tim Hill and Jonathan Loáisiga in recent days, but there remains a good deal of work to be done to fill out the big-leaguer bullpen. There also remains the possibility that the Yankees could reintegrate Cruz and Gil on minor-league deals in the coming days.

title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to have become the biggest entertainment launch in history following the blockbuster video game's debut on Thursday , after a 13-year wait.

The highly anticipated open-world action-adventure saw pre-orders and first day sales total more than 24.5 million units, raking in about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics platform Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas .

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both the firms for comment.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history .

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop , which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.

Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind , which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.

Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.

The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.

If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grown through repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.

GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.

The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.

Its launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.

The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
text:
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off deepens.

The fall in tech stocks continued to weigh on markets, with the S&P 500 down more than 2% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average down 0.7% by lunchtime.

Both US indexes touched correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index also fell more than 3.4% by the middle of trading on Friday.

Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping more than 12% to about $85 by lunchtime, close to its initial public offering (IPO) price of $83.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursday was a crucial test for the industry and was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50.

The maker of the Claude chatbot raised a record $81bn in its initial public offering (IPO), but its share price moved significantly in the first day of trading.

The shares peaked at $115 on Thursday, before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.

Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.

Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.

Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.

While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.

"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.

"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."

Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell.

Nvidia and SpaceX were both down more than 6%, while Tesla shares fell more than 3% and Meta was down 3.4%.

Apple, Amazon and Microsoft experienced smaller falls, while Alphabet was up by 1.2%.

Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks - were also trading lower. Germany's Dax index fell 2% and the UK's FTSE 100 was down 0.5%.

Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.

South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.

Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

title: French police officers found guilty of racist assault on black music producer
author: Angelique Chrisafis in Paris
text:
Beating of Michel Zecler in 2020 sparked outrage over police brutality after it was caught on security cameras

Three French police officers who beat a black music producer they said was not wearing a face mask during the Covid pandemic have been found guilty of intentional, racist violence.

The brutal assault on Michel Zecler, now 47, was caught on security cameras in his building in 2020 and triggered outrage in France over police brutality. The trial this month was considered a turning point for the recognition of racist violence.

The officers were sentenced to between one and two years in prison, with additional years suspended. They were banned for life from serving in the police.

The officers had stopped Zecler outside his Paris music studio on 21 November 2020, accusing him of failing to wear a mandatory face mask. They pushed him into the entrance of his office and violently beat him in an assault recorded by his studio’s security cameras .

Zecler sustained about 30 punches and truncheon blows to the face and body over a five-minute period, according to the investigation. He was left with craniofacial trauma, a wound to the lip and scalp, and a complete rupture of his biceps tendon, leaving him unable to work for 45 days.

Zecler told the court the officers used a racist slur against him on several occasions during the beating. He said the attack had “completely devastated him” and had left a lasting physical and psychological impact.

The three officers, Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Pierre Plantier, 37, and Philippe Tondeux, 50, were found guilty of breaking into Zecler’s studio and committing intentional violence in a group. The judges decided racism was an aggravating factor in the attack.

The officers were also found guilty of forgery after they tried to cover up their actions by falsifying an official police report saying Zecler had been violent towards them. The police used that report to accuse Zecler of attacking them and trying to grab one of their weapons, but the video footage did not back up the claims, showing he was not violent.

The state prosecutor said that without the CCTV footage, the false police report on Zecler could have resulted in him being convicted of attacking a police officer in what would have been a serious miscarriage of justice.

The state prosecutor, who asked not to be named in the media, told the court the case had caused “immense harm to Michel Zecler but also to society as a whole”.

She said the officers had “betrayed” their uniform. She told the judges: “I ask you to believe Michel Zecler, to recognise him as a victim of these racist insults.”

The three police officers, who had not realised their attack was being recorded on security cameras, had apologised in court for beating Zecler, but denied racism.

Zecler’s lawyers and supporters said the trial had shone a spotlight on police violence in France , which victims and researchers say is systemic but authorities and law enforcement unions say is limited to isolated cases. Many members of the public who had come to support Zecler and watch the trial said it was an important moment in confronting institutionalised racism.

One of Zecler’s lawyers, Serge Money, said while summing up the case: “A verdict can force a society to really look at an injustice that up until now had been tolerated, minimised, and I dare to use the word: institutionalised.”

He said: “The Zecler trial is the trial of impunity, for all those who before him and after him will experience the same thing.”

Money told the court: “I want you to give voice to all those who didn’t have security cameras, and to all those who were not believed.”

Nine young performers who had been rehearsing in the basement at Zecler’s studio had been violently arrested when they came to assist Zecler.

Their lawyer, Seydi Ba, told the court that France needed to know how “police violence, lies and racism” would be considered by a court.

text:
Google's flagship search experience is evolving into an AI experience with stunning speed. Even time-tested elements of search are getting AI makeovers, and the latest to get this treatment is the search homepage on Google.com. A redesign that's been in testing for the last few weeks is now official, bringing easier access to AI chats and dropping the dedicated search button entirely.

Google search VP Robby Stein confirmed on X that Google is deploying the new desktop search page after a successful test. The page will now have a few more buttons under the search bar, all connected to AI features. There's an image generation button, one for analyzing files, and one for brainstorming with Gemini. The "I'm Feeling Lucky" button remains, but the Google Search button that used to sit next to it is gone.

The search button has obviously been a part of Google's search page forever. However, it wasn't in a very convenient location in the modern interface. When you begin typing a query, the autocomplete suggestions cover that button. You have to click out of the text field to access the button, which is an extra step compared to simply mashing the Enter key to run your search.

title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous penalties’ for US tech firms that build datacenters abroad
author: Ben Doherty
text:
President gives wide-ranging White House press conference and says he has ‘fantastic relationships’ with Putin and Xi

Donald Trump threatened on Friday to impose “tremendous penalties” on American tech companies that build datacenters outside the US, though he gave no details and told reporters he had not yet informed his own officials about the plan.

In a discursive press conference from the White House briefing room, Trump also said he would “look into” the report that Iran had been planning to possibly detonate a “dirty bomb” in Washington DC, and backed JD Vance over comments the vice-president made blaming Republican midterm losses on the Iran war.

Trump also expounded on his friendship with the Russian president Vladimir Putin, whom he met alongside China’s Xi Jinping at the Apec summit on Thursday, adding he had “fantastic relationships” with both autocratic leaders.

At the White House, Trump told reporters he wanted datacenters built by US companies to stay on US soil.

“We’re not allowing datacenters to go into other countries, because China will take all of them, and we’re not allowing that to happen. And we’re going to put tremendous penalties on companies that try to do it,” he said.

He said Americans should welcome datacenters, and urged communities to extract concessions from developers, repeating a point he made before the midterms.

“You ought to take advantage of the datacenters. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but don’t shut them off,” he said.

With many Americans turning against the datacenters being built near their homes, the US tech industry is making a show of conciliation by promising to take fewer government handouts, to be more transparent, and to give more money to towns and cities willing to allow server warehouses to be built.

The Trump administration on Monday issued new rules to restrict remote access to advanced US computing chips and servers, in a move it said was designed to limit China’s ability to use US chips to train its artificial intelligence models – though a House committee said on Wednesday the US had signed off on sales of nearly 900,000 AI chips to China in six months.

China’s ability to obtain advanced AI chips made by the US firm Nvidia, in which Trump is an investor, has been spotlighted in recent weeks after its CEO, Jensen Huang, was fired over his affair with a woman alleged to be spying for China.

In the same press conference, Trump was asked about reports Iran was planning to potentially detonate an explosive laced with nuclear material – a so-called “dirty bomb” – in Washington DC. The president called it a “rumour” and said: “If they do, we’re going to fight.”

He added: “We know a lot about what’s happening in Iran. We know everything they say. We know who they are, where they are. We’ll find out about it.”

Responding to a question about reports of a rift with Vance, Trump said the vice-president’s remark blaming the Republican collapse on the Iran war was “a very accurate statement”.

“I didn’t say I was unhappy with it,” the president said. “I would have added one other thing if it were asked … would you do it again? And absolutely, the answer is yes, because we cannot allow Iran to have a nuclear weapon.”

Trump was asked whether Vladimir Putin could really be considered a friend to America since Russia is a close ally of Iran.

“I can’t speak to America,” he said, adding: “I consider [that] I have fantastic relationships with Putin. That’s a very good thing. I have fantastic relationships with President Xi. That’s a good thing, and our country is safe because of that.”

He praised Putin as he repeated his grievances over the Department of Justice’s investigation into the Russian attempts to influence US voters ahead of the 2016 presidential election.

“I’ve been dealing with Putin … [since] the fake Russia, Russia, Russia hoax,” he said.

Trump also spoke about two prominent Democrats. He said Gina Hinojosa, who won the race for Texas governor over Trump’s Republican ally Greg Abbott, called him. “She was really nice,” Trump said. “It was a very productive call. And she wants to have a strong border, and I think we’ll be able to work something out.”

And he said Hakeem Jeffries – who Trump previously called a “thug” but is now in line to be the next speaker of the House, and the first Black speaker – is “a smart guy. He’s a streetwise guy.”

The company’s 2026 sustainability report claims that “our long-term ambitions haven’t changed, but our operating environment has,” according to an introduction from Rachel Peterson, vice president of data centers at Meta, and Blair Swedeen, global head of net zero and sustainability at Meta. In the November 19, 2026, report, they attributed the changing conditions and the need for a rethink to how “demand for AI infrastructure has grown faster than almost anyone projected.”

“We are re-evaluating our timelines, sequencing, and interim milestones—including the 2030 timeframe for our net zero emissions goal and our near-term intensity targets—so our approach reflects current operating realities while keeping progress transparent year over year,” Peterson and Swedeen wrote in the report.

title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
author: Lauren Almeida and Graeme Wearden
text:
Nasdaq erases 2026 gains and Asian markets record worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI build-out

Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?

Anthropic’s shares fell at the start of its second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.

As they dropped, the wider stock market fell with them, with the Nasdaq Composite erasing all its gains for 2026. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly entered correction territory.

Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by as much as 12% on Friday. They dropped to $85.12, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.

Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.

US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2.9% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1.66% in morning trading in New York.

Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”

Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.

The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.

In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.

European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.

The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .

Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.

“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.

Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.

Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.

“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”

Nvidia shares fell by 7% after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.

Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.

Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.

Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

title: One Editor Thinks 32-Inch Gravel Is the Future. Another Gives It Five Years.
author: Josh Ross
text:
The Velo Podcast wouldn’t happen without subscribers. We’re offering listeners of the show a special 25% discount on an Outside+ membership. Enter the code velopod at checkout to score these savings, and thank you for your support!

This week, the full crew is together to do some arguing. Host Mike Levy, Lisa Charlebois, Logan Jones-Wilkins, and I (Josh Ross, though Blue Hat Guy works too) are debating Zwift versus everyone and whether 32-inch wheels are actually here to stay.

Before we get to the main event, we dive into a pile of listener comments from last week’s indoor riding and Zwift Plus discussion. That includes everything from TrainerRoad or Strava versus Zwift (and why fearing for life on rollers might be the best way) to whether Zwift will eventually fold Rouvy into a single platform. For the record, I’m putting my prediction on the board now: Rouvy ceases to exist as a separate thing in three years. We also tackle a listener theory that virtual cars in Zwift video routes are desensitizing indoor-first riders to real traffic—a take that leaves Mike and me pretty much speechless before Logan steps in with a much more reasonable explanation.

From there, it is time for the topic everyone loves to hate: 32-inch gravel wheels. Logan just wrapped up 500 miles on the MMosaic GT i55 32—a custom titanium bike built around a proper 32-inch carbon fork—and he is a huge fan. He argues it makes gravel riding noticeably more fun, with better rollover, more traction, and geometry that actually makes sense off-road. Mike agrees, arguing that the best thing about 32-inch wheels isn’t even the wheels themselves, but the longer, more stable geometry they force frame builders to adopt.

I am on the other side of the fence. While I don’t doubt the off-road performance gains exist, my argument is a business one: consumers have wheel-size fatigue, brands don’t want to manage multiple standards, and 32-inch gravel bikes are headed for the same fate as 650b within five years. That leads to a back-and-forth over whether brands can actually pull off two wheel sizes across a single frame run (when they still struggle to spec the right handlebar widths), whether 700c gravel bikes are just turning into “all-road” bikes, and what all of this means for shorter riders who don’t want to feel like they’re riding a monster truck.

Lisa: “This is gonna sound so dumb. I’m sorry, everybody. But it looks like you’re on a Big Wheel… It just looks so weird. The scale is so wrong.” Mike: “We all look so weird. We’re wearing spandex riding bicycles around, talking about watts and carbs. We look stupid and I love it.” Logan: “You know how many people noticed I was riding 32 at Big Sugar? Zero people. Nobody noticed.” Lisa: “Yeah, but you’re tall, dude. You look in proportion.”

As always, let us know where you land in the comments—are you with Logan on the 32-inch future, or are you siding with Blue Hat Guy? And make sure to vote in this week’s poll below to tell us whether you’re actually planning to buy a 32-inch gravel bike when they hit the market in force.

title: Researcher plants 2m canaries into the AI supply chain. A privacy disaster surfaced.
author: Dan Goodin
text:
Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.

The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.

Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations

To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
text:
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.

"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.

"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.

"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."

But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.

"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.

Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.

It also follows an announcement earlier this week that would restrict the export of advanced computer chips and who can access the computing power provided by them.

Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.

The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.

Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back

Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.

As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.

Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.

"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.

"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."

Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.

Meta has already broken ground on a data centre , external in the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.

The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.

In September Google announced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investment in AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.

Last month, building work for two of those centres was halted due to concerns over the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.

Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".

title: YouTube is reportedly preparing to settle social media addiction claims for $3 billion
author: Emma Roth
text:
The potential settlement would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, Bloomberg reports.

The potential settlement would also require YouTube to introduce new safeguards for teens, Bloomberg reports.

YouTube is preparing to pay $3 billion to thousands of school districts to settle claims that its “addictive design” harmed kids, according to Bloomberg . Sources tell the publication that YouTube reached the agreement “in principle,” and that the deal would also include new safeguards for teens.

The settlement would allow Google to avoid a wave of lawsuits filed by US school districts that accuse YouTube, Meta, Snap, and TikTok of negatively impacting the mental health of teen users. The first “bellwether” trial of these federal multidistrict litigation (MDL) cases was supposed to start in Kentucky in June, but all four companies settled for a total of $27 million before it went to court . The next trial is set for February 2027 before an Oakland, California, judge, with Meta, Snap, and TikTok as defendants.

Google didn’t immediately respond to The Verge ’s request for comment.

In August, Meta agreed to pay $17.1 billion over 10 years to settle lawsuits filed by a group of 47 states, along with several districts and territories. It also agreed to implement stricter safeguards for teens, but is pushing TikTok and YouTube to do the same. As part of the agreement, Meta will only shell out the remaining $5.3 billion of its $17.1 billion settlement if YouTube and TikTok roll out similar changes and pay matching amounts. In March, both YouTube and Meta were found negligent in a separate legal battle over social media addiction .

title: Watching as a giant star swallowed its neighbor and exploded
author: Jacek Krywko
text:
In the Andromeda Galaxy, a giant star about seven times as massive as the Sun spent nearly a decade slowly swallowing its much smaller companion. The process, known as common envelope evolution, was proposed in the 1970s to explain how some of the tightest pairs of stars in the Universe form, but no one had ever caught it in the act.

In a new Nature study, astronomers led by Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, finally witnessed the entire spectacle from the decades before it began to the eruption that ended it in late 2025. “It lasts for a few years, maybe a few decades,” Karambelkar said. “Stars evolve on time scales of millions of years. So, it's really like a blip on the entire cosmic time scale.”

Some pairs of stars orbit so close to each other that they could not have formed at that distance, so their orbits must have shrunk. Common envelope evolution is the leading explanation for that shrinkage. When one star in a binary grows old, it expands into a giant, and its outer layers can engulf its companion. The two then share a single, loosely bound envelope of gas. As the engulfed star drags through it, it loses orbital energy to friction and spirals inward. Depending on how much of the envelope gets lost, the pair either ends up in a much tighter orbit or merges.

title: NASA’s new Moon plan is taking shape, but some big questions remain
author: Stephen Clark
text:
SpaceX's successful recovery of its Starship rocket last weekend cleared a major hurdle on NASA's path to the Moon, opening up possibilities for higher launch rates and an all-important, long-delayed orbital refueling demo next year.

For SpaceX's purposes, Saturday's mid-air rocket catch will help engineers learn how to rapidly reuse Starships. That should expedite SpaceX's deployment of its newest generation of Starlink Internet satellites. NASA, meanwhile, believes a higher launch cadence will lead to faster learning as SpaceX develops a deep space version of Starship to ferry astronaut crews to the surface of the Moon.

Early next year, SpaceX plans to bring online a second Starship launch site at Kennedy Space Center, Florida. A second Starship factory is also under construction at Kennedy, joining SpaceX's existing SpaceX production line at Starbase, Texas. With two launch sites, SpaceX will have the pieces in place to take the next leap with Starship.

title: F1's new V8 engine agreed - five things you need to know
author: Scott Mitchell-Malm
text:
Formula 1 will adopt V8 engines in 2030 now key stakeholders have unanimously agreed on the key details that will underpin the new regulations.

A framework has been unanimously agreed by the FIA, Formula 1, the teams and the engine manufacturers to bring in a 2.1-litre, turbocharged V8 with a reduced electric element.

This switch will be made one year earlier than planned, bringing an early end to the V6 turbo-hybrid rules that only started a controversial new era this season with a switch to a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electric power.

The FIA World Motor Sport Council will rubber-stamp the plan at a Shanghai meeting next month.

How key final progress was reached

A meeting of the F1 Commission on Monday, November 16 led to agreement in principle over the framework.

But it required some final progress to be made for the engine manufacturers themselves to accept ending the current rules cycle in 2029 and be satisfied with the switch.

The manufacturers are Mercedes, Ferrari, Red Bull/Ford, Audi Honda and future engine supplier General Motors - which was aiming to belatedly join the current rules cycle before the end of the decade (more on that shortly).

After the Commission, a meeting with the manufacturers – which are represented in the Commission but have their own key discussion group with the other stakeholders – went through key feedback to resolve what was necessary to push the proposal to the next stage.

This is what facilitated Friday's announcement of unanimous agreement of the technical framework.

GM will delay engine to fit

A key consequence of the change of timeline is what it means for GM’s plans.

Its Cadillac team, which GM is a minority owner of alongside TWG Motorsports, joined the grid this year as a Ferrari customer on the condition it becomes a full works entry.

GM had been planning to debut that engine built to the current rules in 2029, which it was willing to accept even though it would be only two seasons before all-new rules came in as originally planned.

To accommodate the next rules era starting earlier, though, GM will delay its manufacturer debut so it does not have to design and build a V6 for one season only.

It is expected to remain a Ferrari customer for an extra year and the rules being agreed is well timed as the purpose-built GM engine facility opens in mid-December this year, which means the full might of its development push can be devoted to the new 2030 rules instead of a split project.

"For a period of time, we were working on both,” TWG boss Dan Towriss said in Las Vegas. “So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8. There are a number of designs that are in motion now.”

Officially, the proposed 2030 engine will be a 2.1-litre turbo V8 that carries over “some geometrical specifics”, will feature limited hybridisation” as well as sustainable fuels, and be married to a lighter chassis.

This is all part of the plan to make the engines simpler, cheaper and louder – although the extent of that last point is still unclear given it will not be a normally aspirated engine.

“I look at the old videos of the old engines, they give me goosebumps – it's just that high-pitch squeal that I'm missing from this era,” said Mercedes driver George Russell.

McLaren’s Oscar Piastri cautioned “I don't know if they'll be exactly like the V8 engines that I grew up watching, necessarily”, but added “I think it's firstly great that we've been listened to”.

The turbocharger stays partly to satisfy manufacturer demand but also to assist with fuel efficiency, avoid larger tanks and more fuel usage at the start of races.

This also helps with the stated aim of making the car and engine around 80kg lighter with almost half of that coming on the engine side.

More details of this will surely come from the “detailed regulatory framework” that will go to the WMSC in Shanghai next month.

However, it does appear to represent a satisfactory compromise between what some manufacturers want in terms of hybridisation and FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem’s initial desire for an even bigger, loud engine without a turbo.

“The return of V8 engines represents an opportunity to reconnect with the DNA of this championship, bringing back the sound, emotion and pure racing that is loved worldwide,” said Ben Sulayem.

“Our vision is clear, lighter, simpler and more affordable cars that put driver skill at the heart of the competition.”

What’s still to be confirmed

The FIA did not specify the hybrid element, which has been known for some time to be heading towards a 100kW base electric power contribution with an extra 100kW available as effectively a push-to-pass overtaking aid.

It will give the engine more than 1,000bhp at full power but crucially, compared to the current engines, not be dependent on the electric element and therefore not at the mercy of the energy limitations that have dogged the 2026 rules since their debut.

Why the hybrid element has not been exactly specified is unclear – “maybe it have some KERS or stuff like that”, as Alpine boss Flavio Briatore put it – but it stands to reason that this is being delayed until more detail can be shared about how it will work.

With the 2026 rules, the engine regulations were designed first, then the chassis and sporting regulations were contorted around them - leading to a fundamentally compromised product, all because the engine rules had to be set early to get all the targeted manufacturers committed.

This time the core V8 engine plan should be much simpler to align with the car design and operation, but there are still elements to decide - like exactly how a push-to-pass system should be managed and whether the active aero with movable front and rear wings is worth retaining when that was primarily adopted to assist with making the current cars more efficient on the straights.

Drivers are excited - with minor caveats

Every single driver on the F1 grid has, publicly or privately, expressed their displeasure with the 2026 engines and their consequences.

So, unsurprisingly, all who have been asked about the return of V8s have welcomed the plan - from the general concept to the fact that there was a good degree of consultation with the drivers themselves.

Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar said he was very excited for a “full attack racing car” and went as far as adding “I don't see why that would not be the most fun cars of all time in 2030”.

His team-mate, four-time world champion and vocal 2026 rules critic Max Verstappen, indicated he would have liked it to go further though.

"If it's fully up to me, of course you go back to like a V10 or whatever,” he said. “That sounds even better, but I know that that's not something realistic.

“So this is good, this is for sure in the right direction."

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton’s own caveat related to the detail of the as-yet undefined regulations that will define how the engines actually work – although what he hopes for most should naturally be achieved simply by stripping back the electric side so much.

“It's all good and well going to V8, it depends on how they design it, regulation wise,” he said.

“And going back to the good sound because that's I think been lacking since we've been in the V6 era. Bring back the smaller exhaust and get that sound back.

“And as long as we don't have the engine dying halfway down the straight, then I think that will be better.”

title: Prisons get OK to jam contraband phones. CTIA says nearby phones will be jammed too.
author: Jon Brodkin
text:
The Federal Communications Commission yesterday voted to let state and local prisons use jamming technology to block contraband cellphones, despite warnings that jammers will also block lawful phone calls outside the prisons.

Wireless industry lobby group CTIA said a recent test it conducted with the Virginia Tech Applied Research Corporation and South Carolina Department of Corrections confirmed concerns that the jammers would block legitimate communications, including 911 calls. CTIA told the FCC in an October 1 filing :

The pilot test was limited in the number of micro-jammers deployed, the spectrum bands they were authorized to jam, and the power levels at which they were permitted to operate. Even with these constraints, the micro-jamming system blocked 911 calls, interfered with public safety and other communications, and caused interference that impacted wireless network infrastructure up to two and a half miles away. At the same time, the pilot results show substantial gaps in jamming the targeted “contraband” devices, with testing scenarios in outdoor inmate recreation areas showing failure rates—meaning “contraband” device call completion—in one-half to two-thirds of call attempts.

CTIA said the pilot test shows "that current jamming technology seems to be both over and underinclusive at once—it risks blocking lawful communications even as it fails to block a significant portion of the targeted contraband device communications."

title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
author: Alex Daniel
text:
Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6%

Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair.

Speaking at an event in London on Thursday, Dimon said he would seek to claw back the increase and was “setting an example so that [governments] understand the trade-offs of these unfair penalties”.

The bank surcharge is to rise from 3% to 6% in January as a temporary 15-month measure. It was unclear how JP Morgan , which employs 23,000 people in the UK, would make up for the extra cost.

In comments first reported by the Financial Times, citing people who attended the event, Dimon said he would set an example in making up for the added costs, and that the decision was “more in sorrow” than in anger.

Dimon has repeatedly lobbied Labour against raising taxes on banks, and suggested in May that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn tower in the Canary Wharf district of London that is expected to serve as JP Morgan’s UK headquarters.

Shortly after the chancellor, John Healey, announced the policy during his inaugural budget in October, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian that plans for the 279,000 sq metre (3m sq ft) building were still going ahead. But the bank also said at the time that the policy “lacks principle” for singling the sector out, adding that it operated in a “highly competitive global marketplace”.

JP Morgan also has a sprawling campus in Bournemouth, where it employs more than 5,300 staff who process more than $1tn (£750bn) worth of global transactions each day. Earlier this month, the Guardian reported fears that the advance of artificial intelligence could put their jobs at risk.

Lenders in the UK pay a 28% corporation tax rate, higher than the standard 25%, and the separate surcharge on their UK balance sheets, which is set for the temporary rise. JP Morgan, the biggest bank in the US, expected to pay £120m more in taxes because of the increase, the FT reported.

Bank share prices rallied after Healey’s October announcement because the increase was less than many people in the industry had expected. The chancellor said at the time that he was “looking to our banks to help fund breathing space for British families”.

title: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79 billion in its first day

GTA VI earned $3.79 billion in its first day of sales, which set “a new record for entertainment across any medium,” according to an announcement from Rockstar Games . The game also sold 32.5 million preorder copies.

The news follows leaks, delays, and a huge amount of interest ahead of GTA VI ’s launch. (Many other games steered clear of GTA VI to get their time in the sun.) But even with the weight of anticipation placed upon GTA VI , it actually lived up to the hype, my colleague Andrew Webster said in his review .

title: Yankees Mailbag: The DH question
author: Madison Pavich
text:
People have been asking it, so it’s time we talked about it: should Aaron Judge get shifted over to DH?

Good afternoon everyone, it’s time to dive back into the mailbag and answer some of your questions. Remember to send in your questions for our bi-weekly call by e-mail to pinstripealleyblog [at] gmail [dot] com .

jmack175 asks: With Judge getting older and needing to stay healthy, do you see a scenario where he gets more at bats at DH this season, and at some point when Stanton has his annual muscle strain from an intentional walk, Judge is fully transitioned to DH and Stanton is released? If that doesn’t play out, how many more seasons do you see Judge playing RF?

Not right away, at least not with how the roster as constructed stands. The Yankees have their designated hitter spot locked up between Stanton, Ben Rice, and Luis García Jr. at the moment, though the team’s future with Stanton is currently cloudy at best. For now, the team is going through with bringing Stanton to spring training and seeing what he’s got left in the tank, but even removing him from the equation still leaves the position filled up with a hitter that the team wants in the lineup more often than not. There’s also been some speculation that the Yankees could turn around and flip García after acquiring him at the deadline as part of their effort to find a quality third baseman to complete the infield, shifting Rice back to first base. Rice admittedly wasn’t that good of a defender despite working with Paul Goldschmidt though, and the team certainly won’t risk moving him back behind the plate at this point with how valuable he is to the team’s offense.

Personally, I don’t think it’s worthwhile to lose García’s bat unless there’s no other avenue to upgrade third, and with the team’s incredible starting pitcher depth as well as the prospects they could part with I think there are plenty of other routes they can consider. As for Judge, while it is concerning that the last two major injuries he’s sustained have been on maximum-effort plays in the outfield (I’m still willing to consider the Dodger Stadium wall collision as more of a freak accident, but c’est la vie) he’s still a tremendous outfielder when healthy and the team would do well to maximize the value he can bring by playing him out there as long as they can. Cody Bellinger provides excellent defense in left field, but we saw how much of a struggle the other two positions were for the team on a regular basis last year, and they may not be able to find a true center fielder this offseason to improve the defense with most options for the outfield being bat-first players. I don’t know if Judge can still be Judge out there if he’s giving 80-90 percent effort out there, but his cannon arm shouldn’t be too affected by telling him to avoid a full-out dive for the ball and that change alone could be enough.

jws85 asks: Forget rumors of Seager, Bohm, Skubal, Jeffers, etc. Boone has one year left and to spend money on long term contracts to get the same old results — start the year on fire, sleep through the summer, make the playoffs, and get bounced early — makes no sense. Why hamstring a new manager with contracts that jam the roster, let the current roster with the addition of kids or one year cheap players get through 2027, and then go crazy for 2028.

We’re making a lot of assumptions here, so let’s break this down. Aaron Boone is on a lame-duck contract, yes, but there’s no guarantee that means they’ll move on from him at the end of next year — or replace him with someone fundamentally different. If the team can’t accomplish more than another ALDS flameout three years in a row, I do think it’s unlikely that Boone gets handed another contract, but why set yourself up for failure just to move on from Boone when he’s at worst a minor part of the problem? The organization should be in win-now mode with their superstars getting up in age, and while they shouldn’t take on a bloated contract for a player that’ll only have one or two more positive years at best they should certainly be aiming to put together a World Series-caliber team instead of trusting that the kids can fill the gaps. They developed Rice and Cam Schlittler from unheralded prospect status into stardom, sure, but they made it to the majors by making the team unable to ignore them much like George Lombard Jr did this season.

Dax Kilby is a rising star in the organization but he’s still years away from the majors, and after him the rest of their top 10 prospects are all pitchers. The best-case usage of the kids in this scenario is finding smart trades to fill out the lineup, as they simply can’t all play. The only argument I’ll make in favor of not adding too much to the payroll for 2027 is that the team likely won’t be in the Tarik Skubal sweepstakes anyway and the other big ticket names don’t impress me as much, but if they were I wouldn’t hate it. Hand him a bag and the Yankees would instantly have the best rotation in baseball bar none, and still have depth to trade away to improve around the margins.
