title: Martin admits 2021 crash memories still slow him at Portimao
author: Eden Hannigan
text:
Jorge Martin has admitted that he is still losing lap time at Portimao’s Turn 7, the site of his life-threatening MotoGP crash in 2021.

This weekend is Martin’s first Portuguese Grand Prix since his 2024 victory, after missing last year’s edition due to injury.

In his rookie campaign in 2021, Martin crashed heavily at Turn 7 in a free practice session, which had left him uncertain whether he would be able to return to racing.

The then-Pramac rider was hospitalised with multiple fractures from the incident, but eventually returned to racing later that same season.

Since the incident, Martin has raced at Portimao three times with mixed success: recording two further DNFs before his 2024 victory.

However, the now-Aprilia rider has conceded that he still struggles at the corner and is still yet to regain full confidence while riding.

“For sure this track is not easy for me because I crashed quite hard in the past,” Martin admitted after ending Friday practice in 10th. “Even if I won last time, I'm not feeling super confident. I see the risk everywhere but I'm trying to get that confidence.

“It's just every corner, every lap I go on that corner I feel it and I know. So I am a bit more careful than the rest but I'm just losing maybe half a tenth there.”

Martin was reluctant to say that the time lost from the corner was what could have cost him an automatic Q2 spot in practice - where he finished 10th - suggesting the loss of time was “more on the last sector.”

The Aprilia rider did concede though that he is more vulnerable in that specific part of the track compared to his rivals.

“When you have a crash like this, like I don't know, [Turn] 12 from Qatar, [Turn] 7 here. I always, every time I go through that corner I remember.

“So this is part of my life. For sure it's nice that I can, you know, I'm safe now and I can do that corner fast, but for sure I am not the strongest in that section.”

When asked what it would take to overcome his fear of the corner, Martin revealed it was mostly down to “accepting that you can crash again.”

“At least I try to be ready a bit more,” he explained. “Trying to get more strong in the bike at that point in case I lose the front or whatever, I can recover that crash.

“But for sure it's not easy to go to that corner and think again about everything. It's not easy. Everything is so fast. For sure it's just maybe one or two seconds. But for sure till I go through that place, it's not easy."

title: Army delays detonating "catastrophically hazardous" lead azide amid fear, anger
author: Beth Mole
text:
In a swirl of questions, fears, and outrage, the US Army announced Thursday that it would delay a plan to blow up 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide, which would launch toxic gas and lead into the air. A federal appeals court further halted plans later on Thursday with an emergency order. The plume, containing neurotoxic lead, could potentially drift 100 miles north of the Army installation housing it in Middletown, Iowa, according to modeling released by the Army earlier this week.

The Army had planned to carry out two controlled detonations, set off simultaneously around noon Friday, to destroy the barrels where they lie, which is in earth-covered concrete containment structures (called earth-covered magazines or ECMs). Prior to the court stay, the Army rescheduled the blast until November 23 to provide more time to communicate about the situation with Iowans, who have reported being unaware of the detonations until earlier this week.

"Public communication is essential to public trust," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a post on social media at 7:31 pm ET Thursday . "Therefore, the Army will continue to actively engage with state and local officials throughout the region to distribute accurate, up-to-date information."

title: F1 bosses agree V8 engines deal from 2030
text:
Formula 1 bosses are close to a deal that will see V8 turbo hybrid engines replace the current controversial engines in 2030.

McLaren chief executive officer Zak Brown said an "agreement in principle" had been reached by engine manufacturers and F1 bosses on the new rules.

These will be for a 2.1-litre V8 turbo engine with a smaller electrical element than this year, as first revealed by BBC Sport last month.

Some details remain to be resolved but the main core of the rules has been agreed.

The electrical element will be for a maximum power output of 200kW - compared with 350kW this year.

But only half of that will be available at all times, with the remaining half used only for an overtake mode.

A key element of the rules will be to remove the issue of energy starvation that has been criticised by the drivers this year for taking away "pure" racing.

But the overall power output of the engines will be similar to now.

The combustion engine will have about 780bhp, while 200kW is 270bhp.

That means a total power output of 1,050bhp in overtake mode or just over 900bhp in standard running.

Brown said: "Everyone is very, very excited. Now it's about kind of dotting the i's and crossing the t's.

"I'm excited for the new engines, I think everyone will be, the power units. But there's a lot more also going on to continue to evolve the sport. So, between the FIA and Formula 1, they're doing a great job."

Russell fastest in Las Vegas practice after rain

How to follow Las Vegas Grand Prix on the BBC

Alpine executive director Flavio Briatore said: "We have the agreement, basically. It's not signed, but it looks like everybody's agreed to 2030 V8s, and I'm very happy.

"It's the right way to go. We need an engine with a lot of noise, and a simple engine, and we need to be racing with that."

The ruleset amounts to a compromise reached by manufacturers after FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for a naturally aspirated engine without turbo or electrical components.

But these were required to reduce overall fuel consumption, and therefore weight at the start of races.

That means Ben Sulayem's desire for a return to the loud volumes of the previous V8 era from 2006 to 2013 will not be achieved. The engines are expected to sound similar to now.

This was important because a significant increase in engine noise would have put at threat some races in city centres that are commercially important to F1, such as Miami and Las Vegas.

The 2.1-litre capacity has been arrived at because it amounts to adding to two cylinders to the current 1.6-litre V6 blocks, with the aim of reducing development costs.

Cars are expected to start races with about 110-120kg of fuel, up from about 100kg now. A total weight limit of 150kg for the power-units will be imposed, down by about 30kg from the current engines.

There will be a fuel energy flow limit to keep the power of the combustion engine under control, and a budget cap figure for engines set at $190m (£145m) per year.

As part of negotiations, General Motors, backers of the Cadillac team, will delay the production of its new engine until 2030. It had been scheduled for 2029.

In return, GM will lose its voting rights on current engine rules and be classified as a new manufacturer from 2030.

The team will continue to use Ferrari customer engines through 2029.

Cadillac F1 chief executive officer Dan Towriss said: "For a period of time, we were working on both. So, they've already got a V6 base to build off of, and working towards the V8.

"There are a number of designs that are in motion now, and so there's a lot of good foundation for what we're trying to build and the direction we're headed in."

Hosting Thanksgiving can be fun, but cleaning up afterwards? Not so much. The Verge’s smart home reviewer Jennifer Pattison Tuohy named the Eufy Omni C28 one of her top picks after testing 16 robot vacuum mops . She thinks it’s a particularly great fit for apartments and smaller homes. title: F1 set for V8 return from 2030
Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
author: David Hytner
text:
Argentinian has excelled in man-management – but will need his powers to energise new squad and impress owners

M auricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does . Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all.

For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll.

Pochettino’s PSG players were at the party. There was no need for anything from them. But there were loads from those he had coached at his previous clubs: Espanyol, Southampton and Tottenham. One by one, the faces flashed up; too many to mention. And, of course, there were the jokes about how old he was getting. But the tone was of pure affection; appreciation, too. Some of the players laid it on thick. They could not help it. They know what Pochettino has done for them.

This is what total buy-in looks like and this is how Pochettino gets you when he finds out which buttons to press. It might be a third-choice goalkeeper. Or a global superstar – for example, Kylian Mbappé, who Pochettino had at PSG. There is a story from those days that is worth sharing. Pochettino was due to give an interview and told the TV crew he would get Mbappé along to speak to them as well.

Everybody knows this is not how it works, that it would not be possible because Mbappé, well … he has his time and commitments tightly managed. They appreciated the sentiment from Pochettino, though. When the hour came, Pochettino took out his phone and messaged Mbappé. “Come to the media centre.” Five minutes later, there he was. A line from one of the production staff was gold. “Err, we’ve got Kylian Mbappé outside.”

This kind of thing is not confined to the dim and distant past. Remember when Pochettino left Chelsea in 2024 and the tributes some of the players paid to him on social media? One stood out because it came from Nicolas Jackson, who Pochettino had punished for getting too many silly yellow cards by ordering him to sprint around the training ground, reducing him to a face-in-the-ground mess when it was over. “Love you coach,” Jackson wrote. “Thanks for the advice and support. You’re a true lion and a fighter.”

It is easy to feel Pochettino has signed up for his biggest fight because it is not only that United have one Premier League win, a place in the relegation zone, no confidence, questionable fitness levels and a trip to Liverpool on Sunday which has the makings of root canal surgery without the anaesthetic.

Hanging heavy over everything is the fan fury towards the Glazer family, who have owned the club since 2005. It is obviously not a new thing. The diehards were passionately against them even before the takeover. But we are going through another period where the frustration has spiked and the malevolence can be heard in the chants. It is the insoluble problem, with the efforts of the minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe and the director of football, Jason Wilcox, making it worse. They have also been targeted by the Stretford End.

Pochettino knows managers do not tend to enter clubs when everything is rosy. There are reasons why the vacancies arise and they are almost always bad. He has told himself this. What he intends to do is what he has always done: create connections, starting with the players; inject his trademark positivity into every pore; build belief.

The Argentinian is obsessed with what he calls energia universal . It is a guiding life force that influences everything, which touches on concepts such as karma and what these days would probably be called manifestation. He once said it helped to explain, for example, why the London-born Harry Kane usually scored for Spurs in London derbies.

Pochettino wants to release the pressure from United’s beleaguered squad and his early messaging has come from his tried and trusted playbook . He will treat each player as a human being, first and foremost, with individual needs. And, if necessary, individually tailored programmes. At Southampton, he put one together for Luke Shaw, then an emerging player. He has been reunited with the left-back at Old Trafford.

Pochettino talked at his media conference on Friday of having had three hours of one-on-one meetings with the players on Thursday; trying to understand what was happening with them on and off the field. Previously, in his opening address to the United fanbase via the club’s in-house channels, he stressed the importance of everybody “connecting together”.

“The responsibility I feel is energy, it’s excitement,” he said. “To connect with the game we need to feel free. The players need to express their talent and we need to create the environment for them to perform. That is the priority.”

Pochettino has been close to the United job before – most notably in the summer of 2022 when he left PSG. It was either him or Erik ten Hag to take over from the interim Ralf Rangnick, who had declared that United needed “open-heart surgery”. What do they need now?! The club went for Ten Hag.

Pochettino was in United’s thoughts when they looked for a successor to Louis van Gaal in May 2016; he had lunch with Sir Alex Ferguson at Scott’s in London that month. It was believed Ferguson was pushing him as a candidate. United appointed José Mourinho. There was also the period after Mourinho’s dismissal in December 2018 and the interim hire of Ole Gunnar Solskjær when Pochettino was tipped to go to Old Trafford. In the end, Solskjær earned the role on a permanent basis.…

title: Police arrest teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction
author: Caroline Davies
text:
Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s

Police are searching for a missing chemistry teacher convicted of sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s after she did not turn up to her sentencing hearing.

Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, was not found at her Hemel Hempstead home by Metropolitan police officers after her failure to attend Harrow crown court in north London on Friday, where a warrant was issued for her arrest.

Bowen’s barrister, Mark Kimsey, told the court she was in contact with solicitors on Thursday and had engaged with a pre-sentence report, adding there had been “concerns as to her welfare due to the content of the messages” from her.

The former teacher, who was in her 20s when she had sex with one pupil up to 30 times and kissed a second boy when they were aged about 14 to 15, was convicted in August of seven counts of indecent assault and granted bail before her sentencing.

Judge Karim Ezzat issued a warrant for her arrest, which he said was “not backed by bail”.

Neelam Gomersall, prosecuting, said Bowen’s partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, was at the home address when officers arrived, but Bowen was not.

Gomersall earlier told the court there was “no evidence” that Bowen could not attend the sentencing, and that information from her partner was “suggestive of refusal rather than inability” to attend.

The Met said: “On Friday 20 November, officers were made aware that a 65-year-old woman had failed to appear at Harrow crown court for sentencing. A warrant has been issued for her arrest, and inquiries to locate her are ongoing.”

The trial heard that Bowen was in her mid-20s when she taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London.

Jurors heard she had worn short, tight skirts and flirted in class, with one former pupil comparing her behaviour to “a Sabrina Carpenter video”.

One victim told jurors he had had sex with her “about 20 or 30 times” over several months, considered her his girlfriend and kept it secret. He said it had led to “the destruction of my education”.

The second victim described spending lunchtimes with Bowen in a cafe, where he was “goaded” into kissing her by other boys and recalled touching her breasts.

Bowen denied the allegations as “total fabrication” and claimed a medical condition made sex difficult and painful. She denied flirting, saying: “I didn’t flirt with students, I was just friendly.” Defending her clothes, she said she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher”.

title: Trump threatens ‘tremendous tax’ for moving AI data centers outside the US
author: Lauren Feiner
text:
While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿

While policymakers across the country are putting new restrictions on the data center buildout, Trump is making threats.﻿

President Donald Trump promised to put a “tremendous tax” on companies that build data centers outside of the US, even as states and cities around the country are placing restrictions on new applications to build them.

“We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country,” Trump said at a press conference Friday following his summit with China President Xi Jinping and Russia President Vladimir Putin. “They allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.” Should the US allow data centers to be built outside of the country, Trump warned, “China will take them all.”

Trump didn’t share many details behind the plan, and apparently was floating the proposal publicly for the first time. “I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people,” Trump said, flanked by Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. “But I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here.”

Trump’s promise could be difficult to fulfill with a new Democratic majority Congress being sworn in within a couple of months. Even members of his own party recognize that the data center buildout has become an unpopular issue across the board. With states installing moratoriums and new restrictions on data center proposals, companies may be forced to look outside of the country, but Trump’s threat is an attempt to make that a less attractive alternative.

Here’s a transcript of the key part of Trump’s remarks:

Whoever wins SI wins. And you ought to take advantage of the data centers. Make them pay you. Make them pay your community. But take advantage. Don’t shut them off. And there’s always somebody else in this country. But if it’s not this country, there’s somebody else outside.

We’re not going to allow our companies to build data centers outside of our country. We’re not going to allow that to happen. You know, they allowed that to happen with chips and everything else, and it was very destructive to our country. It’s where we started going behind.

So I just, I don’t know if that’s a breaking story. But I haven’t even said that to my people, but I’m telling them now. They’re here. Many of them are here. And we’re not going to allow companies to build data centers in other countries. If they do that, they can, but we’re going to put a tremendous tax on them.

title: Stinner Frameworks Launches Stoic Components With Three New Wheelsets
author: Logan Jones-Wilkins
text:
If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside. Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Stinner Frameworks has a lot more wheels to build with. The metal frame builder based in Santa Barbara has launched Stoic Components, a sub-brand within the company, to manufacture carbon wheels built to match the bikes in Stinner’s catalog.

The component brand is a long time in the making for Stinner. In the press release, Stinner said the brand has been in the making for a decade, stemming from a collaboration with Jones Wheel’s late founder John Jones.

“John and I planned to start a component brand together,” Aaron Stinner, the founder of Stinner Frameworks, said. We lost him to cancer in 2021, before we got the chance. Stoic Components is that brand. We’re starting where he would have: carbon wheels, each matched to a Stinner frame and laced to Stoic hubs.”

Each wheelset will start at $1,499 and use the same basic ingredients: Pillar PSR Triple Butted J-bend spokes, Toray T700/T800 carbon, and in-house hubs. The wheels also have a 265-pound rider weight limit, sealed cartridge bearings, and specific asymmetric rim profiles.

Beyond the new wheels, Stinner has also unveiled a collection of other updates. The Stinner Select range of bikes now uses higher-quality Columbus Life tubing and improved specs. Stinner Select 2.0 framesets will now cost $2,599, while complete builds start at $5,499.

Additionally, if you have wondered how I capture my bike imagery, I have been a long-time user of Stinner’s Photo Stick. The small titanium tool is built to easily prop a bike up for photos while packing down small enough to fit in a carry-on bag or a rear pocket. It uses a three-point construction to provide a strong lean point to prop the bike up wherever seems fit.

Stinner has released a new Photo Stick 2.0, also called the Photostique, which is available now for $109.99 MSRP.

To learn more about the Stoic Component wheels or the brand’s other upgrades, check out Stinner’s website .

title: Florida mechanic found guilty of murdering British woman who attorney says came to US to die
author: Edward Helmore
text:
Dwain Hall was convicted of stabbing Sonia Exelby, a music teacher who prosecutors say suffered from mental illness

A Florida mechanic has been found guilty of stabbing to death a British music teacher, whom he convinced to travel to the United States.

Dwain Hall, an auto repair and tow truck driver, groomed 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Portsmouth, England, on a fetish website before luring her to the US.

Hall had pleaded not guilty to the charges of kidnap and first-degree murder.

At trial, jurors heard from several witnesses, most of them law enforcement officials, who detailed Hall’s email, phone records, social media accounts and other records to trace his movements after Exelby travelled from the UK to meet him.

Exelby’s disappearance from her home sparked an international investigation. Prosecutors this week described how she suffered from mental illness. Investigators said that Exelby had traveled to Florida after posting online about wanting someone to end her life.

Hall’s arrest affidavit said that Exelby had previously expressed suicidal thoughts and investigators alleged that Hall knew about her struggles and used that vulnerability to bring her to Florida, the Ocala Starbanner reported .

The authorities said Exelby boarded a flight to the US seemingly with an intention “to be possibly sexually abused, tortured and murdered by unknown individuals living in the United States”.

After Exelby traveled to the US in October 2025, authorities say Hall picked her up from the Gainesville airport in central Florida .

He drove her to an Airbnb rental, where investigators later found evidence they say connected him to her disappearance and death, including transactions on her bank cards and a video of Exelby on Hall’s cellphone.

According to the Times , Junior Barrett, Hall’s attorney, argued that Exelby took her own life. “She came here with the intention of dying, she thought she was worthless, useless, a burden on other people,” he said in his closing statement.

“This isn’t a question about what porn he likes. You can disagree with him about what he likes, but the case can’t be decided on you not liking his lifestyle. The fact he did not stop her from killing herself does not make it murder.”

Prosecutor Amy Beth Berndt said jurors should use their “common sense”. She added that Hall targeted Exelby for her mental illness and killed her for his sadistic pleasure.

Berndt said Exelby “was beautiful. She was kind and she was deeply loved by everyone who knew her. And she also suffered from mental illness for most of her life. She should be alive today.”

She added: “No one could save her from the defendant, the ‘Alpha Sadist’. He took advantage of a severely depressed, mentally ill woman who was incapable of making any rational decisions.”

After the verdict was read, Exelby’s brother Barry Wilton said: “This last year has been one of the hardest of our lives. Losing our dear sister Sonia has had a profound impact on me and my entire family. I’m not sure we will ever be the same again.”

Wilton then addressed Hall directly, adding: “You pretended to care for Sonia. You didn’t at all. You used her to fulfil your sick fantasies. You had her life in your hands. You had the opportunity to save her, but instead you preyed on her vulnerabilities and you took her from us.”

title: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
author: Timothy Pratt
text:
Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request

In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities.

Chambers’s case is the first known instance of the US seeking to extradite a citizen over alleged support for Hamas, an accusation apparently tied to an international money-laundering charge in the criminal complaint underpinning the extradition request and donations to organizations helping Palestinians in Gaza.

Speaking outside Madrid’s Aranjuez prison upon his release on Friday, Chambers called the charges against him “baseless”, adding that his release was “hopefully the first step in recognizing that internationally”.

Chambers also said: “Spain is a country that has stood on the right side of this most important issue of our time, that has stood on the right side of the genocide, and where this is some reason and some justice.”

An appeals court ordered the conditional release on Friday due to issues surrounding the legally required US translation of the extradition request’s core documents into Spanish, first reported on by the Guardian. He had been detained since 10 July, when Spanish authorities arrested him in Ibiza.

The order asserts that the translation issues cause “a diminishment, at least for the time being, in the solidity or foundation of the extradition request”.

Chambers’s release follows a separate decision on Thursday by the three-judge panel at the high court tasked with deciding on the extradition to pause the proceedings in order to evaluate the impact of the alterations the US made to the original, machine-made translation of the extradition request into Spanish.

The Guardian detailed four examples of the alterations on 7 November and the US admitted to tampering with the translation, calling them “substantial [and] inadvertent” on 17 November – and citing the same four examples. Chambers’s defense team has asserted for weeks that there are as many as 30 such alterations.

The changes introduced prejudicial notions with specific legal implications that in turn wound up in the Spanish prosecutor’s report on the case, Aitor Martínez, a member of Chambers’s defense team, told the Guardian earlier this week. The judges must consider the prosecutor’s report in deciding on the extradition request.

The high court was expected to rule on the extradition this week, following a 13 November hearing. But as of Thursday’s decision, the deadline has been extended indefinitely as the judges evaluate the translation, including a 345-page report submitted by the defense team that identifies 30 “incriminating changes” Trump administration officials made to a translation prepared by DeepL, “an AI-first translation platform”, according to its website .

The decision also gives the prosecutor an opportunity to address the issue in writing, after dismissing it in the 13 November hearing by referring to “supposed translation errors”.

Chambers’s views and donations to progressive and humanitarian projects have been extensively profiled in US media, including his controversial public comments on Israel and Gaza. A week after the 7 October 2023 Hamas attacks on Israel, he posted on X about Israel’s response: “Stop calling it ‘collective punishment’/There’s nothing to be ‘punished’ for/No faction of the Palestinian resistance, Hamas or other, has done *anything* wrong/It’s simply genocide/Like it has been.”

The heir to $250m from his family’s business, Cox Enterprises, is being sought in extradition because of such views, his defense team has asserted throughout the case.

Meanwhile, the Irish Garda Síochána, acting on a request from US authorities, raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and Schnabel on Wednesday, destroying the front door and removing electronic items and other possessions, according to their attorney in Ireland , Ciarán Mulholland.

Schnabel, who is five months pregnant, said: “It is difficult to see this raid as anything other than a desperate fishing expedition by the US authorities to find evidence to bolster their case against Fergie.”

The attorney told the Guardian that the raid was the result of a “mutual legal assistance” request from the US – and that such a request “wouldn’t give [the Garda Síochána] permission to kick in the doors of someone’s dwelling in Ireland”.

“It’s unusual for the Irish state to be acting in such a clandestine manner,” Mulholland said. He has asked authorities to produce a search warrant and an itemized list of what was taken. “My fear is that whatever was taken has been put on a plane and taken to the US,” he added.

“This [extradition case] shows the complete disregard for due process … that the Trump administration seems to have,” Mulholland said.

title: Indian man sentenced to 19 years in prison for conspiring to kill Sikh separatist in New York
author: Reuters
text:
Nikhil Gupta admitted to plotting with Indian government official to hire hitman to murder dual US-Canadian citizen

An Indian ⁠man was sentenced to more ⁠than 19 ​years in US prison on Friday after admitting to orchestrating a failed Indian government-backed plot to kill a Sikh separatist in New York ⁠City , in connection with what US and Canadian authorities have called a broader effort to target Indian dissidents.

Nikhil Gupta, 55, pleaded guilty in February to murder-for-hire, conspiracy ⁠to commit murder-for-hire and conspiracy to commit money laundering.

The US district judge Victor Marrero handed down the ​235-month sentence at a hearing in a Manhattan federal ‌court.

The discovery of alleged ‌assassination plots against Sikh separatists in the US and Canada has tested relations with India , which has ‌denied involvement in such plots.

Prosecutors accused Gupta of plotting with an Indian government official to kill Gurpatwant Singh Pannun, a dual US-Canadian citizen and lawyer at Sikhs for Justice in New York who has advocated for a sovereign Sikh state in northern India.

Gupta and the Indian government official, Vikash Yadav, arranged to have $15,000 in cash delivered to a purported hitman who ‌was actually an undercover US law enforcement officer, court papers show.

Yadav is also charged in the case but is not in US custody. It is unclear ​whether he has hired a defense lawyer.

India’s government has dissociated itself from any plot against Pannun, saying it was against government policy.

Prosecutors with the Manhattan US attorney’s office had recommended a sentence of about 24 years in prison.

“This case cuts to the very core of American values,” prosecutor Ashley ⁠Nicolas said in court. “We don’t condone the use of violence to silence voices ​in this country, ever.”

Addressing the ​court on Friday, Gupta said ​he regretted straying from the non-violent example set by the Indian independence leader Mahatma Gandhi .

“I’m ​sorry to Mr ‌Pannun, I’m sorry ​to the communities I hurt, ​I’m sorry to my own family,” Gupta said.

Pannun told the court that he was grateful to the US for prosecuting Gupta and said he would keep advocating for Sikh sovereignty.

“Self-determination for my people and my homeland, Punjab, is my lifetime goal,” he said.

title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
author: Peter Walker Senior political correspondent
text:
PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope

Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.”

This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well.

Seeking to push his deal on food checks, emissions trading and a new youth exchange scheme, Burnham was at first in full consumer politics mode, saying it would bring cheaper food – with a namecheck for Tesco, Asda and other supermarket chains – as well as lower electricity costs and a claimed 0.5% boost to overall growth.

But as the Brussels press conference went on, the prime minister became more misty-eyed, particularly in describing the youth exchange scheme as a gift to a generation stripped of choices by the 2016 referendum and then Covid. “Hope is a word,” he intoned. “And it starts now.”

For all that Burnham is a skilled political salesman, his oratory is backed up with some helpful political context, matched with cooperative allies.

To begin with, not only politics but polling results are now different. A new constituency-level survey released on Friday showed that of 394 constituencies estimated to have voted leave in 2016, voters in 274 of them would back rejoining the EU – including Burnham’s Makerfield seat.

Standing alongside the UK prime minister in the venue, Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, and António Costa, the European Council president, at times resembled proud parents, beaming at every positive phrase.

They, of course, began work when the EU reset was the personal project of one Keir Starmer. His name was not mentioned on Friday, and it is undeniable that Brussels finds life easier dealing with a UK leader who is both bold and popular.

Speaking to British reporters later in the day, Burnham openly challenged political opponents to rebuff a plan that, he said, could add 0.5% annual growth to the economy in the long term – more, he said, than any other single intervention.

“Why would anybody turn their back on that?” he said, with particular focus on Nigel Farage, who was, soon after Burnham spoke, hosting a retaliatory press conference of his own, 10 minutes’ walk from the EU building.

Even with the tight timing – Farage had to delay his event as the summit timetable slipped – the Reform UK leader drew a decent crowd of reporters. But there will be a sense in No 10 that beyond Farage, most of the formidable Brexit forces of 2016 have melted away.

Kemi Badenoch, who has been advised by her team to talk more about the economy and less about Brexit, spent the day on a visit in Essex. The Conservatives did send out a condemnatory press release about the EU deal, but it focused more on Burnham “reopening the divisions of the past” than the specifics.

More trenchant was a statement from Stay Out, the recently formed Brexit purity group , which floated its argument that rejoining the EU would cost the UK £750m a week.

For all that the dominance of vote leave alumni in Stay Out gives the campaign the slight air of a historic battle re-enactment society, Burnham cannot ignore them. A resonant sidenote of the summit was how he was happy to talk about the specifics of the deal, but not much beyond that.

While it was the PM himself who provoked a debate about a future in which the UK rejoined the EU, the brakes were firmly on in regard to any discussion of such ideas.

Pre-summit talk of possible closer future links with Brussels was replaced by much vaguer language about mutual “brainstorming” on what would come next, with UK officials saying any progress could be months in the making.

Another sign of the caution embedded within Burnham’s ambition was the lineup of UK cabinet ministers who watched as the prime minister, von der Leyen and Costa arrived on Friday morning.

Alongside those you might expect – Ed Miliband, the foreign secretary, John Healey, the chancellor, and Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary – was Anneliese Midgley, a close ally of Burnham who has the job of chief whip, No 10’s liaison with Labour MPs.

She was there because a bill setting into UK law the new EU deal will be presented to parliament next week. Most Labour MPs agree with Burnham that the world has changed since 2016. But, as with the voters, he needs to bring them along with him.

title: Marquez's plan to ensure he wins MotoGP 2026 title early
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
MotoGP 2026 title favourite Marc Marquez is prioritising a minimal-risk approach to the Portuguese Grand Prix at Portimao, where he has the chance to become an eight-time premier-class champion.

Marquez needs to score 14 points over the rest of the season to ensure he is crowned champion.

Though he can only pick up 12 on Saturday, with a win in the sprint, this would guarantee the title as it would also deny crucial points to main title rival Jorge Martin.

But Marquez made it clear on Friday this is not his priority. And when asked whether other Ducati riders being competitive - and thus potentially siphoning points off his remaining championship rivals - was a boon to him, he insisted this was irrelevant.

"I mean, I need to score one point to 'game over' [Marco] Bezzecchi, and I need to score 14 to 'game over' Martin," he said matter-of-factly.

"So, this is my main target. Tomorrow, to try to score one point in the sprint. And then Sunday, to try to score 14 points."

What Marquez needs (independent of others)

in the sprint, GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GP in the sprint, or better in the GPor better in the GP if the sprint is a

Since his return to MotoGP action at Mugello, after mid-season surgery, Marquez failed to put up 14 points in only two full-schedule rounds - Assen and Silverstone (excluding the Phillip Island weekend given the cancellation of the main race).

Marquez was only sixth-fastest on Friday, describing it as a day "that you can lose a lot and you can gain nothing" - but also admitting that he was particularly aware of Portimao's propensity for causing mistakes (which are then often punished with severe crashes).

"It's true that I would like to ride in a different way, but I'm human, and I was stiffer than in previous races because I'm looking at the dangerous points too deeply, everywhere - but it's normal.

"I remember last year [the title-clinching weekend] in Motegi - I had a lot of races to go [to get it done], but even like this, during the weekend, I was not riding in the best way possible, because when you have that kind of advantage, you feel that you can only lose.

"I'm in a point that I can only lose, so I need to take full concentration to, how to say it in English, try to control all the risks that are in my hands.

"But then we'll see. As we saw last year - at Motegi I won, and then in the next race I got injured, and I was out for four races."

Marquez said he "felt relief" to conclude the day of running because it's "one day less of risk" - and named the second row of the grid as his "optimistic" target for qualifying, with front-row speed not really on the cards.

He said he told Ducati: "Don't be crazy with [changing] the bike because it's me. The bike is the same as Malaysia, as Qatar. It's me that I'm not flowing well, and on this bike if you are not playing well with the body, you are more stiff, then it's turning less."

title: Two men killed after glider crashes into Loch Leven in Scotland
author: Severin Carrell Scotland editor
text:
The pair had flown from the Scottish Gliding Centre at Portmoak on a training flight

Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning.

Police Scotland said their bodies were recovered from the loch by the emergency services after the alarm was raised at 11.05am on Friday.

The force said next of kin had been told and the incident was not being treated as suspicious. Two Coastguard helicopters and an air ambulance were sent to the scene, along with a fire service appliance and a specialist crew.

The pair had flown off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at Portmoak airfield near the loch’s eastern shore in a Perkoz two-person glider on a training flight.

A spokesperson for the gliding centre said: “The incident is currently under investigation by air accident investigation branch of the Department for Transport and the police in conjunction with the British Gliding Association.

“Our club is co-operating fully with these organisations. At the present time, there is no indication as to the cause of the accident.”

An Air Accidents Investigation Branch spokesperson said: “A multi-disciplinary team including inspectors with expertise in aircraft operations, engineering and recorded data have been deployed to gather evidence and make inquiries.”

The police said airspace restrictions had been put in place after the crash was reported.

title: What exactly is in the deal between the UK and the EU?
author: Jennifer Rankin and Alexandra Topping
text:
The two sides have come to agreements on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth exchange scheme

Burnham has agreed EU reset deal with tuition fees issue unresolved, says No 10

After months of on-off negotiations, leaks and late nights, the EU and UK have agreed a 12-page statement setting out the next steps in their relationship. What exactly have they agreed?

The UK agreed to work closely with the EU’s “Channel action plan”, which aims to crack down on smugglers who organise small boat crossings. The agreement will see law enforcement intelligence sharing between the UK and the EU, working closer with agencies such as Europol and the European border agency Frontex, and improved maritime surveillance from French authorities.

The agreement promises “a new structured dialogue” on migration, with both sides pledging to disrupt smuggling networks, strengthening border management in the Channel to stop small boat crossings, and work more closely with countries along migration routes. Both sides will require “shared financial commitments” given the “shared nature” of the challenges, according to the agreement.

Von der Leyen said Britain and the bloc would work together along the entire migration route and to prevent dangerous Channel crossings, which she argued would also save lives. Burnham also expressed interest in the plans of five EU member states to negotiate an offshore “returns hub” with Rwanda for people with no right to stay in the EU.

In a significant win for the UK, the EU has agreed to “explore further mutually beneficial solutions” on touring artists.

This does not sound like much. But the Labour government has spent more than two years making the case for easier access to the EU for travelling artists, musicians and performers, who face cumbersome work permits and complex rules for tour vehicles and equipment. Government-commissioned research suggests Brexit touring barriers have cost the UK sector £208m and nearly 2,500 jobs.

The EU has long refused to open discussions, so an agreement to talk is a breakthrough. Nonetheless it might not seem much to artists snared in red tape when working on the continent. The Musicians Union general secretary, Naomi Pohl, said members would be “extremely disappointed”, adding that she hoped “resolving this issue will be a priority”.

The document details plans to launch a new bilateral agreement – the EU-UK digital partnership – early next year. It will aim to increase cooperation on technology issues such as AI, connectivity, critical technologies, digital wallets and online safety with both parties maintaining “regulatory autonomy”.

In a potential advance for the UK, the EU appears ready to expand talks on the mutual recognition of professional qualifications, beyond existing negotiations on architects.

The statement welcomes “significant progress” on mutual recognition of professional qualifications for architects under the trade and cooperation agreement (TCA), and both sides agreed to “explore” arrangements in other professions.

title: Multiplying your Switch 2’s storage costs less than usual right now
author: Cameron Faulkner
text:
SSD costs are still sky-high, but at least there are decent deals on microSD Express cards.

SSD costs are still sky-high, but at least there are decent deals on microSD Express cards.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Expanding your Nintendo Switch 2’s 256GB of built-in storage with a microSD card is pricier than it was with Nintendo’s original console. That’s because microSD Express cards , while physically identical to ones you might have lying around, have faster read and write speeds. Thankfully, Samsung’s 256GB model has dropped to $44.99 at Amazon ahead of Black Friday, which is a few bucks off its usual price but still well below its $79.99 MSRP. Sandisk’s 256GB card, meanwhile, is available for $49.99 ($10 off Amazon’s typical list price) from Amazon and Sandisk , if you prefer one brand over the other for some reason.

For those who don’t want to think about upgrading their Switch 2’s storage again, both brands’ 512GB microSD Express cards are selling for a fair $99.99 on Amazon . That gives you double the storage for roughly twice the price of a 256GB card, as it should be.

I suspect the 256GB option will be enough for most Switch 2 players, unless you buy a lot of games. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is 24.9 gigabytes, for example. Other Nintendo-developed games tend to be similar in install size, though it’s all over the place for third-party game makers; Resident Evil Requiem (which also recently dropped to $39.99 on Amazon ) is relatively small at 28.7 gigs, while The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt — Remastered is about 50. Some games take up even more storage.

title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
author: Editorial
text:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than increased closeness to, Europe. Both rightwing parties face a dilemma: how to oppose the better relationship when even Mr Farage acknowledges its benefits?

title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
author: Kevin Rawlinson and Aisha Down
text:
News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks

A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged.

An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable.

News of the operation led by Whitehall and the National Cyber Security Centre, first reported by the BBC, follows a cyberattack this month of supermarket chains in at least seven European countries.

Another wave of attacks also affected hundreds of retailers across France in October in an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” for which Paris has publicly blamed Iran . The Pentagon is also investigating a suspected hack after a series of fridge malfunctions hit at least six US military bases in August.

Experts told the Guardian that if the vulnerability in UK-based devices had been discovered and exploited before a fix was found, the consequences would have been serious.

“This incident should serve as a wake-up call for the entire refrigeration industry,” said Garry Turner-Smith of Omega Solutions, a refrigeration consultancy firm whose employee, Neil McCourt, found the vulnerability in devices manufactured by Resource Data Management (RDM).

He said: “Had these weaknesses been discovered and exploited by someone with malicious intentions, they could have gained full control of vulnerable RDM data managers and used that access to interfere with refrigeration systems across multiple sites. This raises the prospect of attacks similar to those seen in Europe.”

After Omega was alerted to the weakness, the firm called in the cybersecurity consultants Pen Test Partners to investigate. Both firms then raised their concerns with the manufacturer, RDM.

Ken Munro, Pen Test Partners’ managing partner, said: “We determined that there was an urgent requirement to alert supermarkets and the food supply chain to the issue and fix. “However, we also had to work quietly to avoid alerting less ethical hackers and nation states of the likes of Iran, who are active in this space.”

Munro was attending a retail industry cyber event the day the vulnerabilities were found, enabling him to meet National Cyber Security Centre representatives in person to share the intelligence.

That triggered a series of briefing calls between retailers and officials from the National Cyber Security Centre, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs and the Food Standards Agency, among others, Munro said.

He added that Pen Test Partners had also tried to alert the owners of exposed devices. “Some controllers were easy to identify and thus contact the owners, but many thousands at small stores are still exposed,” he said.

“The vulnerability is not easy to find for a number of reasons, but once the method is known, it’s easy to recreate. We have not published that method, so there is still time for small operators to take their controllers off the public internet and/or apply the updated firmware.”

A National Cyber Security Centre spokesperson said it had “shared important insight and security advice to ensure that organisations understood potential risks to their networks, and were taking the appropriate measures to mitigate them”.

RDM did not respond to a request for comment. Its chief executive, Ged Evans, told the BBC the vulnerability was “identified in a test environment” that “went beyond” what such exercises usually involved as it “included dismantling our hardware”.

Evans saidd: “In any event we have acted at pace to address this issue and have already deployed first patch releases and have been in proactive contact with our customers to flag any issues and recommend mitigatory steps.”

title: Google says it’s going to shut off Google Assistant on smart speakers next year
author: Jay Peters
text:
Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿

Google is making some big changes to its smart home offerings, including killing the Nest app.﻿

Google is announcing some significant changes to its smart home software. Starting next year, the company will shut down the Nest app in favor of the Google Home app and retire Google Assistant on its smart home devices.

The Nest app shutdown takes place on January 25th, 2027, meaning you’ll have to manage your Nest products, including Nest thermostats, cameras, and Nest Protect alarms, from the Google Home app instead. If you get the Google Home app set up, Google will move over your Nest devices, including cameras and video history, to the Home app on that January 25th date. The company will also automatically transfer Nest Aware (1st Gen) subscriptions to Google Home Premium. Google says it will begin deleting Nest account data on March 25th, 2027.

The changes for Google Assistant will take place later: On August 2nd, 2027, the Gemini for Home voice assistant will replace Google Assistant on smart speakers and smart displays, the company says. Google argues that Gemini for Home allows users to ask more complex questions and speak naturally instead of needing to use dedicated commands or specific language.

Gemini for Home was announced last year , so it’s not exactly a shock that Google is going to move on from Google Assistant in the smart home (especially when the company also killed Google Assistant on phones earlier this year ). The company says it plans to share more updates about the changes ahead of the August 2027 transition.

title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
text:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."

On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.

Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".

The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

Burnham's push for closer EU ties causes ripples in his party and others

title: Here are the Apple deals actually worth picking up ahead of Black Friday
author: Sheena Vasani
text:
A new pair of AirPods or the latest Apple Watch can make a great holiday gift, but they can also take a pretty big dent out of your budget. That’s especially true this year, as rising hardware prices have made MacBooks and other Apple devices even more expensive. Fortunately, Black Friday offers a chance to save, especially since great deals are already available on a wide range of Apple devices. Some discounts even extend to recent releases like the Apple Watch Series 12 and touchscreen MacBook Pro , which have dropped to new lows.

Most of the discounts below are promoted as Black Friday deals, but we’ve also included a few that aren’t part of the shopping event but have “coincidentally” dropped in price in the last week or so. Black Friday isn’t until November 27th, however, so some prices could fall further in the coming days. Apple is also kicking off its own Black Friday shopping event that day, offering up to $300 in gift cards with select purchases. That said, if you don’t want to wait, we think the deals below are already worth taking advantage of.

Earbud and headphone deals

Apple’s last-gen earbuds lack active noise cancellation, but they still deliver good, relatively bass-rich sound, even if they don’t quite match the newer AirPods 5. They also offer voice call quality on par with the latest AirPods Pro. Read our review .

The are down to $419 ($130 off) at Amazon , which is $19 shy of their best price to date ( Best Buy and Target also have them for about $10 more). Like the original, Apple’s latest over-ear headphones feature a luxurious build consisting of aluminum, steel, and a mesh fabric, but they offer better sound and noise cancellation. The new H2 chip also enables features like adaptive audio and live translation. Read our review .

If you want over-ears and are comfortable going without active noise cancellation, the are down to $79.99 ($120 off) at Target in pink and white through November 22nd, marking a new low price. Amazon also has the pink headphones on sale for $79.99, while other colors are $20 more at both retailers. The headphones are a noticeable improvement over their predecessor, delivering more detailed sound and support for lossless audio. They also last up to 50 hours on a single charge, while their memory foam ear cushions make them comfortable enough for long listening sessions. Read our review.

The are down to around $89.95 ($80 off) at Amazon , Best Buy , and Target , nearly matching their lowest price to date. The wireless earbuds feature a slick, eye-catching transparent option and solid noise cancellation, especially at this price. They’re also exceptionally comfortable, with four ear tip sizes to help you find a secure fit. Sure, you don’t get wireless charging, but they offer IPX4 water resistance and up to nine hours of battery life on a single charge. Read our review .

The recently released 16.3-inch MacBook Pro with a PROLED XDR display, 24GB of RAM, and 1TB of storage is on sale starting at $3,249 ($150 off) — a new low price — at Amazon and Best Buy . The redesigned laptop is Apple’s first with an OLED touchscreen, which allows for rich colors and deep blacks. Read our review.

AirTags, chargers, and other deals

title: Tadej Pogačar Hints at Monster 2027 After His Brutal Vuelta Crash
author: ahood
text:
Pogačar hinted that Flanders and Roubaix could be in the cards for 2027. (Photo: Gruber Images)

If anyone is doubting Tadej Pogačar and what his brutal crash at the Vuelta a España might mean for 2027, rest assured.

Don’t worry, Pogi fans, it doesn’t appear that anything will change.

Pogačar sounds as ambitious as ever and said a return to the Tour of Flanders and Paris-Roubaix could be in the cards in 2027.

“There is a good chance that I will be at the start again, yes,” he told HLN . “I am already looking forward to it, because they are fun races.”

“Fun” for Pogačar usually means misery for everyone else, but fans absolutely love seeing the world No. 1 race the iconic northern classics .

Pogačar has already singled out the Tour de France , unfinished business at the Vuelta, and a run at a record-tying third worlds in Sallanches as major goals for 2027.

Some wondered if that loaded back-end calendar might mean an easier start to next season, especially since he hasn’t raced since his crash on August 29.

But from what Pogačar told the Belgian outlet Het Laatste Nieuws at the annual padel tournament hosted by his agent Alex Carera in Italy, it doesn’t sound like it.

The quick grab with journalists provided some fresh hints of what next year’s comeback season might look like.

Pogačar admitted the obvious that the 71km of time trial kilometers in the 2027 Tour suits Remco Evenepoel. He also made it clear that he still sees Jonas Vingegaard as a contender on any course.

King Pog doesn’t appear to be losing any sleep over it either, even if some are hyping the 2027 Tour as the “Anti-Pogačar” course .

“I haven’t really looked at the course in detail yet, but there is indeed some time trialing involved,” he said. “That is good for Remco, but as I always say, in the Tour, you can’t hide anywhere. You have to be strong for three weeks in every discipline.

“Whether that’s uphill or on the time trial bike. And you have to be able to maintain focus. That won’t be any different next year.”

The Tour is all but certain to be at the center of his calendar for 2027. After winning the record-tying fifth yellow jersey, he wants to make official history by going for number six.

If he does show up for the Flanders-Roubaix double again, that’s the best indication yet there won’t be any lingering physical impacts from the Vuelta crash.

Roubaix and the Vuelta remain one of the few major races Pogačar has yet to win .

After a few weeks off the bike following surgery in September, Pogačar is back to training after the heavy crash that ended his Vuelta and cut short his 2026 season.

After missing the worlds in Montréal, his UAE teammate Brandon McNulty will be racing in the rainbow jersey , so this season Pogačar won’t be donning the stripes.

“I enjoyed the off-season. The first training sessions didn’t go very smoothly, but things have been going better for the past week,” he said. “My rides are getting longer and I can already pick up the intensity a bit.”

Pogačar’s social media feed has been filled with weddings, trips, coffee rides, sessions in the gym, some jogging, lots of food, and yes, a few longer bike rides.

After two documentaries recently dropped , Pocačar is enjoying his last few days of quiet home life before joining his UAE Emirates-XRG teammates in Spain next month for the team’s first winter camp.

That’s when Pogačar’s official racing calendar will be sketched out.

We’ll see what team boss Mauro Gianetti has to say.

He tapped the brakes on Pogačar’s desire to return to racing for the European championships in Slovenia, and it was a good thing too, because doctors later found other neck fractures from his Vuelta spill .

From the sounds of things, if Pogačar has his way, he won’t be slowing down at all in 2027.

title: 'I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders' - Lombardia protest ringleader Ben Healy emboldened as he calls for change on rider safety
author: Owen Rogers
text:
The five minute delay before the start of Il Lombardia at the close of the European season demonstrated the power riders have in forcing better safety in races, according to Ben Healy (EF Education-EasyPost).

Rider safety has been the hottest topic in road cycling since the terrible death of Finlay Tarling at the Volta a Portugal in the summer. And when that incident was followed by a series of further near-misses during the Italian autumn Classics, something had to give.

Healy was the driving force behind what he calls a 'stand' rather than a protest, the peloton delaying the start of Il Lombardia, the season’s final Monument, by five minutes. But, as powerful as the delay was, and as hard hitting and articulate as Remco Evenepoel’s (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) words were, the demonstration was an example of the power riders have.

"I think we just really wanted to show as riders the power that we had, and that we're not happy," he told in a café close to the bustle of the Rouleur Live show, where he was fulfilling sponsor commitments.

"We didn't want to just go at the Lombardia organisers, for instance. You know that's why we chose to do a five-minute stand before the race actually started, and just delay the race, and just show that if this continues, that this is what we can do if we choose to."

"I think after that happened [with Tarling] everyone expected something to change, you know, and when we went to Italy, there were what, three cars on the course in separate races over three or four days? And that was pretty clear then that nothing had changed," Healy said.

"There has to be a process to make things safer. And I mean, for sure, the UCI is aware of it, but I don't know how aware they are, they’re not on the ground every single race. This is clearly something that is recurring, and it just shouldn't happen ever, having a car on the course, let's just hope the UCI will listen and work with us to make change."

If Lombardia was the example of what unity within the peloton can do in bringing an issue to notice, Healy prefers not to commit to what might happen if and when such a dangerous situation occurs again, or worse, should another rider die.

"I just really hope it doesn't come to that, you know? I just have to reiterate the power that we have as riders and ultimately what we can do if we choose to.

"Mistakes can be made, and as long as we're working towards making racing safer, I think that's the most important thing. We don't want to point blame or, like, kick and scream, it’s about being productive and working together to improve the sport for everyone."
