title: Teenage Engineering’s first CD player puts the spinning disc on display
author: Andrew Liszewski
text:
The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.

The EP/BC–1 can wirelessly stream audio to Bluetooth headphones or multiple devices using Auracast.

Teenage Engineering announced what it describes as “a modern take on a classic CD player” with its new EP/BC–1 featuring a slab-like design that leaves the spinning disc exposed instead of hiding it under a lid or inside a slide-out tray. The company says the EP/BC–1 is the first entry in its new broadcast series of products and was designed to bring “physical audio formats into a modern context, evolved from a shared obligation within the company to preserve the formats they grew up with.”

The EP/BC-1 is available now through Teenage Engineering’s online store for $299. The CD player joins the company’s existing EP–series of audio devices and has the same dimensions as its KO II synthesizer that launched in 2023 so it can be paired with, and connected to, other Teenage Engineering gear including the recently-announced EP-35 battery-powered amp .

Although it’s designed to play a nearly 45 year old medium, the EP/BC-1 features modern conveniences like variable speed playback, cue markers, a jog wheel for forward and reverse search, and built-in beat detection. There’s a very retro-looking series of digital displays showing track, index, time information, and audio levels, and around the edges you’ll find both digital and analog audio connections including a headphone jack and a USB 2.0 port.

If you want to go completely wireless the CD player has a rechargeable battery and supports both Bluetooth connections to headphones and Auracast streaming to multiple devices that support it. The EP/BC-1 is compatible with standard CDs as well as discs full of MP3 files, and when using the former it can rip tracks to 44.1 Hz/16-bit WAV files. If you want MP3s or other formats, you’ll need to convert them yourself.

title: Yankees Birthday of the Day: Clark Griffith
author: Kevin Winterhalt
text:
The inaugural manager of the Yankees, Clark Griffith is a titanic figure in the early history of baseball.

Though Clark Griffith is the first man to manage the New York baseball team we now call the Yankees, his time in New York is merely one chapter in a story of one of the giants of baseball’s early history. That’s no shot at Griffith’s time in New York and his importance to the franchise. It’s just he had such an amazing life and career.

He was already an accomplished hurler when he came to New York and became the player-manager of the club, in its first season in The Big Apple. And long after he hung up his cleats, he remained an integral part of baseball in the first half of the 20th century.

Clark Calvin Griffith Born: November 20, 1869 (Clear Creek, MO) Died: October 27, 1955 (Washington, DC) Yankees Tenure: 1903-07 (player/manager), 1908 (manager)

Clark Griffith was already a grizzled veteran when American League President Ban Johnson named him manager of the New York Highlanders (often called the Americans in the press) prior to the 1903 season. It was the inaugural campaign for the club, which relocated from Baltimore after the Orioles folded following two seasons.

The diminutive Griffith (listed at 5-foot-6) was a right-handed pitcher, and a good one, at that. Between 1894 and 1901, he won at least 20 games in a season seven times. His first season in New York was also his last one as a starting pitcher, and he tossed more than 200 innings while managing the club to a disappointing fourth-place finish.

Griffith’s pitching days were not over, however. He transitioned to the bullpen and continued to pitch at a high level while trying to steer the Highlanders to a pennant. In 1904 and 1906, he came close, with the club finishing in second place each season, mere games from wining the American League.

Modern Yankee fans are used to skipper Aaron Boone getting himself tossed from games, though he was shockingly well-behaved in 2026. He’s far from the first Yankee manager to get the hook, of course. Griffith, by virtue of being the first manager, gets that honor. Like his modern successor, Griffith also got himself suspended for his conduct toward umpires.

On Monday, August 27th, 1906, Griffith took umbrage with a safe call at first base while playing St. Louis. As a result, the umpires ordered Griffith off the field. The Highlanders’ skipper took his sweet time about it. Unfortunately for him, AL President Johnson was in the crowd, and the next day he suspended Griffith indefinitely. Yeesh. “Savages in the Box,” this was not. Seems a little harsh. But wait — there’s more. The indefinite suspension might have something to do with Griffith fighting umpire Tim Hurst earlier in the season, which also got him suspended. For that round of fisticuffs, Griffith received a five-day suspension. His ban in August lasted a week.

The Highlanders bottomed out on Griffith’s watch in 1908, and in June he decided it was time for him to move on. Owner Frank J. Farrell tried to dissuade the disheartened Griffith, but to no avail.

“It was fighting against fate,” Griffith told The New York Times , “And I knew when I had enough. I do not know who my successor will be, but I understand [Kid] Elberfeld is mentioned for the place. If that is so, I wish him the best of luck, and I hope my successor will pull the team out of the rut and place them where they belong.”

Griffith’s warm feelings for the club definitely did not last forever. At his death, the Times noted, “Mr. Griffith had two pet dislikes in his lifetime. One was John McGraw and the other was the New York Yankees.”

Griffith’s time in baseball was by no means done when he left New York. Most famously, he eventually found himself in Washington, where he leveraged his assets to obtain a 10 percent stake in the notoriously bad Senators. “First in war; first in peace, and last in the American League,” the old saying went.

Griffith won five pennants in nine years before again relying on his assets to buy a majority share in the franchise. By 1920, he’d transitioned out of the dugout and into the owner’s box, ending a 20-year managerial career where he won 1,491 games (26th most all-time). In 1924, his Senators finally won the World Series, upsetting the New York Giants. They would win further pennants in 1925 and 1933 as well.

Clark Griffith is almost certainly the most important person in the history of Washington baseball, with all due respect to Walter Johnson. He’s also the answer to an obscure yet important bit of trivia. Who was responsible for the tradition of US presidents throwing out the first pitch? It was Griffith, who in 1910 asked President William Howard Taft to toss out the first ball. Taft obliged and the rest is history.

Griffith was also key to baseball’s relationship with the U.S. government and military during both world wars. In World War I, he organized an initiative to get baseball equipment for every American soldier overseas. He even got President Woodrow Wilson to chip in. During World War II, he was one of the people who helped convince President Franklin Roosevelt to keep baseball playing.

He’s the only man in baseball history to have played, managed, and owned a team for at least 20 years each. Clark Griffith was elected to the Major League Baseball Hall of Fame in 1946. His Senators would eventually pass to his son, Calvin, who would move them to Minnesota in 1961 to become the Twins (and become rather infamous in his own right).

Clark Griffith died on October 27, 1955, in Washington, D.C. In its obituary for the legend, The New York Times noted what former president Harry S. Truman had said about Griffith in 1946 when he had thrown out a presidential first pitch, the tradition Griffith started decades earlier.

“Mr. Griffith is a shining example of what this great country of ours can produce.”

Happy birthday to the Yankees’ first skipper.

See more of the “Yankees Birthday of the Day” series here .

title: Man Utd fan criticism has gone too far at times - Berrada
text:
Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada says some of the criticism aimed at the club's hierarchy has "crossed a line".

In a rare interview to Sky Sports as head coach Mauricio Pochettino prepares for his first game in charge, at Liverpool on Sunday, Berrada said he "understood" the frustration of supporters at United being 18th in the Premier League. He also said some of the criticism was "fair".

However, he feels some of it has gone too far.

"Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and scrutiny we're going to get," he said. "We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line.

"We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that."

United's director of football Jason Wilcox has been singled out by supporters at recent games. There have also been social media calls for both Wilcox and Berrada to lose their jobs.

In addition, songs are now sung regularly calling for minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe to leave, while opposition to the Glazer family has remained intense since their leveraged buyout in 2005 saddled debt on to the club that now exceeds £1bn.

Wilcox, in particular, has been blamed for what is perceived to have been poor summer recruitment. After the 2-0 defeat by Atletico Madrid in September, defender Lisandro Martinez said he "expected more from the technical director".

Ousted boss Michael Carrick felt he was let down by a transfer strategy that targeted midfield, while not addressing issues at left-back and in attack - which has been compounded by injuries to Luke Shaw and Benjamin Sesko.

Carrick wanted to target Elliot Anderson and Mateus Fernandes, but United backed off when Nottingham Forest and West Ham's demands went higher than they wanted to pay. Anderson eventually joined Manchester City for £116m, with Fernandes moving to Tottenham for £85m.

Instead, United paid a combined £118m for Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos, who have started seven Premier League games between then, and triggered Youri Tielemans' £35m release clause at Aston Villa. Tielemans scored his first United goal in the 4-4 draw with Aston Villa on 8 November and has one assist.

However, Berrada has defended United's transfer business, saying: "When we look at the summer transfer window of 2026, I know we're receiving a lot of criticism for it, but we're actually happy with the players we bought.

"We think that Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos, and Karl Darlow - and let's not forget that we've also welcomed back Marcus Rashford, who had a very good season on loan at Barcelona - these are five additions that we think have made the squad fundamentally better.

"We went in knowing what we needed to do. Of course, there have been different dynamics at play and we've said consistently in the last few years we need to stay disciplined. We need to take the right decisions. We need to buy the right players, for the right value at the right time - in terms of what the squad needs.

"When we find the right opportunities, we will spend. But what we don't want to be doing is spending just for the sake of it. So, could we have signed an additional defender to straighten the depth and the quality? Yes, but we have to find the right players at the right value.

"There's no point in us spending £40m, £50m for players we're not convinced are going to add value to the team."

When he spoke to the wider media for the first time, 30 minutes before Berrada's interview was aired, Pochettino said he hoped to have a say in all areas of the playing side, even though his official title is head coach.

"I know that, being a head coach, I am the guy that is going to decide the squad for Sunday," he said. "I'm going to pick the starting 11 and I'm going to make the changes.

"Of course, in the future, I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad."

Berrada said there had been little option other than to dismiss Carrick given United's plight and the team had "dropped off in many areas".

Pochettino has spoken individually to virtually every player to get an understanding of what the issues are.

He said he was wary of reading too much into data that shows United's players have not been running enough, arguing "if you don't put context on the data, it's very dangerous to talk".

The 54-year-old also said that, despite talking extensively about culture in his first in-house interview on Thursday, it could take 10 years to build one.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear," he said. "It's a historic club, one of the best in the world. It's difficult to find another club the size of Manchester United.

"The culture of the club and the identity of the club is very clear. It needs to be in a different place than we are now."

Pochettino did confirm Bruno Fernandes will remain as skipper for the trip to Liverpool.

Fernandes has struggled for form and, with the 32-year-old's contract due to expire in the summer, there has been no breakthrough in negotiations over an extension.

United do have the option to trigger an additional year on the Portugal playmaker's present deal but, given the massive dip from the levels that earned him all last season's major player of the year awards, there are some who wonder whether a clean break might be best.

Pochettino preferred to deflect the wider aspect of Fernandes' future and concentrate on the immediate.

"Bruno is our captain and he's a very important player," he said.

"I think we will have time after to talk about the [other] things that you are asking me."

title: Shirin van Anrooij to make cyclo-cross debut with Canyon-SRAM alongside Zoe Backstedt next week
author: laura.weislo@futurenet.com (Laura Weislo)
text:
Shirin van Anrooij will make her debut with Canyon-SRAM in the upcoming UCI Cyclo-cross World Cup in Ostrava, Czechia, next week, racing alongside Zoe Bäckstedt at the start of a 13-race schedule, the team announced on Friday.

She has been training in Malaga, Spain alongside her new teammate and former under-23 cyclo-cross rival Bäckstedt in preparation for the intensive campaign of 11 World Cups, the National Championships and culminating with the World Championships in Oostende, Belgium in January.

"I'm just really excited and looking forward to starting the season because we've been watching CX racing on TV for a couple of weeks now, and I'm really curious to see how it is amongst the girls again," Van Anrooij said in the team press release.

"I think Zoe and I are having a good preparation camp here in Malaga, so I can't wait to be on the start line myself, and to see where my level is at."

"I'm hoping that I'll reach my best level in cyclo-cross again, and then I'll just have to discover what results this will bring me," Van Anrooij said.

"I think the biggest goals are, for sure, the Christmas period with a lot of races that I really like – Koksijde, Zonhoven, Gavere, and then the World Championships in Oostende. Worlds is always a big goal for everyone, but I especially look forward to that, with it being a race on the sand in Belgium."

After her first year racing in the elite fields last season, with nine races from the end of December through Worlds, Bäckstedt is looking forward to a longer campaign. "I'm really excited for this cyclo-cross season. It feels like it's been two years since I properly raced CX as last year was an extremely short season for me.

"It's super fun having Shirin as my teammate. Already for training, it's been really beneficial for me to follow her and learn from her. I'm now excited to do our first race together."

Although both riders have goals for the early part of the 2027 road season, Canyon-SRAM's performance director Dan Fleeman supports their off-road ambitions.

"I think cyclo-cross offers several important benefits. From a physical perspective, it develops the ability to repeatedly produce high-intensity efforts, accelerate out of corners, change pace and deal with constantly changing demands. It also requires a high level of anaerobic capacity and the ability to recover quickly between efforts.

"Technically, the benefits are equally important. CX develops bike handling, balance, coordination and the ability to make decisions under pressure. Riders are constantly adapting to different terrain and conditions, managing their effort and finding the quickest way through a course.

"Also, I think that there is a mental benefit. CX is an incredibly demanding discipline where you have to be prepared to push yourself outside your comfort zone, deal with mistakes, and keep fighting throughout a race."

Their calendar has been designed to focus only on the major races, skipping the Superprestige, X2O Trofee, and HG Cross.

"The main consideration is quality over quantity. The World Cup offers the highest level of competition, the best opportunities to measure ourselves against the world's leading riders, and the experience of racing on some of the biggest stages in cyclo-cross.

"We also have to consider the overall demands of the season. Both riders have important road objectives, so we don't want to overload the programme with racing simply for the sake of racing. We would rather be selective, target the important events, and make sure that they arrive at them in good physical condition."

title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
text:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

Anthropic mathematician claims to have solved prestigious Millennium Prize problem with Claude
author: Robert Hart, Emma Roth
text:
An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.

An Anthropic mathmetician’s latest breakthrough is another sign of how quickly AI is transforming mathematics.

If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge claims he has proved the Riemann hypothesis, one of mathematics’s most notoriously difficult problems, with the help of Claude, cracking a puzzle that has eluded some of the world’s best mathematicians for decades. If verified, it would mark yet another seismic achievement for AI in mathematics and add to the upheaval already unleashed by OpenAI’s previous, often inelegant forays into the field.

Alpöge’s solution has yet to be verified independently. Anthropic has not commented or involved itself in Alpöge’s announcement. In a document on his website , Alpöge says he texted Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei about the solution “late Sunday night” and suggests he held off publication until after the company’s IPO on Thursday .

The Riemann hypothesis is one of seven Millennium Prize problems, which are widely considered some of the most formidable open challenges in mathematics. First proposed in 1859, the Riemann hypothesis concerns the distribution of prime numbers and how zeroes of a function are involved. It’s regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics.

A statement on Alpöge’s website says Claude was integral to developing the proof:

I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof 1 of the Riemann Hypothesis. In fact, the method easily extends much further, resolving the so-called Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, and I expect, with more time, the Extended Riemann Hypothesis too. Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions. It is natural to feel that this is an end, in my case a loss of a principal guiding light, but what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater.

The Verge reached out to Anthropic but didn’t immediately hear back. Anthropic said it was working on the Riemann Hypothesis with Claude in August , but noted at the time: “We don’t expect that the techniques Claude used will lead to proving the Riemann hypothesis.”

Alpöge’s solution, presented in Lean, has only been published on his website and has not yet been publicly accepted by the Clay Mathematics Institute, which administers the Millennium Prize and offers a $1 million bounty for each problem solved. Under the institute’s rules , a proposed solution must be published and withstand at least two years of scrutiny before it can be considered for the prize, during which time it must have “received general acceptance in the global mathematics community.”

In the quarter-century since the prize was established, only one problem has been officially solved: The Poincaré conjecture , a topological problem concerning three-dimensional spheres. In September, OpenAI claimed to have cracked another, the Navier-Stokes problem, which concerns the flow of fluids.

OpenAI said it pursued Navier-Stokes after hearing rumors that rival researchers were closing in on a solution. Alpöge had been working on the problem with New York University mathematics professor Tristan Buckmaster. Buckmaster claimed OpenAI produced a solution for Navier-Stokes using the route he and Alpöge were working on with OpenAI’s Codex and Claude.

OpenAI spent millions of dollars and deployed 10,000 agents in the attempt. The result is widely considered credible, though it has yet to receive formal recognition. But the achievement has been marred by allegations of questionable research practices, including claims it used unpublished work from mathematicians who had shared their research with its AI tools. OpenAI has strongly denied wrongdoing, but this has done little to quell the uproar.

Though most of the spotlight has been on OpenAI’s movement in math, Alpöge said in July that he solved the Jacobean conjecture using Claude. The deluge of findings has left mathematicians scrambling to digest the material and figure out where they belong in what is rapidly becoming a profoundly different mathematical landscape.

title: Forbes releases 2026 F1 team valuations
author: Samarth Kanal
text:
The report puts Ferrari highest at $9.5bn to Mercedes's $9.2bn, putting those two most valuable F1 teams on par with the top half of the NFL's teams, the three most valuable NBA teams, and Real Madrid.

F1's 11 teams are therefore valued at an average of $5.2bn and, not including Cadillac - which was absent from the 2025 rankings - the average is up to $5.4bn, a gain of 53% from last year.

Haas has made the largest increase in value - of 87%, from $1.5bn to $2.8bn - while McLaren's value has increased 73% to $7.6bn. Scroll down to view the full valuations table.

Forbes uses estimated revenue as part of its calculations: from 2024 to 2025, estimated revenue rose 15% to $530m per team.

Its report says that McLaren and Mercedes expect to surpass $1bn for the first time ever in 2026 - and only the NFL's Dallas Cowboys and football teams Real Madrid and Barcelona have reached that mark.

The report highlights “multiples” as a catalyst for F1 teams' growth: in 2019, F1 teams were valued at 2.3 times their previous season's revenue and the 10 teams (excluding Cadillac) are now valued at 10.3 times last year's revenue on average.

This signals a transformation of F1 teams' business models over the last seven years, implying that the value of an F1 team is tied to their huge potential for growth rather than physical assets and historic cashflow.

Owning a stake of an F1 team is therefore likened to owning that of a valuable US sports franchise, with F1 teams' revenue multiples now closing in on the NFL and NBA - and well ahead of the NHL, MLB, and European football.

The upswing in multiples is, according to Forbes, a consequence of the 2021 cost cap (at $215m for 2026) that limited spending.

The cost cap, plus Concorde Agreements, have led Ferrari, Red Bull, Racing Bulls, Mercedes, Haas, and Alpine to be profitable in 2025 - with McLaren expected to hit a profit of $200m in 2026.

Mercedes is estimated to have the highest profit of $225m.

With just 11 teams on the grid, it's rare to be able to own a piece of an F1 team. Sportico reported in November that Mark Walter's stake in Cadillac is being offered for at least $3bn.

Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang recently said that F1 has made “huge inroads” into the United States, a continued area of its focus, while China and India “represent opportunities” both for F1 and MotoGP.

In 2027, the values of Mercedes and Ferrari are projected to hit $10bn.

F1 teams are 'overwhelmed by interest'

Being on the ground here in Las Vegas, it's no surprise to me that Forbes is reporting a 47% increase in the average value of a Formula 1 team.

I've been talking to Liberty Media CEO Derek Chang for an upcoming interview in The Race Business this week and listening to him you get a sense of how buoyant the people running the championship feel about its prospects in America. Walk through the city and you can understand why.

I've been to all three US grands prix this year. There was a real commercial buzz in Miami and Austin, but here in Vegas it feels like it's reaching fever pitch. As most things do in Vegas.

The team commercial directors I've spoken to are almost overwhelmed by the interest. They're scrabbling around for paddock passes or trying to squeeze one more prospect into the Paddock Club. Everywhere you go there's a brand event. American companies are practically throwing money at Formula 1.

Look at what F1 itself announced in three days. Standard Chartered upgraded its partnership. Nike signed up. So did Whoop. Who would have imagined, even a few years ago, that there'd be a wearables category on F1's sponsorship list? The series is in rude health.

At our Monaco event in June, Aston Martin's Jefferson Slack asked “We're valued at six or seven times revenue. Why is an NBA team valued at 12 times revenue?” Forbes now puts the 10 established F1 teams at an average of 10.3 times revenue. On that measure, much of the gap Jeff saw has already closed.

How much weight should we put on the individual numbers? Forbes and Sportico published eight days apart and disagreed by $1.3bn on Ferrari alone. Over the off season we'll revisit our work on team ownership and valuations and look at how the assumptions behind both reports stack up against the deals people have actually done.

Perhaps the scrabble for passes is a decent KPI for the scrabble for ownership. There are only 11 teams and yet you can usually find one more pass. If either of the rumoured Alpine or Cadillac stake sales gets over the line before Christmas, we might get a firm data point of what it now costs to get in permanently.

title: Boys Noize turns to the club (and an obscure Italian synth) for inspiration on 7LLVSION
author: Terrence O’Brien
text:
‘I always look for the newest machines.’

If you’re wondering how Alex Ridha’s (aka Boys Noize) collaboration with Nine Inch Nails influenced his new record 7LLVSION , the answer is simple: It didn’t. That’s not to say Ridha didn’t learn anything from the virtuosic production team of Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross, but most of the songs on 7LLVSION had been knocking around for some time. And as Ridha is quick to point out, these are not rock songs built for live performance; they’re “battle tested” for clubs and DJ sets. “I was kind of back on the usual kind of thing,” he tells The Verge .

“I do the same I kind of always do. I go make coffee, go in my room, put on the machines, and I’ll start messing around with sounds and build one sound to another and there comes a record,” he says. Like previous Boys Noize releases, a lot of 7LLVSION starts with sound design. “It’s kind of tech-driven, in a way,” he says, “because I always look for the newest machines.”

On 7LLVSION, Ridha frequently turned to an obscure Italian semimodular synth, the Grp A4 . “It’s just so powerful , and it sounds so big,” he says. The routing options, dual filters (which he uses in parallel), and built-in sequencer kept leading him to new and inspiring places. Because of that, the A4 ended up on a number of tracks, including “ Shut It Down ,” “ 1+1+1 ,” and “Ycore.”.

“The exciting part is always to, you know, not repeat myself, even with the drum sounds, and try something new that I haven’t tried before,” Ridha says. For a few tracks, that meant getting away from the rigid, quantized grooves of techno and opting for a more dynamic, live feeling on tracks like “Shut It Down” and “1+1+1” especially. “Live drums are the new 808,” he says.

He looked to German bands of the ’70s and ’80s for inspiration, like Can , Amon Düül , and Deutsch Amerikanische Freundschaft . He also called out Conny Plank, who produced landmark records by Neu!, Kraftwerk, and Eurythmics. But in general he says, “My goal is to not sound like anything you can point to. You know, I don’t want to be a direct copy.” Instead, he was chasing the sound of “electronic punk.” That means aggressive basslines, driving drums, and stripped-down arrangements that avoid overstuffing the mix with too many instruments.

But it all comes back to the club at the end of the day. “Environment has always been the main thing in my music. I need to have a record that I want to play at the party,” he says, and that meant testing the songs off 7LLVSION extensively in his DJ sets and letting the audience tell him what works and what doesn’t. “The club is the most open and objective situation you can have,” he says. “They don’t know what I’m playing, so they hear something for the first time, and you can just look at someone’s face, or someone’s there in the room to get a cool reaction, and that usually makes me feel good about something or not.”

Boys Noize is currently touring the world on the festival circuit, and 7LLVSION is available now on most major streaming services .

title: Everything that happened in Portimao MotoGP practice
author: Eden Hannigan
text:
Alex Marquez provided an upset to the expected order as he concluded Friday MotoGP practice at the Portuguese Grand Prix as the fastest rider on his return from surgery.

VR46 Ducati’s Fabio Di Giannantonio was narrowly behind Marquez in second, as the satellite Ducati riders proved the manufacturer still had the pace to challenge Aprilia.

It provided a slight change to the expected order as Marco Bezzecchi had comfortably led throughout the session, though the rider who was fastest in FP1 was ultimately shuffled to third.

KTM’s Pedro Acosta and LCR Honda’s Johann Zarco also showed solid pace consistently in Friday’s running and completed the top five.

It was a less straightforward session for the other riders still in title contention, with Marc Marquez and Jorge Martin both flirting with a place in Q1 in the first half of the session.

Marquez was ultimately comfortable by the chequered flag as he finished the day in sixth, while it was more touch-and-go for Martin, who narrowly squeezed into the last automatic Q2 spot in 10th.

Brad Binder and Fermin Aldeguer were two of the riders who slotted between Marquez and Martin, who was fortunate not to have been pushed into Q1 by the Trackhouse Aprilia pair, as Raul Fernandez took ninth while Ai Ogura was 11th.

Iker Lecuona crashed twice on the factory Ducati while replacing Pecco Bagnaia.

Pol Espargaro, who came in between sessions for the still-injured Maverick Vinales at Tech3 KTM, also suffered a crash at Turn 1 with 12 minutes left on the clock.

title: Mario Cipollini Stalking and Abuse Case Ends as Statute of Limitations Expires
author: ahood
text:
Criminal case against Mario Cipollini has ended in Italy. (Photo: Tim de Waele/Corbis via Getty Images)

An appeals court in Florence ended the criminal case against former road world champion Mario Cipollini on Thursday after ruling that the statute of limitations had expired on all counts.

Cipollini, 59, was facing a three-year prison term handed down by a Lucca court in 2022, Italian media reported .

The case began in 2017 when Cipollini’s ex-wife Sabrina Landucci filed a complaint. The charges included alleged domestic mistreatment, stalking, bodily harm, and threats.

Landucci reached a separate agreement with Cipollini over damages and withdrew from the proceedings, La Stampa reported.

“Today I can declare, without any fear of contradiction, that I am a citizen with a completely clean criminal record,” Cipollini wrote on Facebook.

He said his lawyers had challenged the Lucca court’s account of events, and that basically time had run out before an appeals court could hear a possible challenge.

Cipollini — nicknamed Il Re Leone (The Lion King) and Super Mario — retired in 2008 after a 20-year pro career. The flamboyant sprinter won the 2002 world title, 160 pro wins, Milan-San Remo , and a record 42 stage victories at the Giro d’Italia.

Cipollini often ran afoul with race organizers and the UCI for his outrageous antics, that included dressing up in a toga ahead of a stage at the Tour de France or racing in a zebra-print skin suit.

In 2008, he was linked to the Operación Puerto doping scandal, an allegation he denied. In 2013, the French Senate released a report that linked Cipollini as one of the riders whose samples from the 1998 Tour de France were positive for traces of EPO when retested in 2004.

Since retiring, Cipollini has remained in the public eye, with appearances on Italy’s version of “Dancing With The Stars” and other reality TV programs.

Cipollini launched his own bike brand in 2010 and November 2025 he underwent heart surgery in Ancona, Italian media reported last year.

title: Valve says it might have to raise the price of supply-limited Steam Machines
author: Kyle Orland
text:
When the Steam Machine first started shipping in June , Valve said it was producing fewer units at a higher price than initially planned because it couldn't secure supplies of scarce RAM and storage components at a reasonable cost. Now, as the last of the initial batch of Steam Machine reservations are finally being fulfilled, Valve says those supply and cost issues will continue into the foreseeable future and may even require a price change.

"We are continuing to build more Steam Machine units, but memory and storage costs continue to increase at unprecedented levels," Valve wrote in a blog post on Thursday . "As a result we don't yet know the number we are able to make, and at what price we'll be able to offer them. The 2TB model in particular will be especially constrained."

title: Airbnb's divisive new house rules come into force
text:
New rules on what Airbnb hosts can reasonably ask guests to do have come into force.

Hosts should now not normally ask guests to wash up, for example, but can appeal to Airbnb if they have a compelling reason.

Some guests have found lists of house rules laborious to complete, with one telling the BBC "it was not relaxing at all".

But some hosts have said that the costs of paying for extra cleaning may have to be passed on to customers.

The new Airbnb rules, announced last month , allow hosts to choose from seven standard house rules, which include determining how many people can stay overnight, and whether or not pets or smoking are allowed.

Hosts can then set additional rules, but guests shouldn't be asked to do the washing up, remove sheets from beds, take rubbish out or avoid using utilities.

Airbnb has begun reviewing listings and will be sending emails to hosts , external "who need to take action" it said.

Hosts can appeal to Airbnb to argue an additional house rule is necessary, and ask Airbnb to approve it.

If the house rule is not approved and the host keeps it anyway, Airbnb will flag this to guests on the host's listing page with a message such as "includes cleaning tasks".

Airbnb said chores can make customers hesitate about booking through the platform, arguing that making house rules "clearer" would increase the number of clients.

But some hosts have said they may have to pass the extra cleaning costs on to guests.

Lisa Clewes, who runs a Welsh holiday let, told the BBC she was "horrified" at the state her guests left the house after a dinner party.

There were broken glasses, drinks cans on the floor, pans full of food on the table and fish guts left in the garden.

Clewes said it typically takes cleaners four hours to turn around her three-bedroom property.

She said guests leaving more mess could mean hiring extra cleaners and increasing costs – expenses that may ultimately be passed on to her customers.

The changes have come as a relief to guests like Jessica Newhook, who says she has been faced with lengthy checkout lists, often on top of hefty cleaning fees.

She booked an Airbnb in Florida for a family reunion of 11 guests and says they had to "leave the property move-in ready for the cleaners", despite paying a $250 (£187) cleaning fee.

"We had rules about everything and it was not relaxing at all," she said.

The new rules have added to growing frustration among owners following increases in Airbnb's commission rates last year.

Many are investing in their own websites and social media to attract direct bookings and avoid platform fees.

Not all hosts are concerned about the changes, however.

Matt Porsz, who hosts and manages other Airbnb properties full-time, told the BBC previously the review system encourages both hosts and guests to behave reasonably.

title: Knicks Bulletin: ‘I was raised by Wolves’
author: Antonio Losada
text:
I thought yesterday’s game was over by the end of the third quarter…

…only for these fools to nearly drop it. Good thing, they did not.

Here’s a bunch of quotes coming off Minnesota as the boys return home once and for all.

On finishing the road trip with a victory over Minnesota:

“Great to finish off a road trip, getting a win in a pretty tough environment by a well-coached team. It’ll make the plane ride a little bit better going home.”

On the Knicks’ fourth-quarter offensive collapse against the Timberwolves:

“Our execution the first three quarters was at a pretty high level against this team. And then you give them credit. Fourth quarter, they did a phenomenal job defensively, kind of bogged us down. The ball and the pace offensively in the frontcourt wasn’t popping like it was the first three quarters.”

On the Knicks winning the battle for loose balls despite struggling offensively in the fourth quarter:

“The thing that saved us was winning the 50-50 ballgame. We were 13-for-14 in that area, and that was huge for us because we had trouble scoring in the fourth.”

On beating his former team as an NBA champion with the Knicks:

“I was raised by Wolves, but it was Knicks in 5 at the end.”

On why the Knicks don’t need to win games convincingly:

“For ‘Dancing with the Stars.’ For us, at the end of the day, as long as we win, this team is just trying to stack the number on the left side.”

On the importance of winning games in different ways:

“If you wanna win a championship, you gotta be ready to win in any way possible, because you never know what the game will be.”

On his uncertain contract situation and remaining focused on his responsibilities to the Knicks:

“I got a job to do, at the end of the day. I gotta come here and put that jersey on and do what’s best for my brothers and the guys they have in my locker room. So, I’m just here to do my job.”

On refusing to let his contract situation distract him from performing:

“I gotta put that jersey on and put the best performance out there for my teammates. So, that’s all I really think about.”

On his emotional attachment to Minnesota:

“I still have so much love for this place. It doesn’t go away. I think it’s actually grown as I’ve been away. I think that, even for me and my dad, we were just driving around the city and just going to places. We went to eat at a spot we love to go here. It always hits home. This is the last place that I got to play basketball with my mom. I got to see the kids be young before now. Jolani, my niece, who was in my rookie of the year photo actually in here, she was a baby, and now she’s in high school. It’s a different part of life, but it’s a part of life that I really enjoy.”

On returning to Minnesota as an NBA champion:

“It’s always great to be home and to be back here. Nine years of my life, some amazing years, amazing moments. Yeah, it’s special to be back. Obviously, it’s bittersweet to come back with a championship because I wanted to win it here so bad for the city, for Minneapolis, for Minnesota, for all the people who haven’t seen an NBA championship here. But it’s great to be able to come back and to be able to see friends, people I call family here.”

On the release of the new Grand Theft Auto game and his excitement to play it:

“I haven’t played the game yet, but I’ve heard it’s a hell of a game. So shout-out to Rockstar [Games] and 2K and Take-Two [Interactive]; they did a good job with that one. It’s fun, man. The world is taken over by ‘GTA,’ as it rightfully should be.”

On his Grand Theft Alvarado nickname and his history with the video game:

“I was a big fan of it before my name. It was just a cool name that I had, so it makes it even better when I play the new one. Got the name for it; now, play the game.”

On how much his life has changed since GTA V dropped:

“Thirteen years ago, I wouldn’t even be talking to you, I promise you that. It’s a long journey, fun journey, one hell of a ride. Still with it.”

On the Knicks nearly blowing their lead against Minnesota:

“It was hectic. We gotta get better at finishing a game like that. But it’s a win, 3-1 on the road trip. We’ll take it.”

On the criticism Karl-Anthony Towns faced during his Timberwolves years:

“Particularly when he started his playoff journey, how much flak he had gotten.”

On Towns leading the Wolves to the Western Conference Finals:

“We don’t do it without him in all facets of the game, whether it be his defense in the Phoenix series, the only guy who held us in the game in Game 7 in Denver when we had nothing else going until we could find it in the second half. Those are the little moments that spring to mind. There are many others along the way. And he kind of grew into that and then was able to build on that with an experienced team where he fit into in New York.”

On watching Towns succeed in the Knicks’ championship run:

“It was fun to see him at the heart of it, too. Especially as they were kind of tweaking their offense going along and all of his skills came to the surface through that.”

On the similarities between Towns and LaMelo Ball :

“They play with a lot of expression to their game and people interpret that or they don’t like that. But it doesn’t mean that A) they’re not super talented players, of course, and B) they can’t play winning basketball. Sometimes it’s as much of the environment that people might be judging them unfairly through, if that makes sense.

“They both are really selfless in the way that they play. But maybe some of their expressions and the way that they carry themselves on the court draws a lot of attention and they get judged unfairly for that, too. They’re actually incredibly selfless. They both play with a lot of joy.

“They’re incredible people. Just great teammates, fun to be around, always bring the same energy every day. Very coachable.”

title: Mauricio Pochettino demands say on all big first-team decisions at Manchester United
author: Will Unwin
text:
Head coach wants control recent predecessors lacked

Indicates he wants more running and focus on fitness

Mauricio Pochettino has told the Manchester United hierarchy he wants a say in all major decisions related to the first team. The club’s transfer business in recent years has received plenty of criticism and the new head coach is eager for a level of control not enjoyed by his recent predecessors.

Pochettino has been given the title of head coach rather than manager but has made plain the power he is seeking, working alongside the director of football, Jason Wilcox, who is in overall charge of player recruitment.

“The way that we work is indifferent to the title description,” Pochettino said. “It depends on the structure, depends on the communication, the relationship with all the areas. I know that being a head coach I am the guy that is going to decide tomorrow the squad for Sunday and I’m going to pick the starting XI. I’m going to make the changes, and of course in the future I would like to be involved in all the main decisions that will happen on the squad. In the end, Manchester United is a football club.”

United’s squad has been heavily scrutinised for being repeatedly outrun by opponents. Pochettino and his staff are known for demanding an intense and relentless style, making fitness a key area of focus.

“That is a debate that I don’t like to go into because I think we cannot talk about things without context, and data is about context,” he said. “If you don’t put context on the data it’s very dangerous to talk and I think it’s easy to manipulate the data, but it’s true that I need to be honest that sometimes data shows something that you can see after on the field. But we are going to be very focused on trying to improve our data, our numbers in every single area of the field, and of course, we are here not to denounce things, we are here to build something.”

Sunday’s game at Liverpool will be Pochettino’s first in club football since he left Chelsea in May 2024. United, 18th going into the weekend , will start bottom if on Saturday Crystal Palace win at Coventry and Sunderland avoid defeat at Aston Villa.

Pochettino has spent the past two years as the manager of the USA men’s national team and said he was pleased to be back in a day-to-day coaching environment. “We were missing [it] a lot,” Pochettino said. “I think we are animals of the grass. We like to feel the grass, we need to smell the grass and try to help the players to improve every day. It’s true that it’s a different job when you are in the national team, but at the same time you learn a lot, and I think we are much better coaches now.”

How does the grass smell in Manchester? “Lovely, because yesterday it rained and today is sunny. It was an amazing morning here.”

Pochettino’s first training session on Thursday was ­overshadowed after it emerged the session had been filmed by a member of the public using a drone . The footage was put on YouTube before being taken down by the person who carried out the filming. They apologised for poor judgment and said it had been “unethical”. United say their security was not breached and will not take legal action but will consider doing so if the same happens again.

United’s chief executive, Omar Berrada, gave a rare interview about the state of the club to Sky Sports on Friday, 24 hours after it was confirmed United’s debt has risen to £1.1bn. “We are laying the foundations for sustained growth to put us in a position where we can be competitive consistently,” he said. “I am convinced that we are heading in the right direction.”

The owners, Berrada and Wilcox have been the focus of criticism from supporters and people outside the club. Berrada believes some of the commentary has “crossed the line”. He said: “Being in this position comes naturally with the criticism and ­scrutiny we’re going to get. We accept it. Some of it is fair, some of it does cross the line. We do live in this world of social media, where people like to generate negative stories about the club because it drives more engagement, and it drives more general noise and activity around the club. But we park that.”

Pochettino is the fourth person to lead the team since Berrada joined in the summer of 2024. Berrada has overseen the sacking of Erik ten Hag, Ruben Amorim and, most recently, Michael Carrick and said of ­Pochettino: “He has a tremendous amount of passion and energy. We see it already in the two days he’s been with us. There’s a buzz about the place, and he’s brought that with his staff.

“He has a very clear philosophy, identity of how he wants to see the team play. And I think he’s coming just at the right time for him and us to be able to help the team and take us forward. He’s equally as ambitious as we are, which is: we want to win titles … I think in Mauricio we bring ­somebody that has just the right amount of maturity and experience at the big clubs to be able to put his arms around the players and to let them perform at their highest potential.”

Berrada worked at Manchester City from 2011, eventually becoming chief footballing operations officer before moving to United. He said in relation to City being found to have breached Premier League rules: “I want to be very clear about this: I wasn’t involved in any wrongdoings. I wasn’t involved in the proceedings. There are no allegations against me.”

title: Filming training by drones should be illegal - Iraola
text:
Liverpool head coach Andoni Iraola says filming with drones around training grounds should be illegal after Mauricio Pochettino's first session as Manchester United boss was captured and uploaded online.

Pochettino and his players were clearly visible in the footage, which was shot above United's Carrington training base from a variety of angles and distances.

The drone operater apologised and later took down the footage, with sources telling BBC Sport they are adamant there was no security breach and that they do not intend to take legal action.

Iraola said he was sent the 12 minutes of footage on Thursday - three days before United travel to Anfield for a Premier League match.

"The important part of this is that it shouldn't be legal," he said on Friday. "It happened to United but it could happen to me.

"Yesterday, when Sky Sports had access to our training and the cameras recorded 15-20 minutes, you know who trained and who didn't.

"It's not the matter of the advantage. It's the fact that someone can do this. There's a reason we train behind closed doors because there are some things that you have to respect. I don't think it's nice for any club."

Ten outfield players were seen working directly with former United States boss Pochettino in the footage, though it seems unlikely they will all start Sunday's match.

"We've faced each other and obviously he [Pochettino] has a lot of Premier League games behind him that we can look at," said Iraola.

"We can look at games from the US but it's true that they have this small advantage that we don't have references to prepare, because they can go different ways that we honestly don't know right now."

Iraola said he expected United to be "well prepared" as Pochettino's assistants travelled to England to work with the players before the Argentine arrived on Wednesday.

"They have this advantage that we don't exactly know - or at least we don't have the references like we do against other opposition," he said.

"Especially the beginning of the game will be important. We have to adapt to certain things. But we know the players very well."

Liverpool are fourth in the table - 14 places ahead of United.

But they have failed to beat the Red Devils at Anfield in each of the past three seasons, and have lost to Arsenal and Manchester City at home already in this campaign.

"You don't find bigger games than this," said Iraola. "I feel lucky to be here and privileged to be a part of these games.

"We have to acknowledge the importance of the game. There are a lot of ingredients. They have a new manager, new challenges for us. This is important for us in a lot of different ways.

"We want to improve our form at home. We have been very good away but not good at home and the first chance we have is United on Sunday."

title: Vinales withdraws from MotoGP Portuguese GP
Yankees 2026 Roster Report Cards: George Lombard Jr.
author: Jonathan Farrar
text:
George Lombard Jr. experienced the highs and lows of a rookie season.

Few positions, or the players manning them, have been debated as intensely as shortstop for the New York Yankees over the last several seasons. Heading into 2026, many fans hoped the club would find a way to move on from the Anthony Volpe experience. However, the club made no external moves and started the season with José Caballero slotted in at the position as the team waited for a rehabbing Volpe to return.

Along the way, injuries and performance, both struggles by the incumbents and red-hot play in the minors, led the Yankees to hand the reins at shortstop over to 21-year-old George Lombard Jr. The rookie would spend August, September, and October at shortstop for the Yankees in what really is the throne of NYC.

In terms of how it went, the staff here at PSA averaged out to a B-minus. In academic speak, that would mean Lombard understood the core material and performed above average, but did not master the assignment.

2026 Stats: 42 G, 166 PA, 23 R, 36 H, 4 2B, 1 3B, 7 HR, 22 RBI, 2 SB, .237/.285/.414, 92 OPS+, 93 wRC+, 0.4 fWAR, 1.1 bWAR.

2027 Contract Status: Pre-arbitration eligible.

Before reaching the show, Lombard was on an absolute tear in the minors. Starting the season in Double-A, he hit .312 with a .971 OPS in 20 games, which earned him a ticket to Scranton. Lombard’s season looked like it might be coming off the rails after an adjustment period, and then he sprained two fingers, which sidelined him for a month and caused him to miss the MLB Futures Game. However, he came back in mid-July and forced the Yankees’ hand right before the Trade Deadline, going on a 14-game heater to the tune of a .377 average, .477 OBP, and 1.081 OPS.

On August 4th, after surviving the Trade Deadline himself, and with the Yankees not acquiring an outside option at shortstop, the club called Lombard up to the show. The kid finished the minor league season slashing .284/.411/.498 with 12 home runs. This performance led Baseball America to name him the Yankees’ Minor League Player of the Year for 2026.

Lombard’s 2026 season at the professional level, and the basis for our grading, really is a story of three parts. The first was a euphoric honeymoon stage. Lombard committed just one error in his first 14 games and racked up eight Defensive Runs Saved (DRS) in his first 100 innings, looking like a potential Platinum Glove winner. This all came as he homered in his first pro at-bat and slashed .320/.393/.560 with a .953 OPS across his first 25 at-bats. It was too good to be true.

After the rise came the fall, as Lombard slumped with the glove and bat. In late August, Lombard made the wrong kind of history, committing an error in six straight games and tying a 105-year-old franchise record. With the stick, big league pitchers started getting him to chase and roll over breaking balls, causing his average to sink to .217 by mid-September. The vibes from some fans really went from “next” to “next Volpe.”

To the kid’s credit, he righted the ship down the stretch and saved himself in the third act. From September 9th through the end of the regular season, Lombard’s defense stabilized to league average, and he hit five home runs in his final 16 games. He carried that confidence into the postseason, going 3-for-4 in the Wild Card opener against Boston and finishing October batting .333 (6-for-18), albeit with an error in the ALDS.

I’ll save the hype train for future preview articles. However, despite only having an 86 mph average exit velocity, Lombard finished the season pacing for 27 home runs over 162 games. There’s also a lot of room for growth, as Lombard had a 17.3 percent walk rate at Triple-A and only a six percent rate in the majors through his first 42 games, or essentially a quarter of a season. The defense, especially when playing beside a big league-quality third baseman, was fine for someone who was just a few months into being able to buy an adult beverage.

Lombard’s minor league season was an A+, while his rookie season comes in at a B-. With some growing pains behind us and a few more likely ahead, here’s to hoping Lombard can continue to improve and develop into a difference-maker. What grade would you circle in red for Lombard’s 2026 season, and what do you predict he’s produce next season?

title: ‘Gloucestershire nouveau’: UK vineyard uncorks its 2026 answer to beaujolais
author: Joanna Partridge
text:
Three Choirs unveils First Release white wine after long, hot summer led to earliest harvest start in 50 years

F orget beaujolais nouveau: a Gloucestershire vineyard has uncorked its 2026 vintage, giving the first taste of this year’s long, hot summer – and an answer to France’s autumn tradition of opening young wine straight after harvest.

Three Choirs near Newent has unveiled its First Release white wine after the earliest harvest in its 50 years of producing wine.

The First Release is what the vineyard calls its “Gloucestershire nouveau” – its tongue-in-cheek nod to beaujolais nouveau, a young, fruity red that is released on the third Thursday in November . Beaujolais nouveau was traditionally made for local consumption and was a way for workers and villages to enjoy the first sip of that year’s harvest.

Vines were first planted on the Gloucestershire site of a fruit farm in 1973, while Three Choirs has been bottling a young wine every November since the 1980s. Customers can buy the wine directly from the vineyard’s shop or try it in its restaurant.

In the 1980s, the harvest used to begin in mid-September, about a month later than it did this year, according to Three Choir’s winemaking director, Martin Fowke.

This year’s prolonged summer of warm temperatures – and rain at the right time – meant the first grapes were picked on 20 August, a week earlier than the previous record set in 2025. The harvest ended on 9 October, by which time 200 tonnes of grapes had been collected across the vineyard’s 30 hectares (74 acres).

The 2026 First Release is a run of 5,000 bottles of a dry, white wine containing solaris, bacchus, siegerrebe and madeleine angevine grapes.

“We now have an extra month to make the wine. We had riper raw material and longer in the winery,” said Fowke, calling 2026 a “record-breaking year”. He added that higher sugar levels and lower acidity allowed winemakers to make a product that was not possible in Britain 30 years ago.

The early timing of the harvest surprised even the Three Choirs winemaker Jack Abbotts, who was on his summer break when picking started. “It’s usually a safe week for me, but this year it all snowballed,” he said.

The changing climate has made it possible to grow grapes on a commercial scale in Britain, but it also brings challenges.

“We found it hard this year,” said Fowke. “People kept saying: ‘This hot weather must be good for you’, but it was difficult because we knew the heat and lack of rain was challenging for farmers. We don’t need it to get any warmer, that’s for sure.”

Vines have been planted as far north as Yorkshire and Scotland , as Britain’s wine industry expands. More than 1,100 vineyards are now registered in Britain.

While Britain remains far down the list of global wine producers in terms of volume – behind countries including Uzbekistan and Tunisia – it is the fastest-growing wine region in the world , according to the property group Knight Frank. The area of planted vineyards in the country has quadrupled since the turn of the century, it reports.

Some of the newer, smaller vineyards do not have their own winemaking facilities, relying on contract winemakers such as Three Choirs. The Gloucestershire vineyard also produces wine for about 40 others, including Llanerch, located west of Cardiff.

English and Welsh wine producers had their second-largest harvest in 2025, when the equivalent of 16.5m bottles, or 124,377 hectolitres, was produced, according to the industry body WineGB.

The data for the 2026 harvest will not be available until early next year, although WineGB said in August it was “optimistic” about the size and quality after the hot growing season.

If the UK climate continues to change and summers such as 2026’s become the norm, Three Choirs may consider growing new varieties. “We can evolve and change, but we would be planting cabernet sauvignon like they did in Bordeaux 50 years ago,” said Fowke, noting the shift from white to red grapes. “But that is not what we set out to do.”

In the fog and damp of November in Gloucestershire, pruning of the vines ready for the 2027 growing season has already begun. “To have two good years in a row is not uncommon, to have three is unusual,” said Fowke.

title: US will soon announce root cause behind FAA nationwide ground stop
author: Jeremy Hsu
text:
The US government will announce soon the root cause of the router outage that led to the third-ever nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration. But questions remain about whether the FAA's effort to modernize the national airspace system is being done with all the proper risk assessments and adequate agency oversight of the private contractors involved.

The nationwide ground stop blocked flight departures and impacted more than 1 million passengers across the United States for more than four hours on Friday, November 13. More than 12,000 flights were canceled on that day alone, with the number rising to more than 20,000 over the weekend as stranded travelers scrambled to find accommodations or alternative transportation. Some international flights were allowed to depart prior to the broader resumption of air traffic.

Nearly one week later, FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told news reporters that government investigators are “very close” to figuring out the root cause of the nationwide ground stop, according to CNN . Bedford also said that Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy plans to announce the findings at a news conference as soon as Friday, November 20.

title: Vinales withdraws after single MotoGP session in Portugal
author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
text:
Maverick Vinales has pulled out of the second-to-last round of the 2026 MotoGP season, replaced by KTM test rider Pol Espargaro.

Vinales, who does not have a ride for 2027 and remains limited by the shoulder injury he sustained last year, is now also in doubt for the season finale in Valencia, which was set to mark his final appearance as a full-time MotoGP rider for the time being.

The 31-year-old has spent the entire campaign struggling to be competitive due to the after-effects of that 2025 shoulder injury at the Sachsenring. A follow-up operation and various courses of treatment have allowed him to recover his fitness for daily life, but when it came to riding in MotoGP he has encountered persistent issues with pain and inflammation.

The lack of any recent competitive track record meant KTM abandoned the plan to promote him to the factory outfit from satellite team Tech3, and he was then left out of Tech3's 2027 line-up, too.

Ahead of Portimao, Vinales said that the weekend off between Qatar and Portugal allowed him to improve his condition - but was wary of how his body would react to riding the KTM RC16 again.

"If I'm riding right now, I mentioned many times, one [reason] is for my salary, and the second is because my team is here, and I want to race for them, and I don't want someone [else] riding my bike."

But on Friday, after placing 19th in the opening practice session, with 17 laps completed, Vinales has called time on his Portimao outing.

"It was a really difficult decision, because I want to keep pushing, but we have decided it is best to stop," he lamented. "The important thing is to avoid any more damage to my shoulder and any dangerous situations on track, and I will continue to focus on my recovery.

"It's disappointing, especially after all the work I've put in to get back here, but I have to listen to my body."

Tech3 says Vinales "will continue to assess his condition" ahead of the Valencia finale.
