title: Yankees sign Jonathan Loáisiga to two-year deal
author: John Griffin
text:
The Yankees bring back an old friend to bolster the bullpen.

So far this winter, the bullpen has been a clear priority for the Yankees, who saw no fewer than four important relievers from the 2026 season become free agents. After re-signing Tim Hill and bringing back David Bednar on the qualifying offer, the team has now made its third addition to the bullpen, coming to terms with old friend Jonathan Loáisiga on a two-year deal with a team option for 2029.

Canal 4 News in Loáisiga’s native Nicaragua had the news late last night, the man himself hinted at it with a picture of the NYC skyline on his Instagram story , and Jorge Castillo of ESPN confirmed it this morning. MLB.com’s Mark Feinsand reported the total outlay of the contract as $18 million across the two years and buyout.

Yankees fans are, of course, very familiar with the man nicknamed Johnny Lasagna. Signed as a minor-league free agent in 2016 after a couple years in the Giants’ organization, Loáisiga spent parts of eight seasons with the big league club, and served as the bullpen’s ace fireman/setup man in 2021 and the second half of 2022. Injuries and ineffectiveness plagued the right-hander for the next three seasons, however, and after a lackluster 2025, the Bombers declined his team option for 2026.

It turned out to be the best thing for him. After sitting on the market for most of the winter, Loáisiga signed a minor-league free agent deal with the Diamondbacks last January. He made the team out of spring training, stayed healthy for a full season for the first time in five years, and put together one of the best seasons of his career, posting a 2.42 ERA in 67 innings. Perhaps more importantly, his advanced metrics were some of the best of his career, and helps explain why there were so many suitors for the recently-turned 32-year-old (the Mets, Phillies, Dodgers, and Blue Jays were all reportedly in on him).

Despite the small time apart, though, Loáisiga is not exactly the same pitcher who Yankee fans remember. Gone are the days where he threw the sinker like Mariano Rivera threw the cutter, i.e., pretty much every pitch. Although it’s still his main offering (he threw it 35 percent of the time last year), that is a far cry from the 54-to-69-percent usage rates from his first Yankees stint; in its stead, he’s upped his changeup, fastball, and cutter.

While nobody would ever consider Loáisiga a strikeout pitcher, these changes oversaw a slight bump in strikeout percentage to 18.4 percent from his 16.6-percent rate between 2022-24 and a slight drop in walk rate to a career-best 5.0 percent, all without sacrificing ground-ball rate. The question will just be how his body holds up after an actual full, healthy season.

Even with Loáisiga, Hill, and Bednar back in the fold, the Yankees are probably not yet done looking at bullpen arms — assuming they ever truly feel like they have enough bullpen arms. At this point, though, the Yankees have successfully turned it from a “need” to a “want,” as they’re no longer so thin out there that Yerry De los Santos and Angel Chivilli were listed as two of the team’s higher-leverage relief arms on the FanGraphs Depth Chart .

One could, of course, absolutely still argue that they still need a big swing-and-miss arm in the ’pen, as they’re still lacking in that regard and not everyone should be a pitch-to-contact guy. As we wait for the league to come to a screeching halt in 10 days due to the owners’ insistence on a lockout, getting some things crossed off the winter to-do list is certainly not a bad thing, and Loáisiga checks another box.

title: SpaceX lenders don’t want Elon Musk launching their collateral into space
author: Michelle Chan, Financial Times
text:
Lenders backing SpaceX’s latest $43 billion debt package, which is secured by its advanced AI chips, have tried to bar Elon Musk from firing the collateral into space as part of his plan for orbital data centers.

The world’s richest man has outlined ambitious plans to power AI models with data centers cooled by the vacuum of space. That will require packing satellites full of advanced chips.

SpaceX has said it plans to use the chips involved in the debt deal on Earth. But lenders have expressed concerns that if the group later decided to shoot the valuable chips that underpin their loans into space, it would prevent them from reclaiming and selling the semiconductors in the event of a default, according to people familiar with the matter.

title: George Hincapie’s Son and Another Rising American Teen Are in Red Bull’s WorldTour Pipeline. How Far Can They Go?
author: ahood
text:
Enzo Hincapie gets promoted to Red Bull's U23 squad in 2027. (Photo: Dario Belingheri/Getty Images)

Two of America’s most promising teens — Enzo Hincapie and Jack Klau — are moving up in the Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe talent pipeline in 2027.

Hincapie, 18, steps up to the U23 Red Bull Rookies after winning the U.S. junior national title.

Klau, 17, signs with the U19 junior team grenke-Auto Eder.

That puts two Americans right in the center of Red Bull’s development train that runs directly from the junior team to the Rookies and on to Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe WorldTour squad.

This is cycling’s version of getting drafted out of high school by the Yankees. Red Bull has one of the peloton’s biggest budgets and is betting big on development, but the odds are still long of hitting the WorldTour.

Could these two up end up as Remco Evenepoel’s teammate in a few years?

Red Bull rolled out its rosters for its two development squads for 2027, and the two Americans both get star billing.

Hincapie — the son of former pro George Hincapie — spent 2026 on Red Bull’s grenke-Auto Eder U19 squad. Standout rides include victory at the U.S. junior title and fourth at the junior Tour of Flanders.

Those results helped earn him one of four promotions from the junior squad to the Rookies for 2027.

That bump is significant because Red Bull is investing heavily on its development programs to build out its WorldTour team.

Four Red Bull Rookies from the U23 squad — Tour de l’Avenir winner Lorenzo Finn , Alessio Magagnotti, Davide Donati and Sebastian Putz — are graduating to Red Bull’s WorldTour lineup in 2027.

“In 2026 we had clear winners. In 2027 we are much more versatile, and that will certainly affect our tactical approach in races, too,” said Tim Meeusen, Red Bull’s director of development. “But the goal remains the same: to develop our talents and bring them to the WorldTour.”

That means Hincapie is now one step behind the WorldTour squad. Two other Red Bull Rookies also signed pro contracts for 2027, so six out of 13 riders will race pro next season.

Budding superstar Finn also raced on the U19 squad and two years on Red Bull’s Rookies before graduating to the WorldTour in 2027 .

Hincapie will have a few years to race at the U23 level, but those are good odds.

The other big U.S. signing is Klau, who signs with Red Bull’s U19 squad grenke-Auto Eder after racing in 2026 on Hot Tubes, one of the top junior teams in the U.S.

Hot Tubes’ alumni list includes WorldTour stars like Magnus Sheffield, AJ August, Artem Shmidt, and Matteo Jorgenson.

Klau also got a taste of European racing this year with USA Cycling’s junior team, with a top 20 at the Course de la Paix Juniors, before a knee injury kept him out of nationals.

“An injury brought my road season to an early end, which definitely wasn’t part of the plan, but it’s also been a year that’s taught me a lot and given me plenty to take forward,” Klau wrote on Instagram.

Talent recruiters saw enough to make Klau one of six new signings on a 12-rider junior squad for 2027. The team also launched a cyclocross program this winter.

It’s a long way from a junior team to the WorldTour, but being inside Red Bull’s structure will give him a good shot.

The promotions also come after a quiet transfer season for the Red Bull WorldTour team.

After signing Evenepoel for 2026, Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe’s only outside transfer for 2027 is Georg Steinhauser from EF Education-EasyPost. The four Rookies getting the bump to the WorldTour squad are Red Bull’s only other 2026-27 market moves.

That makes Klau and Hincapie as the first Americans to be tapped by Red Bull’s cutting-edge development teams.

Like most other major WorldTour operations, Red Bull is betting big on its internal talent program to discover its next generation of stars.

So having two Americans in the pipeline confirms that U.S. prospects are getting noticed by some of Europe’s biggest teams.

Could these two someday races alongside Evenepoel in the WorldTour?

Maybe. At least they’ll start in the pole position.

title: Pontins owner fined £1m over death of woman at Somerset holiday park
author: Matthew Weaver
text:
Wendy Jones, 68, was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at Pontins Brean Sands

The owner of Pontins holiday parks has been fined £1m over the death of a woman who was fatally injured when part of a ceiling collapsed during a bingo game at a fun park in Somerset .

Eighteen people were injured at the Brean Sands site, near Weston-super-Mare, in February 2019 after ventilation ducting and a 40-metre section of ceiling fell inside an entertainment area known as the Fun Factory.

Wendy Jones, 68, a grandmother from Hereford, was sitting in her mobility scooter for bingo with about 100 others when the ceiling collapsed.

She was among six guests to be treated in hospital after the incident and died six months later. A postmortem examination revealed a clear link between the injuries she suffered and her subsequent death.

Britannia Jinky Jersey, the parent company of Pontins, pleaded guilty at Bristol crown court to failing to discharge its duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974.

On Friday the company was fined £1m for the offence. Stephen Bennison, 60, an unqualified contractor who had been employed by Britannia Jinky Jersey to install soundproofing in the ceiling, was sentenced to 10 months’ imprisonment, suspended for 18 months.

An investigation by Avon and Somerset police, Somerset council and the Health and Safety Executive found that the ventilation ducting had originally been poorly installed decades earlier, before the site became a Pontins holiday park. But the immediate cause of the collapse was linked to soundproofing work carried out in 2015 when it was under Pontins’ control.

During that work, Bennison stacked heavy sound-insulation slabs on top of the ventilation ducting, the investigation found. It concluded that the insulation in the ceiling appeared to have been leftover material which could not be returned to the supplier – and stacking it on the ducting served no practical purpose.

The court heard that neither Britannia Jinky Jersey Ltd nor Bennison properly assessed whether the ducting could safely bear the significant additional weight.

Rachael Taylor, a specialist prosecutor with the Crown Prosecution Service, said: “A family holiday ended in tragedy because basic safety responsibilities were not met.

“Wendy Jones had every right to expect she was entering a safe environment. Instead, failures by Britannia Jinky Jersey Limited and Stephen Bennison resulted in the collapse of ventilation ducting and the death of a grandmother who was there to play bingo.”

Taylor said Jones’s death was avoidable. She added: “Those responsible for the safety of the public must ensure work is carried out competently and safely. Our thoughts remain with the family and friends of Mrs Jones, and anyone else affected by this tragic incident.”

title: As the Coalition stares down One Nation in NSW, a new threat is rising: the teals
author: Anne Davies
text:
The opposition’s struggle is creating an opportunity for progressive independents who are boosted by shrewd political operator Chris Minns

Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast

The New South Wales Coalition is facing a renewed threat to its heartland seats on Sydney’s north shore.

This time, the threat is from independent candidates – and they’re backed by the same community activists who put a swathe of teal independents into federal parliament.

The challenge, which has so far remained under the radar, comes as the NSW Coalition tries to shore up its right flank against a surging One Nation before the March state election. This has resulted in the Coalition lurching to the right on issues ranging from gun control to law and order, and, in the case of the NSW Nationals, to abandon climate targets altogether.

As former opposition leader Mark Speakman resigned from the Liberals on Thursday – joining an exodus of MPs announcing they wouldn’t contest their seats in March – he warned his party against becoming “One Nation lite”.

But the move to the right has also created an opportunity for progressive independents running in urban seats usually held by Liberal moderates, with several candidates about to launch their campaigns.

This weekend, Amelia Loye, a management consultant who specialises in stakeholder and community engagement, will announce she is running in the seat of Willoughby, on Sydney’s north shore. She will attempt to oust Liberal MP Tim James, who holds the seat on a 2.6% margin.

Loye is backed by community group Willoughby Votes, which came close to securing an independent in the 2023 election with 47% of the two-party preferred vote.

“Willoughby has already shown it is ready for an independent,” she said. “Nearly half of voters backed one last time. I want to earn their support, and the support of those still deciding.”

She joins high-profile candidate Elouise Massa , a small business owner, who became a household name after campaigning for Northern Beaches hospital to return to public hands after her toddler’s death in emergency.

Massa will run in the Sydney seat of Manly against Liberal Adelaide Cuneo, who is seeking to replace the retiring MP, James Griffin.

The independent deputy mayor of Mosman, Michael Randall, announced last weekend he will run in North Shore as a community independent. Several of the people behind former independent federal MP Kylea Tink’s campaign are supporting him.

Monica Wulff, another independent, has announced a run in Davidson.

Voters on the northern beaches have already sent two independents to Macquarie street – and both have a good chance of being returned.

At the federal level, teal independents Sophie Scamps, Zali Steggall and Nicolette Boele hold McKellar, Warringah and Bradfield respectively. Tink held North Sydney for one term before the seat was abolished .

The NSW Liberal party is not giving up on the northern beaches and the north shore, despite the trend towards independents.

“We’ll keep making our case directly to voters, including why we oppose Labor’s gun buyback that targets law-abiding owners rather than criminals and terrorists,” a Liberal spokesperson said.

This time, however, the independents have a boost in the form of NSW Labor premier, Chris Minns .

During the final weeks of parliament before the NSW election, Minns joked that independent Jacqui Scruby, who won Pittwater at a byelection, should be known as “the member for Mona Vale road” for her tenacity in seeking an upgrade. It’s now being fast-tracked by the Minns government.

Minns has also appeared with Massa, and praised her for her advocacy.

But Minns, a shrewd political operator, has not fallen in love with independents – he’s just hedging his bets.

A year ago, with the Liberals languishing in the polls, Labor could have expected to increase its majority in 2027. But with One Nation storming to a primary vote as high as 30% in some polls, that prospect has dimmed.

In the current parliament, Labor has support of three independents – Greg Piper, Joe McGirr and Alex Greenwich – to ensure confidence and supply for its minority government. An expanded crossbench would give more options and provide a buffer for Labor losses to One Nation in western Sydney, the Hunter and possibly the Central Coast.

If all independents were successful – and that is a big if – almost the entire north shore region would go to state independents, except the seat of Wahroonga.

Most of the commentary about the 2027 election has focused on the likely Armageddon facing the Nationals, who could lose as many eight or nine of their 11 seats in the regions.

But a teal wave also remains a threat to the Liberal party, especially as the Coalition try to position themselves to fight off One Nation in the regions with policies that don’t sit well with urban voters.

One Nation could also prove helpful to independents if it makes good on its promise to run candidates in every seat. The party is more likely to shave votes from the Liberal primary vote, making it easier for the independents to overtake the Liberal on preferences from Labor and the Greens.

NSW’s optional preferential voting makes it hard to predict how strong flows will be – and it depends what parties advocate on how to votes. But in 2023 only 41% of One Nation voters nominated preferences, compared to 70% of Green voters and 49% of Labor voters.

The opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, has not ruled out either a preference deal or a post-election arrangement with One Nation, describing such options as “hypothetical”. But if they do end up preferencing One Nation, it may alienate moderate Liberals and ultimately work against them.

Disclosure: Anne Davies worked as a media and policy adviser to the independent federal MP Sophie Scamps from October 2023 to October 2024.

title: These US fishers see offshore wind as a ‘godsend’. Trump wants to shut it down
author: Hilary Beaumont with photographs by Simon Simard
text:
Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream

O n a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island.

“God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy.

Souza and his three-man crew were fishers by trade, but this trip was different. Instead of fishing, they were working for Sea Services North America, a co-op funded through contracts with offshore wind developers.

It was welcome work for these fishers who weather a legally restricted scalloping season. Sea Services retrained the fishers to work in offshore wind and gave them a second stream of income. But this work put them at odds with other fishers who viewed offshore wind as an existential threat to their industry.

Commercial fishers have sued wind companies, arguing that the projects could displace them from their traditional fishing zones and wreak havoc on marine ecosystems (US fishers are allowed to fish in wind-lease zones , except for 500-metre exclusion zones around construction sites, and construction can have positive and negative effects on marine life).

Yet, now, in New England, a cooperative of about 200 fishers is challenging the idea that offshore wind and the fishing industry are natural opponents. Sea Services North America trains and equips fishers to support offshore wind construction, an opportunity that provides them with a second stream of income.

Sea Services pays each fishing boat $4,500 a day plus fuel. Souza, who was initially skeptical of offshore wind, says the opportunity has been a “godsend”.

That godsend, however, may soon come to an end. Since returning to office last year, Donald Trump has systematically attacked offshore wind projects, saying his goal is to not allow any “windmills” to be built. In January 2025, the president issued an executive order halting construction of five offshore wind projects on the east coast.

Sea Services North America was founded in 2020 by another once skeptical fisher. Gary Yerman, 76, had been fishing for more than four decades when he began hearing about proposed commercial-scale offshore wind projects. He and other fishers feared the windfarms could harm their industry. He didn’t want windfarms in his fishing zone, but he believed they were too big to fail. “They’re gonna win,” he thought, deciding to cast his lot with the projects.

In 2019 he and Gordon Videll, a friend and local lawyer, visited Northern Ireland, where they met with fishers who were working with developers building offshore windfarms and other structures. “We saw how it was benefiting the fishermen there,” Yerman said.

Videll noticed that the local fishers drove nice cars. “This provided a real annual income, which, if you’re raising a family, it means everything,” he said.

They returned to the US eager to find a way to bring similar benefits to their fellow fishers – which meant earning the trust of a skeptical industry.

“There was a lot of fellas that were very angry because we joined in on building these windfarms,” said Videll, Sea Services’ CEO. “Nobody trusted it.”

They convinced just one fisher to give it a shot, and over time, more joined.

The pandemic, which struck just as Sea Services was getting off the ground, may have helped Yerman and Videll’s recruitment efforts. As restaurants closed , demand for seafood fell, meaning fishers in New Bedford and nearby fishing towns were looking for extra work. “People had to make decisions they might not have made otherwise,” Videll said.

They found a relatively eager labor pool in local scallopers, who work on boats that are legally restricted from fishing more than 36 days a year to prevent overfishing, leaving the owners of these highly specialized boats looking for extra sources of income during the off-season, said Capt Jack Morris, who owns a fleet of scallop boats including the Pamela Ann, and joined Sea Services in 2021.

“It’s a huge benefit Sea Services has brought,” Morris said. “With the [scallop] fishing season being so short, they are able to continue buying groceries, paying insurance, taking care of the house.”

Stacy Alexander-Nevells, a business owner who works with Sea Services, runs a 19-boat commercial fishing operation with her father. Their boats mostly harvested scallops, but revenues were inconsistent and federal restrictions were always changing. “Working with Sea Services was another income stream,” she said. “We had to diversify. Now the boats aren’t just sitting at the dock, and the guys aren’t unemployed.”

At first, Souza was on the fence about working in offshore wind because most fishers perceived it as working for the enemy, but two decades of scalloping had taken a toll on him. Shucking scallops at a commercial pace eventually causes arthritis, carpal tunnel and rotator cuff tears. Souza lost the tip of a finger, and said he probably has arthritis. “I saw the writing on the wall that scalloping is more of a young man’s game than us older guys,” Souza said.

To date, Sea Services says it has paid vessel owners and fishers a total of $34m for their work at several commercial-scale windfarms. And those benefits have extended to the broader community, Morris said.

“These boats just tie up after their 36 days, but with the windfarm work, they keep going,” Morris said. That means more work for onshore businesses like mechanics, welders, carpenters, electricians and painters, he said.…

title: From plumbing to Picnic PostNL – The Dutch team's newest recruit with dreams of Amstel Gold Race and riding with Wout van Aert
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The lowest-ranked team in the WorldTour last year, Picnic PostNL , have made plenty of changes to their roster next season, with nine new faces and counting.

Joining the Dutch team in their quest for more success in 2027 is Belgian racer Daan Depuydt , who comes on board from Continental squad Baloise Verzekeringen-Het Poetsbureau Lions.

The 23-year-old, who previously raced at amateur level, enjoyed several standout rides this year, including a Tour de Limousin stage win and three top-10 finishes at the Tour de Wallonie. His rise to the WorldTour has been a rapid one, given he was working as a plumber just a few years ago.

Depuydt, who also did odd jobs as a gardener and electrician, told that, "Actually, I was never really consciously focused on landing a professional contract. I just raced because I enjoyed it."

He primarily raced on the mountain bike as a junior, picking up four Belgian titles before struggling with back injuries. On the road, he raced in Belgium with amateur squad VP Consulting before catching the eye of Baloise-Het Poetsbureau – Sven Nys' team – with a stage win at the Triptyque Ardennais in 2025.

He hit the ground running this year, with June's Tour de Wallonie only the second UCI-ranked race of his career after the Antwerp Port Epic in May.

"I was riding there with broken ribs, because I had a bad fall 2 days before the opening stage," he told . In August, there was another top ride in Limousin, where he finished second on the opening day before winning stage 3.

"After my second place in the opening stage, I wanted to win one of the remaining 3 stages at all costs. And in the third stage, I struck gold," he said.

"After the opening stage, I suddenly started receiving messages from teams. But I never thought I'd actually secure a spot – especially after reading an article about how many riders were still without a team for the season."

Soudal-QuickStep were among the teams to show interest, though they were already full for 2027. Choosing Picnic PostNL was a no-brainer, he said, despite recent reports of a 'culture of fear' at the team.

"When the moment finally came to put pen to paper with Picnic PostNL, I didn’t have to think twice. I had a good feeling right from the start of our conversations. They prioritise the riders' interests and are always open to feedback," he said.

"Sure, it’s a strict team, but name me one WorldTour team that isn't. As a team, you have expectations of your riders, and vice versa. That dynamic can – and should – be a bit strict, provided it’s handled fairly."

Depuydt sees himself as a puncheur who excels on shorter climbs while also sprinting well from a small group. He's hoping to race on his home training roads at Amstel Gold Race next season, and is dreaming of racing alongside his idol, Wout van Aert – a goal which shows just how far he's come since his plumbing days.

"I see myself as a puncheur. Short climbs suit me thanks to my past as a mountain biker. But I have also noticed this year that I am fast. I am not a pure sprinter; I am too light for that. But after a tough race, I can finish well in a reduced group," he said.

"I've never ridden a race with Wout. I would think it's really cool if that happens next year. If we stand at the start of a race together, I will look for Wout and ride behind him for a bit to take a look at him.

"If I could just follow him for a little while on a climb, that would be a huge dream come true."

title: WorldTour team ignored by new Collective Cycling Group reform project
author: Patrick Fletcher
text:
The nascent Collective Cycling Group (CCG), a coalition of teams bidding to overhaul cycling’s economic model, did not seek the involvement of all the WorldTour teams, with Human Powered Health telling they were ignored by the project.

The CCG, which is the new version of the failed One Cycling movement, launched publicly on Wednesday , with 24 teams coming together in a bid to "unlock the value potential of professional cycling".

Not all 32 teams from across the men’s and women’s WorldTour agreed to sign up to the new company, with Tadej Pogačar’s UAE Team Emirates the most notable of the teams who have declined to be involved.

However, one WorldTour team, Human Powered Health, were not even approached.

A spokesperson for the US outfit, which has operated in the Women’s WorldTour since 2022, told that senior management were not made aware of the CCG nor of any opportunity to take part in such a project.

The complete overlooking of an established WorldTour team raises early question marks over the unity of the CCG, which was described by its CEO Oliver Ciesla as a “broad and inclusive initiative”.

Furthermore, it was not billed as a closed shop, with the announcement stating that discussions with other teams are ongoing.

The project is largely made up of WorldTour teams but two second-division men’s outfits, Pinarello-Q36.5 and Tudor Pro Cycling are shareholders in the company, too.

Contacted on Friday in relation to Human Powered Health's position, a spokesperson for the Collective Cycling Group said: "CCG has brought together a significant group of leading professional cycling teams, and we are open for that group to grow over time."

title: Rocket Report: A weekend of ups and downs; Stoke celebrates engine milestone
author: Stephen Clark
text:
Welcome to Edition 9.20 of the Rocket Report! Last weekend was a picture of the US launch business in miniature, and emblematic of the opposing trajectories of two of the nation's most experienced rocket makers. First, on Saturday, SpaceX completed a perfect midair catch of its Starship upper stage at its launch pad in Texas after spending nearly a day in orbit. The Super Heavy booster was lost at sea, but SpaceX proved it can recover that piece of the rocket on previous flights. While SpaceX showed it is well on the way to fielding a fully reusable rocket, United Launch Alliance suffered its first-ever total launch failure with the Vulcan rocket. That is terrible news for not only ULA, but also the US Space Force and Amazon, which have booked some 70 launches on Vulcan over the next few years. Your faithful correspondents will take a break from the Rocket Report next week for the Thanksgiving holiday, so we'll see you again the first week of December.

As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar.

Europe's leading satellite startup eyes Italian rocket maker . Finnish satellite developer ICEYE announced Tuesday that it is seeking to buy Italian rocket-maker Avio for more than $2.2 billion in a transaction aimed at creating Europe’s first true vertically integrated end-to-end space company, Ars reports . Avio builds the Vega C rocket, a solid-fueled launcher designed to carry up to 3.3 metric tons (7,300 pounds) of payload to low-Earth orbit. ICEYE is, by far, the most successful space startup in Europe, with a valuation of more than $12 billion after the company's most recent fundraising round in June.

title: Black Friday Wahoo deals 2026: Kickr Core 2 hits best-ever price, Elemnt computers on sale too
author: josh.croxton@futurenet.com (Josh Croxton)

With summer behind us, thermal bib tights back in rotation, and a winter of hiding from the rain on Zwift on the horizon, that can only mean one thing: Black Friday is fast approaching.

Like mine, I expect your inbox is full of Black Friday promotions, and the latest to land in mine is a huge Black Friday Wahoo rundown; a list of everything we can expect from Wahoo Fitness, the cycling tech mainstay from Atlanta.

Wahoo's own Black Friday sale kicks off today - November 20th - with deals across smart trainers, indoor bikes and treadmills, but there are plenty of other deals if you know where to look.

So no matter if you're shopping for a new smart trainer, a bike computer, a heart rate monitor, or even a treadmill, you're in the right place to find the best price and the best advice.

If you want to take it a step further, you can add on the Zwift Ride v2 smart frame too. This still uses the Kickr Core v2, but the frame replaces your bike, saving you the need to wheel it through your house. It's also more widely adjustable, so you can share it with others in the house. View Deal

Wahoo is slowly branching out into running, and the Kickr Run is its first foray into treadmills. I've not used it, but the general consensus is that it's very good. View Deal

Whether running or cycling, if you're doing it indoors you'll want a really good fan to help keep you cool. This is still the gold standard in that space, and although the price is steep, mine is still running strong after seven years of regular use. View Deal

This is a bit of an odd one as Amazon says its retail price is 624.99. That's not true, it's actually $499.99. However, it's still a nice discount on the biggest model in Wahoo's GPS computer range. View Deal

In our opinion, it's likely the best for most people. Great navigation, great features, and very user friendly. View Deal

This one's the smallest model in the range. It's perhaps more of a racer's choice, but it also packs more or less all the features of the Roam into a smaller package.

That means it's cheaper still, but the smaller screen can be limiting in some cases. View Deal

This is the same as the product above, but with the Zwift Cog and Click add-on, which replaces the cassette with a single-speed cog that's compatible with all modern groupsets. The 'Click' then lets you shift virtually in-game, which is silent, unlike the loud clunk you sometimes get from a derailleur. View Deal

But before you commit to the V6, consider this, which is potentially better and currently the same price.

The Kickr Move uses the same internals as the current Kickr smart trainer, but adds a moveable track to allow you to roll forward and backward under high load, and a few degrees of left-right tilt too.

In use, the left-right tilt makes for a slightly unusual ride feel, since it doesn't self-centre like a bike. I often felt I was fighting it with core strength or simply sitting at an angle. View Deal

The Zwift Ride V2, paired with Kickr Core 2, is the whole-bike indoor solution, saving your own bike from the wear and tear. Its broad adjustability also means you can share it with others in your home, or try out new positions without changing the fit on your main bike. View Deal

If you want to go even more premium than the Zwift Ride and Kickr Core pairing, this Kickr Bike Pro is it. It's broadly adjustable, tilts back and forth to mimic gradients, it's belt-driven so had a completely silent operation, and shifting is silent too. View Deal

Or a halfway house between the two, the Kickr Bike Shift, which offers the quiet operation and broad adjustability, but foregoes the tilting and a few other features to keep the price down. View Deal

Wahoo is primarily a cycling-focussed company, but it's slowly branching out into running, and this Kickr Run is its first foray into treadmills. View Deal

The Kickr Climb lets you simulate gradients of up to 20%, by literally lifting the front of your bike up and down, to make things feel all the more realistic. It's a useful addition to your setup if you're trying to train for riding up long climbs and you want to mimic the position. View Deal

The Roam barely needs an introduction. It's the goldilocks GPS in Wahoo's range, balancing price, screen size and battery life nicely. View Deal

This one's the baby of the range. More of a racer's choice, but it also packs more or less all the features of the Roam into a smaller, cheaper package. View Deal

And finally, if you want the biggest screen possible for your bike computer then it has to be the Elemnt Ace. It's really very large, the battery is bigger, but of course, so is the price. View Deal

You can easily make do with a simple fan for indoor training, but if you want to have a better time you can get a smart fan like the Kickr Headwind. It'll either work as a dumb fan (just turn it up and down as needed) or you can set it to increase power in line with with your heart rate monitor, so it'll blow stronger the harder you ride. title: An entrepreneur fights for workers’ protections after his mom was fired after being assaulted at her Saks Fifth Avenue job
author: Victoria Bekiempis in New York
text:
Jeff Vinokur is using his newly minted wealth from the sale of his edtech company to hold the retail store accountable

L ate in the afternoon of 28 June, Jeff Vinokur received a call from his mother that sent him running. “I was assaulted,” Vinokur, a popular science educator known as the “ Dancing Scientist ”, recalled his mother saying.

Vinokur’s mother, Laza Susuni, was working in the women’s ready-to-wear section at Manhattan’s Saks Fifth Avenue that day when a client attacked her in the dressing room. A court document reviewed by the Guardian corroborates that a woman was arrested at that location on assault and harassment charges.

Vinokur, 36, who was in New York City visiting Susuni, bounded out of bed, threw on clothes and rushed to the famed department store – not even taking a moment to brush his teeth. Susuni, who said she was kicked in the stomach, was evaluated at a hospital.

While Susuni, 62, was discharged from the hospital later that day without permanent physical injuries, she reeled from panic.

“I could not sleep at all,” said Susuni, who came to the US from Russia as a teen. “I was just so afraid that … she would just come back [to] hurt me, to punish me, and just send somebody to stab me because they put her in handcuffs in front of her own children.”

Susuni said she asked Saks for five days off to recover from her anxiety. She claims that the company instead terminated her.

Vinokur sprang into action, contacting lawyers because he believed that surely such a firing would be illegal. When an attorney said there wasn’t anything he could do, Vinokur thought: “This guy is an idiot, this cannot be, let’s go talk to other lawyers.”

They spoke with about 10 attorneys. “They all say the same thing: that there is no law that protects [against] this,” Vinokur said.

Now Vinokur is taking it upon himself to push for change in New York law to provide broader legal protections for workers against firing if they have been the victims of violent crime on or off the job.

While an employer almost certainly would not tell an employee they were fired for being a crime victim, a workplace might effectively do so by taking issue with things like time off or medical requests, or make spurious claims about lapsed job performance in the wake of the crime.

Alice Jump, a partner at the Reavis Page Jump law firm, said “it doesn’t seem rational” for an employer to behave in such a way, but imagines they might use “taking a lot of time off, or being distressed or emotionally or physically compromised”, as an excuse to terminate a crime victim.

While there are some laws on the books in New York state and city that protect workers from firing in relation to being crime victims, there are limitations. New York state human rights law bars employers from discriminating against, or firing, people because they are victims of domestic violence.

New York state law also prohibits employers from penalizing or firing crime victims for taking time off to appear in court or meet with prosecutors, so long as they give notice of the absence. New York City law makes it illegal for an employee to be fired because they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, said Jump.

“So if it’s a non-sexual assault, then you’re not specifically covered,” Jump said. “The law doesn’t extend to all crime victims.”

For Jump, it seems that amending legal protections to shield employees who suffer other assaults or violent physical attacks wouldn’t be difficult. “Any kind of assault or violent physical act – you shouldn’t be fired because you’re a subject of that.”

There is no federal law providing termination protections for crime victims, Jump also said.

As part of Vinokur’s campaign for change, he launched a website, Saksfiles.com , outlining not only his mother’s situation but several other alleged instances at Saks stores where former employees have claimed they were fired in relation to being purportedly victimized.

Vinokur, who holds a PhD in biochemistry from UCLA, is also using the media savvy that propelled him from quirky science educator to edtech founder – and vast resources following the sale of his company – to launch an ongoing, in-person protest against Saks.

From 12 November, Vinokur is paying anywhere from more than one to several dozen people to stand outside Saks every day toting signs with text such as “MY MOM IS THE 7th VICTIM. BEATEN AT SAKS. THEN FIRED. I WANT ANSWERS.” Vinokur said that he will pay them to hold signs outside Saks every single day from 1 to 7pm throughout the holiday shopping season – and potentially indefinitely.

“There’s a power element of this – a billion-dollar corporation, the disposable minimum wage worker who is my mom,” Vinokur said. “To me, it’s like: wait a second, I have power now.

“I have this $100m startup exit. I was majority shareholder,” he said. “I don’t have a boat. I don’t fly private. It’s not my style – but I can hold them accountable in a way that I think maybe nobody else can.

“It’s a paid protest. We’re owning it,” he continued. “It’s a very unusual way to go about it, and that’s because I thought: well, if we just go hold signs for a day, nobody cares.”

Vinokur didn’t originally set out to change the system. He wanted Saks to be held accountable. “It was the realization that they got away with this, that they did this to my mom, and they got away with this because there’s no law against it.”

When they couldn’t take legal action, Vinokur then set his sights on the possibility of protest – maybe signs that said “My mom was beaten here and fired.” He then started thinking through the plan “as a scientist” – would anyone care about a beating? “It’s shocking, but that’s not crazy.”

Vinokur started doing research to see whether anything similar had happened at a Saks store. An internet search yielded another example, so Vinokur deployed AI to further research other allegations of crime-related termination and found more.…

title: From aero pockets made on a dining table to skinsuits worn by Mark Cavendish – How one rider took Nopinz from Devon to a world-leading 'everyday aero' brand
author: Andy McGrath
text:
A couple of thousand years before bike racing even existed, Plato had it right: necessity is the mother of all invention.

An elite racer in the UK finishing at the sharp end of the country’s time trials on highways and byways, Blake Pond was getting into an unwanted routine. He would lovingly spend several minutes getting his race number pinned perfectly for every time trial. It was a need, driven by aesthetics, aerodynamics and fastidiousness.

When he jumped on the bike, rode off and heard a ripping noise, he knew what it meant: gigantic pinholes in a speed suit which had cost a week of his bike shop mechanic wages. The alternative fate was just as undesirable: he would pass riders with numbers flapping like parachutes. "On the drive back, I was thinking there’s got to be a better way of doing this," Pond tells over coffee.

His solution: a stretchy pocket, as you’d find on a documents-enclosed envelope, stuck on a skinsuit with special adhesive. Initially, the idea went in his training kit drawer for a few years, doubting its mass appeal. But he was drawn back to it after hearing other racers airing their frustration or even yelps of pain from competitors accidentally getting stuck by a pin-wielding friend trying to give them perfectly flat race numbers.

In 2014, Nopinz was born with the SpeedPocket. At first, it was just Pond, his computer and a heat press. The next iteration involved using a seamstress to sew in this aero addition before posting the garment back.

In little more than a decade, his company has gone from the dining room table in the Devon town of Bideford in the south-west of the United Kingdom and a self-explanatory brand name to more than 50,000 orders and the WorldTour , with a range of apparel and aerodynamic accessories tailored for TT, road racing, triathlon, running and indoor cycling. The WorldTour teams and riders supported along the way include Mark Cavendish on his record-breaking 'Project 35' stage-win quest at the Tour de France .

Nopinz wouldn't be where it is today without the community’s explosion of interest in aero gains over the last decade. "How optimised everyone’s got in TT is crazy. When I was racing back in 2014, I had a lot of watts but not a lot of aero," Pond reflects. "And now it’s shifted the other way completely. I’m going the same sort of speed as I was back then, off 15 per cent less power."

An aero obsessive, Pond climbed a lamppost at the 2015 Tour de France prologue in Utrecht to take photographs of riders from above. This obsession feeds their comprehensiveness, testing products in the wind tunnel at Silverstone, prototyping in-house and doing fabric tests.

WorldTour recognition for 'everyday aero' kit

"We always test and market the averages. If we test at 40, 45 and 50 [km/h] and nought to seven degrees of yaw, we’ll average it out across the speeds we’re aiming that product at," he says, implying that they do not cherry-pick certain data for marketing. Alongside the weighted model designed to better reflect real-world riding conditions that he mentions, theirs is a competitive price point: their popular Sonic socks cost £24.99.

Pond has tried to keep their pricing reasonable, though he is aware of the perverse "reassuringly expensive" philosophy that can pervade in the sport. More expensive does not necessarily mean better. "We need to make the margin in the suit and obviously get profit out of it, but it comes to a stage where you’re making it up, really. Sometimes that does happen with other brands – I can’t understand why the suits are so pricey when we can do it [for cheaper] and do all the R&D," he says.

For the founder, Nopinz suits are for the person who can’t spend £20,000 in a wind tunnel. "Maybe we’re doing it more cost-effectively. There’s a ceiling price: we want to be that reliable sort of partner: you know you’re getting a really good product and it’s not stupidly expensive. That’s how I see it really: NoPinz – everyday aero."

As the framed and signed jerseys around their HQ in the Devon town of Barnstaple attest, the WorldTour wanted a piece of their watt savers too. Starting with support for LottoJumbo-NL in 2015, riders from the likes of FDJ, Israel-Premier Tech and AG2R have all benefited. Alex Dowsett bought his own skinsuits from the company and wore one to win a 2020 Giro d’Italia stage .

The company became an official TT partner to WorldTour team Intermarché the next season, giving it visible "additional credibility" after years of secretly supplying ingredients to the bunch, without recognition or under an NDA.

Pond says Nopinz was offered a full clothing partnership with the Belgian squad but couldn't accommodate the approximate £500,000 outlay, nor the quantity of kit. "That sort of commitment would be crushing," he says.

Still, teams or riders came calling with projects – and you might be surprised at how disorganised and last-minute pro cycling can be. One of the company’s latest nights on the job involved working with takeaway boxes after Israel-Premier Tech realised several days before the Tour de France start that they had sent the wrong designs for their special edition skinsuits. One of their coaching team drove from the south of France to Devon, got a few hours’ kip in Pond’s campervan while Nopinz put on a production run of 50 suits, turning it around in 24 hours in time for him to drive to the Grand Départ.

Cutting-edge materials and UCI pushback

There is a knick-knack sign in Pond’s home which says 'One bike ride away from a good mood'. He was inspired to get in the saddle by hearing tales of the sport: his grandfather, Lew Pond, was a rival of British track sprint icon Reg Harris and was selected for the 1948 Olympics in tandem racing.

After starting in triathlons, he moved to the family’s legacy sport and quickly noticed his bike leg was his strongest. Becoming an elite-licensed racer, he finished seventh in the British national TT championships, although being knocked off by a car led to a back injury which stopped competition between 2014 and 2024. Now back pinning on numbers using his own SpeedPocket – and winning time trials galore in the UK’s south-west – being in the racing environment helps him to understand his customer base and generate ideas.

Pond regards himself as a "fake CEO" and more a hands-on, jack of all trades, doing everything from business direction, budgeting, R&D, product design and social media to fixing machines, using his old bike mechanic nous. Reinvestment in his company has often been preferable to status symbols: when he had the money to consider buying himself a Porsche, a new laser cutter for Nopinz took priority.

Investing in the cutting-edge was worthwhile for their latest skinsuit, the Hypersonic Mk2, building on their original, double-layered (base layer and skinsuit) aero iteration. "We dared to be a bit different with it," he says.

Top speed-suits use a lot of the similar striped fabric on the sleeves, which he dubs 'Super Stripe'. Pond and Nopinz collectively spent four years looking for an aero, textured fabric that would be faster.

A year and a half ago, he found his Eureka material from a company on Italy’s Lake Como and christened it Speedcell. It wasn’t cheap, coming in at roughly £45 a metre at orders of 250 metres minimum, but worth every penny. From a rudimentary aero test, switching from the former material to the new one, the basic prototype showed measurable gains, and they made improvements to the fit. It looks different – sci-fi, even – it feels different, and their testing proved that it saved watts.

An ongoing challenge for Pond is keeping up with UCI regulations . In 2022, the sport’s governing body banned the SpeedPocket at mass events after a consultation with a working group of manufacturers. It was a bitter pill to swallow. "Brands started to cotton on to it and were doing their own versions, but the trouble was, you could hardly see the numbers," he says.

Economic challenges, sustainability, and 'Project 35'

Governing body caprices are just one blast in the face for a business that has faced "one headwind after another" in the last five years.

The vast majority of the cycling industry can relate.

He estimates raw fabric costs have risen "15 to 20" per cent, likely due to the increasing cost of oil and the raw materials used. War has a knock-on effect, with the Russia-Ukraine conflict causing a spike in prices.

Shipping costs have also risen considerably, and Brexit added complications. While Pond produces in the UK, fabrics are bought from European nations or ones outside the continent, bringing pressures associated with import and export.

"Because the industry has been so negative and there’s been so much discounting, you can’t pass it on or win it back," he adds.

From Nopinz’s side, wage inflation and increased National Insurance contributions have added approximately £90,000 to their wage bill across a team of 15, which has been streamlined in recent years.

It all means the customer feels the pinch. A European client will have to pay VAT and additional tariffs as well as possible fuel charges and surcharges from delivery operators, even though Nopinz do customs duties and taxes paid now (i.e. settled by the sender) to try to mitigate nasty surprises. With all the added costs, a would-be buyer might easily abandon their shopping basket and drop off. "That’s been quite hard to navigate," Pond says.

It has become harder to manufacture in the UK and make a profit. Nopinz has been flat in terms of growth in recent years, but making a profit, which he perceives to be rare. "We’d obviously love to see Nopinz go back on that growth trajectory, but we don’t want to do it at the expense of being a sustainable business," he says.

In a crowded market of apparel makers at similar price points, Pond expects they will focus more on the high-end side of the sport and the pinnacle. "I feel that’s where we can differentiate ourselves as a brand," he says.

"We want to have products that people go ‘I’m racing, this is super important, I’ve trained really hard, and I want to make sure I invest in the kit.’ We want them to think Nopinz when it comes to cycling products."

"Being small is good. We’ve got the Speedcell now, and we’re already looking for the next thing – we’ve acknowledged we’ve done that, now someone else is going to do that, and the only way we can stay one step in front is being able to rapidly prototype and produce something," Pond says.

"In a company with a lot more management and structure, it might take two years for a product to be conceived and actually find its way to market. Whereas for us, it can be 10 days if we have to, like something to do with Cavendish."

Ah yes, collaborating with the greatest sprinter in the sport. As office dogs Rodney and Cassandra pad in and out of the HQ boardroom to the whirr of air compressors, Pond locates a pair of surprisingly small white shoes with a blue Nike tick which belonged to the sprinter extraordinaire.

Yes, Nopinz was part of 'Project 35'. Nopinz brand ambassador Alex Dowsett, a fellow aero geek, went to the wind tunnel with Cavendish in the middle of 2024 and called Pond, wanting to fine-tune every possible aero gain in his pursuit of the record.

Turning round prototypes and testing them at Silverstone rapidly, Nopinz worked up toe overshoes ('Hypersonic Tovershoes') and eye-catching textured, shoelace covers. "We tried to simulate the texture of the laces, while also tidying up the aero around the Boa [dial]," he says.

There was also what would become the Hypersonic Mk2 socks, initially called P35, with V-shaped aero chevrons. However, Pond was mindful that, due to UCI equipment rules, anything used for competition has to be on the market. "I said ‘put them on [the website] for £1,000 so nobody buys them’ – and somebody did," he says.…

title: Only the Seminole Tribe can offer online gambling in Florida—and they're furious at DraftKings
author: Cyrus Farivar
text:
Last week, DraftKings asked a federal court in Florida to take over a lawsuit recently filed against it by the Seminole Tribe, opening another front in the nationwide online “swaps” debate .

In the new lawsuit, the Seminole Tribe contends that two of DraftKings’ current online offerings—the fantasy sports-style “Pick6” and the “Super App” sportsbook—are “illegal" in Florida.

title: MLB, college sports, and the sports propaganda moment
author: John Griffin
text:
When we’re in school, we hear a lot about propaganda. American history textbooks show us political cartoons from the late 19th and early 20th century about the abolition of slavery, the rise of industrial robber-barons, and the progressive movement. European art historians discuss how Louis XIV used paintings and sculptures to present himself as the “Sun King” as he strengthened the power of the French crown over the First and Second Estates. In my own Roman history classes, I spend multiple weeks demonstrating how the emperors employed literature, history, sculpture, and construction projects to assert the supremacy of both Rome and the imperial household. Whether in middle school, high school, or college, students regularly grapple with propaganda in their history classes, learning how people with access to communicative resources have been able to present their own version of reality to sway public opinion in their favor.

Once we’re out of school, though, propaganda falls by the wayside, and ceases to be a concern. It exists, in the public consciousness at least, not as a part of our lives, but as a historical oddity, the behavior of a bygone era — or, when it’s acknowledged in the modern world, as something that happens in the nebulous “over there,” not “here.” And yet, what else can we call the flood of political advertisements in every commercial break that made the World Series borderline unwatchable if not propaganda? After all, are they not trying to sell their version of reality, as opposed to that of their opponents, in an effort to sway voters?

Propaganda is most often understood in terms of politics, but it doesn’t have to be. And right now, we’re living in what I call a sports propaganda moment, as two major entities — the NCAA and Major League Baseball — have gone on the figurative warpath, spending millions of dollars in advertising not to get people to watch their product, but to generate outrage from fans on their own behalf against that of their players.

Whether you’re a fan of a power conference school who competes for the national championship every year or a small liberal arts college who celebrates when their team gets blown out during the March Madness tournament because that meant they made it in the first place, you’ve almost certainly been exposed to commercials sponsored by the Saving College Sports organization in support of the Protect College Sports Act. Since the start of the 2026 college football season (and in truth, since last bowl season, as commercials in support of the bill ran even before it was officially introduced in Congress back in June), they have run a massive ad campaign encouraging fans to contact their congressional representatives and pressure them to vote yes on the bill. Backed by multi-million athletic programs and employing household names such as Deion Sanders and Nick Saban (a current coach and a former one, respectively), these ads center the conversation about the bill on the legitimate concerns fans have about today’s Wild West NIL era — namely, the constant transfers — while ignoring the fact that the bill attempts to, as much as legally possible, reassert the extreme levels of control that the conferences and schools used to have over their athletes.

Starting in the middle of the summer, Major League Baseball has rolled out their own ad campaign in preparation for the upcoming lockout, which is now just a week and a half away. Focused on MLB.tv and social media, the “Level the Playing Field” campaign directly argues for the implementation of a salary cap and floor, claiming that the league cannot have competitive balance due to the payroll disparities that exist between small- and large-market teams. These ads ran all summer, during the All-Star Game festivities, the postseason, the World Series, and the awards season. While, ironically, this meant that t he league plastered everywhere a chart in which the team with the second-highest payroll, the Mets, missed the playoffs as the team with the second-lowest payroll, the Rays, won the pennant, the very fact that the league spent time and energy publicly fighting the players during what should be the biggest annual celebrations of the sport is a testament to their priorities — and the important role that these ads played in their pre-lockout preparations.

Now, obviously, these two situations aren’t 100 percent comparable. Decades of corruption and a refusal to negotiate common sense solutions with its players forced college athletes to turn to the courts for assistance, and once the courts got involved, federal involvement and oversight was all but guaranteed, and all the political machinations that entails. Major League Baseball, meanwhile, is attempting, for the second time this decade, to use the expiration of the Collective Bargaining Agreement as an opportunity to break the power of the players’ union and implement the salary cap that they believe will see franchise values skyrocket . Sure, the almighty dollar may be the driving force for both the NCAA and MLB — both the Protect College Sports Act and the salary cap are, at their core, attempts to rein payrolls in and ensure cost certainty — but each organization is so fundamentally different from the other that their financial systems are incomparable.

Nonetheless, the fact that both collegiate athletics and professional baseball have adopted the same tactic, large-scale propaganda campaigns meant to turn the fans against the players, reflects the unique historical moment we are in. As we saw during the last CBA negotiations, social media has allowed players to interact with fans directly, allowing them to, for example, directly argue against the league’s propaganda, much like Jameson Taillon did last week.

Last time around, this direct connection between players and fans appeared to help the players in the negotiations, as the players were able to successfully mock the league’s insistence on removing all evidence of players’ likenesses on all media. That being said, should there be a disconnect between the fans and the players, this has the potential to backfire on the players, and perhaps this is what Major League Baseball is going for here. Baseball may be in the midst of a renaissance, but that doesn’t mean the fans don’t think that some things need to be fixed. Deferred money, especially when done to the extent the Dodgers have in recent years, has been regularly mocked in baseball-related online spaces. The rise of gambling has resulted in real, concrete ethics concerns. Blackouts, TV restrictions, and an ever-increasing stable of required streaming services have made watching the games a veritable chore. Solving none of these problems requires a salary cap, and yet, the league has tried to use their media machine to tie all of them to it, to limited success. In fact, it may have backfired just a bit: the frequency with which they have said “this proposal is contingent on the players accepting a salary cap” has sparked quite a bit of mockery online.

Of course, what has sparked such a large push for a cap at this time is the fact that this CBA negotiation might be the league’s best guaranteed opportunity for one in the foreseeable future. The Dodgers and the Mets have giftwrapped the league two bogeymen to use to sway fans to their side in the negotiations: between the former’s willingness to exploit deferred money and their acquisitions of Shohei Ohtani, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Rōki Sasaki, Blake Snell, Kyle Tucker, Edwin Díaz, Tanner Scott, Tyler Glasnow, Teoscar Hernández, and Tarik Skubal over the last three years, and the latter’s willingness to ignore all luxury tax thresholds and common sense to sign whatever hot free agents they can, there’s quite a bit of ammunition to turn fans of small- and medium-market teams against the owners. The Players’ Association, meanwhile, has been in a bit of disarray this year, with Tony Clark one of several union executives shown the door within the last 12 months; while it’s unclear whether this will actually harm the union in negotiations, turmoil at the top can at least give the impression of weakness to an ownership group looking to make major gains.

Together, these scenarios have things ripe for Major League Baseball to push all their chips to the center of the table and try to get their salary cap, as it might be their best opportunity for a while. And so, the propaganda machine spins on.

title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
author: Mark Sweney
text:
Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies

Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said that the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month-on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency.

The surge in sales is a welcome bounce back for the industry after a poor September , which the ONS has revised down from a 0.4% fall to a 0.6% fall, fuelled in part by poor online sales of autumn and winter clothing because of unseasonably warm weather.

“Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government’s ‘Be Ready’ campaign,” said Grant Fitzner, chief economist at the ONS.

Food store sales, primarily supermarkets, rose by 0.8% month-on-month, the fastest rate since the 1.4% rise in April.

Textile, clothing and footwear stores reported a 1.5% month-on-month boost. An increase in visits to galleries, and a jump in sales of sports equipment, games and toys, lifted sales across other non-food stores by 3.1% month-on-month, the biggest rise since January.

The total non-food stores category – which includes department stores, clothing, household and other non-food stores – increased by 1.1% month-on-month in October.

Non-store retail sales, primarily online but also sellers such as street stalls and markets, bounced back too, rising 0.9% as a turn in the weather last month drove sales of autumn and winter ranges.

However, sales volumes of motor fuel fell by 2.2% last month, the steepest rate since April, as prices at the pump rose.

“October’s retail sales have exceeded expectations, despite low consumer confidence and growing pressure on household finances from higher interest rates and inflation,” said Erin Brookes, European retail and consumer lead at Alvarez & Marsal.

“Retailers will be feeling optimistic as the sector approaches the critical Black Friday and Christmas trading period, with October’s sales growth suggesting consumers are still willing to spend this festive season.

“Despite this positivity, retailers are caught between increasingly price-sensitive consumers and mounting operating costs.”

title: 'There is certainly no bitterness' – Case against truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin won't continue due to his ill health
author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
text:
The hearings into the case of Wolfgang Rieke, the truck driver who struck and killed Davide Rebellin , have concluded with no charges brought.

Two years ago, a first-instance trial concluded with Rieke being sentenced to a four-year jail term after hitting and killing Rebellin in 2022. However, the Venice Court of Appeals ruled last week that Rieke is unfit to participate in an appeal trial, so the case has been dropped, according to the news agency .

Rieke, 66, currently resides in a nursing home after suffering a stroke in 2024, and this summer his lawyers obtained a doctor's report on his psychological and physical ability to participate in the trial. The report concluded that Rieke is mentally unable to stand trial.

"The family acknowledges what happened. There is certainly respect for the judicial decisions and today's. There is certainly no bitterness; there is acknowledgement and respect for his health," said Rebellin's family's lawyer, Davide Picco.

"Justice has certainly worked, given that the Prosecutor's Office transferred the defendant from Germany to Italy. He served several months in prison and then under house arrest. His health condition then led to today's sentence."

Rieke, who had previously pled guilty to a non-fatal hit-and-run and drunk driving, struck and killed Rebellin as he was on a training ride in Montebello Vincentino on November 30, 2022, shortly after he retired from racing. He then fled the scene, leading authorities to launch a multi-country search.

He turned himself in to German police in June 2023 and was later handed a four-year sentence after the judge rejected several initial plea deals. After suffering a stroke two years ago, the case against him will not continue.

"We are satisfied that the judges have accepted our requests, acknowledging Mr. Rieke's current health conditions, which prevent him from consciously participating in the trial," said Rieke's lawyer, Andrea Nardin, according to the Corriere del Veneto .
