title: Science has a home here at Ars—please help keep it that way
author: John Timmer
text:
It's now been 21 years since I first published an article at Ars Technica. It has been the only home I've known as a writer, and it has been essential to my development from scientist to blogger to journalist. It's no exaggeration to say that Ars has helped make me who I am today.

So, asking you to support Ars via a subscription is very personal (and a bit selfish) for me—I'd like to stay here! Jobs that give you this sort of independence, that let you both edit and write, are very rare in journalism, and I'm unlikely to find another. Helping secure Ars' future through your support will mean I don't have to.

But I'd rather make a case for why you'll benefit from supporting Ars. In fact, I'll make three: the writing, the people, and the community.

title: Knicks 102, Timberwolves 99: “3 straight on the road, what’s up…”
author: Moritz Wollert
text:
As their beautiful offense waned the Knicks’ D took over against Minnesota.

LaMelo Ball hit one of his patented three-pointers from the left elbow early in the third quarter against the New York Knicks last night and as the crowd cheered, he proceeded to jog back on defense. Of course, the only not totally broken Ball brother couldn’t let the moment pass without completely indulging himself into a thoroughly scripted “ice in the veins”-gesture that feels as original these days as a two-handed set shot. Just a moment later Josh Hart rained on the parade, running directly by Vanilla Ball’s D and finishing an easy backdoor cut with a simple layup. And just like that the Knicks were up 14 again, ignoring the protocol of how cutting a deficit to 12 in a game where your team got handsomely dominated up to that point needs to be celebrated.

It feels good to root for a professional team, doesn’t it? It will allow you to say things like Real Clydes Wear Plaid shared in the Postgame Thread and which I unapologetically stole for the headline of this recap. The Knicks won their third game in a row at Minnesota last night and they probably made it a lot harder than it needed to be. Their opponents certainly had something to do with it, no matter how ill-advised some individual emotions might have been. The Timberwolves can play tremendous defense, are as long as those trees in their logo and have an aggression you could certainly link to that name-giving animal of them. They got a good albeit cranky coach, a proven system, years of winning experience. Yet in the end they also got LaMelo Ball now.

We get that he is a talented, at times iconic passer; we also get that he has found his footing fairly well on the frozen tundra near the Great Lakes so far. But we really can’t get convinced that you can ever really win big with a “talent” like that. His play can remind one of the game young kids play before they really get a hang of Dr. Naismith’s rules. They also take two steps before every dribble, then four after they pick the ball up. They also couldn’t care less about a repetitive shooting motion or dribbling the ball without palming it every time. With the kids it’s okay and fun, we let them discover themselves as players and excuse it. But Lamborghini LaMelo should be held to a different standard, he is supposed to be a professional NBA player after all.

Luckily for the Knicks, they got plenty of real pros on their roster, guys who truly care about winning and treat their profession like it means something - not only to them but to others. It certainly seemed that way when they played most of the game last night with a level of calmness and concentration that has been a hallmark of theirs ever since they went on that beautiful championship run last year. But despite all their dominance over that two-month stretch in the playoffs, you can’t ignore that they are a team with plenty of cracks in their armor, many of which showed themselves last night as well. It’s the kind of weakness that are often the reason for the Bockers falling behind big only to have the opportunity to stage their beloved monumental comebacks later on.

Yesterday the Knicks offense completely bogged down late when Minnesota went to more switching on D (raise your hand if you’ve seen that before), neutralizing all the beautiful team basketball that helped the Gotham Gang run up an almost 20-point lead earlier. Not even Karl-Anthony Towns, once again mesmerizing for most of the night against a traditional five at his old stomping grounds, couldn’t regain his first-half form. Maybe he rode the pine a little long, Mr. Brown? Well, you can’t play him all 48, we get it. A lineup that included Jose Alvarado, Andre Drummond and Josh Hart was still an interesting choice, to say the least. For all the individual chops it’s quite a load for Jalen Brunson to carry that group offensively, it almost feels like him heaving big AD up K2 or some other majestic mountain. It might get you to the summit against certain defenses but considering some defenses are as long and physical as the Wolf Pack, it can also get cold rather quickly. Especially when Brunson still hasn’t found his touch inside the paint yet.

That New York could still pull it out in the end is a testament to timely plays and a gritty, opportunistic defense that at no point in the game relented to the physically imposing Wolves coming at them. When LaMelo Ball couldn’t find someone open downtown, the canines’ only plan was to ram their oversized combo forwards ahead. It worked here or there but never consistently. Watch out, there’s an extended arm coming at you - boom, another offensive foul! It’s an interesting yet understandable choice by the league to make the off arm a point of emphasis this year (sorry, SGA). Why didn’t they do the same for palming the basketball or taking more steps than a dressage horse? Your guess is as good as mine.

For the moment, though, let us not worry about it - there is a win to be celebrated. For all we know though, our guys are probably watching some film right now and preparing for their next opponent (Portland on Saturday). Maybe they are also speeding race cars through some busy pedestrian zone or practice their one-legged step-back fadeaway jumper that has netted them less than 42 percent shooting for their career?

Nah, we leave that to the guy with ice in his veins.

title: Trump admin still won't let Wi-Fi giant TP-Link sell its latest routers in US
author: Jon Brodkin
text:
TP-Link, which may be the top provider of wireless routers for US homes and small businesses, isn't allowed to sell its latest Wi-Fi routers in the US. The Trump administration imposed a sweeping ban on foreign-made consumer routers in March 2026, and TP-Link hasn't been able to obtain an exemption.

The rules prevent the import or sale of all new router models that are manufactured, assembled, designed, or developed outside the US. The Trump administration has control over which router makers receive special permission to import and sell new products through a waiver-review process involving the Federal Communications Commission, the Department of Defense, and the Department of Homeland Security.

While some of its competitors have obtained exemptions to the ban, TP-Link appears to be having a hard time making its case to government officials. Its routers approved before the March 2026 ban remain available for sale in the US, but its newly released Wi-Fi 8 routers cannot be imported or sold.

title: US reacts cautiously to Myanmar genocide ruling as EU praises ‘critical’ role of UN’s top court
author: Jason Burke
text:
Reactions to ICJ ruling underline global divisions over court with China raising concerns about judicial overreach

The US has greeted with caution the world’s highest court’s ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority, while China has raised concerns of judicial overreach.

Reactions to Thursday’s historic ruling underlined deep international division over the role of the court and similar institutions. The international court of justice (ICJ) had never previously found a state responsible for genocide and the decision could set a precedent for future genocide claims, notably a case against Israel .

The EU hailed a “landmark” judgment from the ICJ, while the UK reaffirmed “full support” for the court and the international legal order. Australia called on Myanmar to comply fully with the judgment and its obligations under international law.

But China, which has offered rare international support for Myanmar’s military rulers since they seized power five years ago, highlighted “issues such as jurisdiction overreach and expanded interpretation”.

“China … believes that such practices are not conducive to the settlement of disputes,” the foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, told a news briefing when asked about the ICJ ruling. “The international community should make joint efforts in this direction to avoid complicating this issue.”

Western nations cut ties with the unstable and poor south-east Asian country after the 2021 coup that ousted a civilian-led government.

Myanmar’s presidential spokesperson said on Friday that the ruling was “unfair”, noting the judges’ nine to six vote. The country’s military rulers have denied carrying out a genocide, claiming their actions targeted a Rohingya militant group that conducted insurgent attacks.

“When we look at the result, not all 15 judges agreed with the decision,” said Khaing Khaing Soe, speaking at a press conference in the capital, Naypyidaw. “So this was not a unanimous decision … I would say it is not fair.”

The US state department said on Thursday that Washington was examining the judgment, while stressing the need to avoid “politicisation” of the ICJ.

Donald Trump’s administration has taken a dim view of international law, vowing to dismantle the international criminal court (ICC), but has yet to question the legitimacy of the ICJ.

The state department reiterated US support for the people of Myanmar and said it shared “grave concerns over the continued abuses of human rights against Rohingya Muslims and members of other minority groups”, noting that the US was the largest single humanitarian donor to the Rohingya humanitarian crisis response.

In Brussels, the EU said Myanmar must fully implement the ICJ’s ruling “without delay” and that “compliance with ICJ’s decisions is not optional, it is an obligation under international law”.

“The European Union holds the ICJ in the highest regard and remains steadfast in its support for its critical role in the peaceful resolution of disputes and the upholding of the rule of law at international level,” an EU spokesperson said in a statement .

“The Rohingya people have endured immense suffering, including displacement and violence, and their plight must not be forgotten. This landmark ruling underscores the imperative of justice for victims and the necessity of upholding international law.”

The UN secretary general, António Guterres, called the ruling “a demonstration of international justice and a reaffirmation that impunity for such horrific acts must not stand”.

The UK expelled Myanmar’s defence attache and called for measures to “ensure the court’s ruling sends a clear message that such crimes cannot be committed with impunity”.

The ruling caps a lengthy legal campaign since August 2017 when Myanmar’s military launched what it called a “clearance campaign” in Rakhine state in response to an attack by a Rohingya insurgent group. Reports rapidly emerged of mass rapes and killings by security forces, as well as the burning of thousands of homes.

Judges rejected Myanmar’s claim that its actions were primarily intended as counter-terrorism operations, or even that they were an attempt to punish or forcibly displace the population but without committing genocide.

The country’s leader, Min Aung Hlaing, who headed the military during the 2016-17 attacks, has a pending arrest warrant from the ICC – which, unlike the ICJ, prosecutes individuals and not states – on allegations of crimes against humanity.

The former general overthrew the elected government of Aung San Suu Kyi, triggering a civil war that has left tens of thousands dead. He was installed as civilian president in April after elections that were widely discredited .

While the ICJ does not have the power to enforce rulings, its decisions are considered binding, carry diplomatic weight and can shape international action, including sanctions.

Under the 1948 convention, to establish that genocide occurred the court had to find that there was an intent to destroy the Rohingya “in whole or in part”.

About 1.2 million Rohingya refugees now live in Bangladesh, primarily in crowded camps across the Cox’s Bazar district, where they endure harsh conditions marked by fire hazards, infectious diseases, monsoon landslides, inadequate sanitation and strict work restrictions.

Judges at the court based in The Hague have also been asked to rule on other allegations of genocide.

South Africa has accused Israel of breaching the genocide convention during its offensive in Gaza, a claim Israel vehemently denies. That case is years from completion. An interim ICJ judgment in 2024 ordered Israel to ensure its forces do not commit acts of genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.

Ukraine also has a case pending against Russia . Shortly after Moscow’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, Kyiv accused Russia of fabricating genocide claims against Ukraine to justify the attack.

title: China Offshore Tax Clampdown Pushes Budget Into Rare Surplus
author: Bloomberg News
text: China’s budget swung into a rare surplus in October, as tighter scrutiny of offshore wealth produced a one-off bonanza of individual income tax receipts and offset a long-awaited increase in fiscal spending.

title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
author: Bruce Schneier
text:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

I t’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system – and that’s where the core problems lie.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.

Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies – and, additionally, all other positive intangibles – out of a company in pursuit of those profits.

Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.

From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful … until something bad happens.

But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.

The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyber-attack – both human and AI-fueled – and more susceptible to random mistakes.

The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.

We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation – with enforcement and meaningful fines – and stringent antitrust enforcement.

But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to implement – especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.

Bruce Schneier is a security technologist who teaches at the Harvard Kennedy School at Harvard University and the University of Toronto’s Munk School

title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
author: Henrietta Moore
text:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

A I is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

The World Economic Forum finds analytical thinking is now the skill employers value most, and estimates that 59 in every 100 workers will need training to adapt to this shift by 2030.

In September, I found myself at the first Global Brain Economy Summit in New York asking a hard question: how much room is there for creativity and learning when one’s mind is consumed by anxieties about paying rent or for food to last through the week?

There are two new indices that rank countries and US states on brain capital, using about 60 indicators ranging from child poverty to the prevalence of Parkinson’s disease. Yet they both possess a flaw: neither measures whether people’s livelihoods are secure – whether income is predictable, debts are manageable or homes are safe. The World Health Organization counts safety and security among the foundations of brain health, but nobody building these indices asked people what drains their mental capacity.

I call this missing liability “cognitive taxation”. It is a tax no government voted for, levied on attention, memory and the capacity to learn, and collected through rents, debts and welfare paperwork. Worry over insecurity runs in the background like an app draining a phone battery, and over years, the chronic stress wears down the brain itself. And AI is raising the rate.

Livelihood pressures stack up to exceed what one mind can handle. Poverty manufactures its own interest payments. Imagine a week in which a worker’s rent goes up and she loses a shift at the last minute, something common for workers without guaranteed hours. She puts the shortfall on a credit card. Preoccupied with finding the rent, she returns a benefits form late and loses part of her benefits payment as a penalty. Three small setbacks leave her household poorer in money, headspace and health.

Financial scarcity measurably impairs how well people think, but the effect lifts when the pressure does too, according to a 2024 analysis of 112,000 people in the Journal of Economic Psychology. Low-paid workers in rural India who received their wages a few days early were 7% more productive and made fewer mistakes. When South Africa lowered the pension age for men from 65 to 60, those who became eligible earlier showed slower memory decline and were about five percentage points less likely to develop dementia.

Though AI is increasing the value of human judgment, it also increases cognitive taxation. Automation makes work less predictable, shifting and shortening schedules, long before it eliminates jobs, as Walmart staff dealing with AI-set schedules have found. Meanwhile, overseeing AI tools also adds mental fatigue, according to research by the Boston Consulting Group. Workers required to retrain for the AI economy will struggle to learn new skills if their minds are already occupied by worries over pay, housing and debt.

Britain shows what insecurity already costs before AI adds to it. About 2.7 million people there are out of work through long-term sickness. And my institute’s research found that people facing insecurity across several areas of life carry an earnings penalty as large as the gender pay gap, one that roughly doubles after seven years. Those findings suggest that worry erodes how well people work. Now the UK’s AI minister says the government must seriously consider that the tech could have “ an unprecedented impact ” on the jobs market. Worries abound and compound.

When Elon Musk told reporters at the White House in September that AI would bring “universal high income”, he offered Silicon Valley’s favourite answer to job losses: cash. Yet a study funded by Sam Altman, giving low-income Americans $1,000 a month, found that mental health gains faded after the first year. Extra cash helps, but it cannot guarantee a place for your child at a nursery or a bus that gets you to work on time. These pressures already tax the minds of people in work, and no payment removes them.

The better answer to cognitive tax and job loss is universal basic services, providing childcare, housing, transport and digital access, free at the point of use. The principle is the one behind the UK’s National Health Service: people should be able to rely on essential support without facing a bill when they use it. Extending free childcare alone is expected to bring 60,000 non-working parents into jobs in the UK.

Every government should ask this question of every fiscal policy: how will this policy affect the cognitive load of the poorest people it touches? Britain, which takes over the G20 presidency after December’s summit in Miami, should put it to the world’s largest economies. This question belongs in every treasury’s fiscal plans, brain-capital indices and AI-powered public services before they launch.

Sixty years ago we learned to count the damage economies do to the air and water, and it has changed how we build infrastructure for the better. Now that AI is making our minds the most valuable thing we have, it is time we count the damage done to them.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

title: ‘Weak and dizzy’: the secretive ICE force-feeding tactics that ended a Cuban father’s hunger strike
author: José Olivares
text:
Exclusive: Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez says in messages to Guardian from inside Texas facility pain of force-feeding caused him to break strike

T he text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border , on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment , and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants , a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Pérez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.…

title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 11/20/26
author: Madison Pavich

After locking down David Bednar’s contract for 2027, there were overnight musings that Jonathan Loáisiga reportedly is coming back to New York after a year away in Arizona. title: Why a 37-year-old Primož Roglič is still a great signing and how more freedom at NSN can unlock his five-time Grand Tour-winning best
author: James Moultrie
text:
The further into the off-season it went, the more likely it seemed that five-time Grand Tour winner Primož Roglič 's career was going to end before he wanted it to.

It wasn't like most of the big-name moves in modern cycling, which are signposted months in advance, but it did finally bring an answer to the question that Roglič had been answering with "We'll see, ah" and "I don't know yet" ever since July, when Red Bull team boss Ralph Denk confirmed he would be leaving.

The idiosyncrasies that have made him one of the peloton's most popular and compelling riders won't be going anywhere, instead just repackaged in the Swiss team's colours for, as they described it, the "final chapter".

Though it should be noted that Roglič hasn't ruled out a similarly complicated re-up of his time in the sport 12 months from now, more openly putting it down to needing "some time to figure out how to make a chapter in my life where I am peaceful, but the answer is actually simple with the team name: Never Say Never."

Tudor, Pinarello Q36.5, Unibet Rose Rockets, and XDS Astana were among the other speculated landing spots for the Slovenian, but clearly none could muster up the perfect mix of financial resources, a fitting contract, or the desire to bring him in, but NSN have found room for the GC star.

Importantly, it means that instead of a nondescript 68th-place finish at Il Lombardia, 37-year-old Roglič is now in control of where his final chapter as a professional comes to an end, and he certainly won't be looking to go out with a whimper.

"I still believe I have some work to do – in both racing and with myself," he said, when his surprise move to NSN was announced on Wednesday evening. "I have the drive and also the attitude not just to race, but also achieve things."

After his home heroics in Slovenia late in the season, Roglič will start his 12th year in the WorldTour as the reigning European time trial champion , which he wasn't even sure he'd get to wear in a race after he won it: "Maybe I'll only wear it at home. Because we haven't decided yet what I'll do next, but no matter what, I'll wear it."

Off the bike for 10 days and unsure if he would have even taken the start if it wasn't where he lived, Roglič's late-season results should be looked at with the context that what he did was nothing short of miraculous when it came to recovery. This is far from the sort of moves that saw the then Israel-Premier Tech – which was rebranded as NSN a year ago – criticised as something of a "retirement home ".

Roglič may be a veteran, but he is still one of the top riders in the world.

Roglič raced 53 times in 2026, with mixed success, but importantly, still with success.

He opened up his campaign with a solid performance at Tirreno-Adriatico, finishing fifth overall and helping teammate Giulio Pellizzari to third on GC behind winner Isaac del Toro, and followed that up with more success in Italy by taking third at Milano-Torino.

From here, things slowed down for the Slovenian, finishing 16th at Iztulia Basque Country, and failing to impress at the Tours de Romandie and Suisse as compatriot Tadej Pogačar dominated the racing to take both titles. Roglič only managed 18th and eighth overall, respectively.

He turned things around at the Slovenian national championships, ramping up his performance with a win in the ITT and fourth in the road race, ahead of his already confirmed major goal of the Vuelta, where he was looking to stand alone at the top of the history books for the most overall titles – which he currently shares alongside Roberto Heras on four.

However, it was soon after, on July 31, that Roglič revealed he had been halted in his plans: "Got hit by a car few days ago…" read a post on his Instagram. "I won't be participating in San Sebastian and in Burgos unfortunately... not the best scenario, but it's life, eh. Now it's all systems go towards La Vuelta; we work and hope things will turn around!"

He did make it to the Vuelta, and while there were no of old – as it was Enric Mas who stepped into the spotlight and claimed red after Pogačar crashed out – when all was said and done in Granada, Roglič could only describe second as feeling "like a victory to me".

Mas rightly took the majority of headlines as he made history for Spain, but there was a more visceral reaction from the press room as second-place Roglič answered his final question in the longer post-race press conferences. It felt like a goodbye to the race where he had enjoyed his most successful moments, with no one in the room, nor he, knowing where he'd end up next as the room filled with applause and matching gratitude from the Slovenian.

The same feelings returned at European Championships and Il Lombardia, where the enigmatic Roglič was none the wiser, still saying, "You never know when is the last one. Like everything in life, it can be a bit emotional," as he conceded that the Italian Monument could be the endpoint.

Into the off-season, Roglič next resurfaced at the Taiwan Cycling Masters, where a KOM challenge south of Taipei saw the Slovenian drop no hints at whether he'd signed a contract – instead, he continued to be cryptic in his comments.

"The people that you collect on the way, or they collect you, that you have around, they help the influence at the end on you," he said in a promotional video for the event.

"I think yes, they left a mark on me, like I said I'm always open to learn, to know more, and the more you know, the more you know that you don't know, so it's a never-ending process."

Well now we do know, as does he, that life in the pro peloton will be continuing, and while those previously ruthless punchy legs perhaps lack the same bite they had five-eight years ago, he has a diesel engine that can still power him up the highest mountains.

In his best results at the Europeans and Vuelta, it's key not to forget that it wasn't against weak fields by any means; at the former, Bruno Armirail, Stefan Küng, and Jakob Söderqvist were among those unable to live with Roglič's time, and at the latter he emerged ahead of Giro runner-up Felix Gall, new teammate Richard Carapaz, and Oscar Onley for his second place on GC.

How he could fit into NSN's plans

Even with Roglič clearly proving his worth as an asset into his late 30s, there still remains the question of how NSN will deploy their new leader and fit him into their schedules after such a late pick-up.

The team's media day is next week, and the thoughts will already be on December and January training camp ahead of the start of the 2027 season on January 1, with rider schedules among the news set to be confirmed in the coming weeks.

With Carapaz, Santiago Buitrago, and Lennert Van Eetvelt, NSN had already been looking to improve their stock as a GC-hunting outfit, having failed to finish in the top 10 of all three Grand Tours in 2026. Their best results were 12th at the Giro, 68th at the Tour, and 15th at the Vuelta, but with those three mentioned above and Roglič, they suddenly have a chance at finishing in the top 10 and potentially higher of all three.

Carapaz has already suggested that it is a return to the Giro where he wants to target an overall placing, and while this would seem to interfere with a potential Slovenian homecoming for Roglič, it's actually the Tour and Vuelta that look like more likely targets.

Sharing the leadership among their new star signings lessens any chance for internal bickering, and also opens the door to Carapaz potentially chasing GC at one Grand Tour and then stages and the mountains classification at another – as he'd been doing successfully for EF in recent years.

NSN's new foray into the GC hierarchy also represents more freedom for a rider like Roglič, who has been bitten by bad luck and crashes several times in the most pressure-filled moments riding for Visma and Red Bull – teams where you to maintain GC success to keep your spot.

Roglič should get the freedom to pick the plan which suits him best and allows him to build up in the ways he knows will work for GT success. NSN will also offer up what Red Bull didn't in his final Vuelta for them this past summer, where a young team lacking in climbing support saw them struggle to front up numbers to muster a major challenge consistently against Mas – even if it likely would have had no effect on the final red jersey standings.

NSN can commit their younger riders Buitrago and Van Eetvelt, and the experience of George Bennett and Nick Schultz to a full-blown Roglič bid, be that at the Tour or Vuelta. And while in an age of Pogačar, Vingegaard, Evenepoel, Seixas, and Del Toro, any entrance into the top-five seems unlikely, this summer proved that anything can happen, even to the big stars, with Pogačar crashing out of the Vuelta and Vingegaard from the Tour, so it's not out of the realms of possibility that he is able to score one final Grand Tour podium, which would be his 10th, or indeed a sixth victory.

In reality, Roglič's goals could become a final stage win at the Tour – to add to the three he already has, 10 years after his first into Serre-Chevalier on stage 17 of the 2017 race – the GC title at the Tour de Suisse, which remains the only major one-week stage race missing from his palmarès from the seven, or indeed that elusive fifth Vuelta title.

Even with Pogačar probably taking the start, living by the words "Never say never" has got Roglič this far, and he'll be hoping his new team's name can carry him to the last hurrah which he deserves. There's a degree of risk in not allowing that European title win on home roads to become the denouement to his great career, but as one Slovenian famously said en route to one of his Vuelta titles: "No risk, no glory."

title: How to get a bigger Black Friday bargain: cashback, price matches and gift cards
author: Hilary Osborne
text:
From cashback on what you buy to cut-price gift cards, we offer tips on how to maximise savings on your shopping

With Black Friday on the horizon, retailers are already offering discounts, and over the next few weeks you can expect to see more price cuts as they attempt to entice us to open our wallets.

It could be a great time to snap up the things on your Christmas list or buy household items you need yourself. And there are ways to maximise your savings on Black Friday – which this year falls on 27 November – by doubling up on discounts, or earning cashback on your purchases.

Assuming you have shopped around for a good price and are sure you really want what you are about to buy, here are some ways you can make the bargain even better.

There are many ways to earn cashback – and you can often stack up more than one.

Some of the big banks pay cashback on purchases made with their debit cards, with offers linked to specific retailers. Lloyds, for example, runs the Rewards programme, which has cashback deals with a rolling cast of retailers. Santander has the same type of programme called Santander Boosts and Barclays runs Blue Rewards.

Current deals for Lloyds customers include 14% cashback on purchases from Dyson, 8% on the smart-ring maker Oura and 10% on FatFace. If you take advantage of Dyson’s Black Friday deal for a Ball Animal multifloor cleaner, for example, on top of the retailer’s £100 discount, you will get another £39.20 back when you use your Lloyds card to pay – bringing the price down to £240.79.

Many credit cards have similar offers. Barclaycard Rewards, for example, offers a range of deals with different retailers. You need to register in the app before you can start earning money. It also pays 0.25% cashback on other spending.

Typically you have to activate the deals before you spend money. (If you have just bought something and it is showing as pending on your statement, it might not be too late to do so.)

Before you spend anything, check if you need to shop via a specific link. This will be signposted on your bank’s website or app.

Quidco and TopCashback offer cashback from a large number of retailers, including, at the time of writing, up to 10% from the Lego shop and 5% from Boots. The sites require registration, and cashback is available either when you buy via a link or if you buy a gift card (see below).

You might be able to double up by buying through a cashback site and paying with your bank card.

Barclaycard is offering 4% cashback at Currys, while Quidco has a range of cashback offers at the same retailer, including up to 10% on selected wearable tech. Activate the offer on Barclaycard, then use your plastic to shop via Quidco, and you will get back 14% in total.

Quidco and TopCashback also offer cashback on retailers’ gift cards, which means you can benefit from the effective discounts in shops as well as online. Currently, for example, TopCashback is offering 6% back when you buy a Primark card to spend in store.

Another place to look for discounts is your workplace intranet. Many employees are offered cut-price gift cards, or access to special discounts, as a perk. Often you can buy instantly usable vouchers for high street shops at below their face value.

There are similar discount schemes aimed specifically at key workers such as teachers and nurses. These also offer gift cards at below face value.

Health Service Discounts and Discounts for Teachers sell discounted gift cards for 170 retailers, and you can use one to pay for something that is already discounted. Current offers include 5.5% off when you buy a Marks & Spencer card and 11% off one to spend with Adidas.

You cannot use these gift cards to buy via cashback sites – you have to go directly to the retailer. The good news is that you do not need to round up to the nearest £10 but can buy what you need to cover your purchase.

At the time of writing, a GHD Gold hair straightener bundle from Argos has a third off and is reduced to £159. Health Service Discounts and Discounts for Teachers are offering 3% off an Argos gift card, saving you another £4.77 – more than enough for a couple of rolls of wrapping paper.

Some retailers offer to match prices being charged elsewhere, and it is worth looking at these if you have a specific retailer you want to shop with. It is also worth keeping an eye on prices after you have made a purchase.

You may live near a John Lewis or like to earn the points you get on its credit card, and if so, its price promise could save you money. It pledges to match the prices being charged by a list of 25 other retailers including Currys, Argos and The Entertainer. John Lewis actively reduces prices to match, but if you spot something it has missed within seven days of making a purchase, it will refund the difference. It does have a caveat for Apple products, and will only match products bought directly from Apple or those sold elsewhere with a minimum two-year guarantee.

AO.com has extended its price match guarantee for Black Friday. It says if the price of your purchase drops on its site or you see it cheaper elsewhere, you can claim back the difference any time up to 23 December.

Several retailers including Argos, Currys and Very have a special Black Friday guarantee on some discounted products that only applies to their prices.

Argos, for instance, says that if something is marked with a “price guarantee”, it will not be reduced further before midnight on 25 December – but if it is, you will get a gift card for the difference. You don’t need to invoke the promise – just make sure you give the right email address when you buy.

At Currys, the promise lasts until 1 December, and you need to register your purchase. Once you have done that, it will automatically let you know if the price drops and will arrange a refund into your bank account.…

title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
author: Garrison Lovely
text:
Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm

You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams.

Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack.

But last month, several freezers in France burst into flames after temperature controls in hundreds of shops were hacked , spoiling tons of food and causing an estimated tens of millions of euros of damage. Similar cyber-attacks then hit freezers in six more countries .

Even if the recent outages weren’t the result of malicious behavior, it’s all a visceral reminder that the border between the digital and physical worlds is more porous than ever. And the digital border walls are crumbling – with the AI industry to blame. Frontier AI models can find and exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them, and the rush to patch raises the risk of exactly the kind of disruptions we’re now seeing.

The AI industry is built around relentlessly scaling AI models, discovering what new capabilities emerge, then deploying the models for commercial gain. So far, this process has wrecked education and sloppified the internet; now it threatens to break it altogether.

Instead of waiting to see what the companies break next, we should freeze the reckless gain-of-function experiments they call “frontier AI development”.

Already, hackers are “all using AI now”, declares Ireland’s cybersecurity chief. Google’s top threat analyst agrees : “At this point, we can assume that all threat actors are using AI in some capacity and their operations have benefited.”

And benefit they have. In recent months, apparent amateurs have used AI to hack more than 100 companies, from the tractor maker Deere to South Korean banks , with the hackers spending as little as $50 per successful infiltration.

Suspected North Korean hackers carried out the biggest heist ever, stealing $6.3bn from the crypto exchange Binance, less than half of which has been frozen or recovered.

Cyber-attacks took down hospital emergency rooms in New Mexico and Germany . AI-enabled hackers broke into the European Commission, disrupting services for more than 10 days.

And on Monday, attackers exploited a flaw in third-party software to serve malware to visitors of 178 organisations’ sites, including the BBC, CNN, Zoom and HSBC.

Last month, researchers using AI discovered a severe flaw in the programming language powering 70% of all websites. (The NSA outage, officials now say , was caused by a rushed patch for that very flaw.) The CEO of internet security provider Cloudflare said he knew of “a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities that are present in other pieces of critical software … I think we’re going to have a couple years where every single week it’s going to feel like the sky is falling.”

“The cyberspace that I built with my colleagues … is now on the verge of being completely destroyed by malicious actors,” the CEO of a multi-billion dollar Japanese financial services company said after his company was hacked last month.

While AI has been accelerating cybercrime for years , the recent deluge can be largely attributed to highly capable, easily modified open-weight models released by Chinese developers.

But the AI industry on both sides of the Pacific is responsible for the internet’s “ Black October ” and whatever other cyber horrors await us.

In their quest to render us obsolete , Anthropic and OpenAI were the first to develop and release superhuman hacker AIs – knowing that Chinese developers would piggyback off their progress to release guardrail-free hacker AIs in a matter of months.

The US companies’ plan was to use AI to fix the world’s critical software in time. They didn’t. “I no longer think we’re going to be able to patch all bugs,” OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said last month. His new plan is to use AI agents to defend against AI hackers. In other words, the flamethrower industry decided to start selling firehoses too.

When a Twitter/X user told Anthropic’s deputy cyber chief: “You and your cohorts created this monster,” his reply was shockingly candid: “yes. it was always going to be this way. we tried to warn the world.” Thanks for the heads up.

These hacks and disruptions may soon appear quaint. “Given the accelerating rate of AI capability development”, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in September, “it’s my worry that in 6–12 months [an AI agent] swarm could be capable of taking over the entire internet with a persistent botnet .”

But accelerating AI capabilities aren’t actually a “given” – they’re a product of trillions of dollars in investment and deliberate effort, which is predictably producing enormous new dangers. Anthropic’s IPO filing acknowledges that the entire insurance industry may not be big enough to cover the catastrophic or existential risks the company is creating.

Those risks extend beyond the cyber realm. This summer, researchers at Stanford University synthesized the first AI-designed viruses, and Anthropic quietly set up an automated biology wet lab – a space for physical experiments – in what it says is a bid to find treatments for rare diseases. Meanwhile, AI models steadily improve at assisting in the development of bioweapons. We’ll survive superhuman hacker AIs, but maybe not the bioterrorist variety.

All of these risks will arrive faster if the industry achieves its primary goal: turning AI development over entirely to the machines, in a process known as recursive self-improvement.…

title: Drone operator sorry for filming Pochettino’s first Manchester United training session
author: Reuters
text:
‘I fully accept it was unethical,’ he says

A drone operator who filmed Mauricio Pochettino’s first ⁠Manchester United training ⁠session on Thursday has apologised for what he called a “total error of judgment” and removed ⁠the footage from ⁠his ​YouTube channel.

The footage was uploaded online under the username “CC OVERVIEW”. In a statement posted on his YouTube channel ⁠on Friday, the drone operator said that while the flight ​was legal under drone regulations, ‌filming the session ‌had been “unethical”.

“My aim was to picture Mauricio Pochettino in his ‌United training kit for the supporters to see for the first time,” he said. “I fully accept it was unethical on my part. I would like to apologise to Manchester United , Mauricio Pochettino and the players for my actions and sincerely ‌hope those actions do not affect the outcome of any match.”

The operator said he had wrongly ​assumed only warm-up activities would be visible and that the training session would be open to various media outlets. He said neither Liverpool – United’s opponents on Sunday – nor any other football club had been involved ⁠in his decision to film at Carrington.

“The video has been ​removed from ​my channel,” he said.

Pochettino arrived ​from the US men’s national team this week ​after United ‌sacked Michael Carrick, ​and faces ​an immediate test at Anfield . United are 18th in the league after winning one of their 10 games. Liverpool are fourth.

title: Tinned food and long-life milk boost retail sales after 'Be Ready' campaign launch
text:
Retail sales rose in October, driven by people buying long-life food such as tinned goods and UHT milk, according to official figures , external .

Sales volumes were 0.7% higher as people responded to the government's emergency preparedness "Be Ready" campaign, the Office for National Statistics (ONS) said.

The campaign encouraged people to stock up in case of disruption to essential services by severe weather or cyberattacks.

Separate research released last week suggested that while households were stockpiling essentials, they were not panic buying .

The government campaign encouraged people to keep three days-worth of food and water in their homes.

Wet wipes, a torch and cash were also recommended.

"Supermarkets have told us that sales of long-life food items such as tinned food and UHT milk were boosted by the government's 'Be Ready' campaign," ONS chief economist Grant Fitzner said:

"Meanwhile fuel sales have been recovering from earlier low levels, despite pump prices rising again."

The rise in retail sales last month beat some economists' expectations - they had predicted a slight fall - and the uptick came after a 0.6% decline in September.

As well as sales being boosted by people buying essentials, visits to art galleries and clothing purchases were also higher in October.

The boost in sales comes at the beginning of the festive period, which is normally the busiest time of the year for retailers.

Jacqui Baker, partner and head of retail at auditing firm RSM UK, said that "retailers will want to see out the year with some Christmas cheer before consumers batten down the hatches in the New Year as energy costs skyrocket and inflation ramps up further".

Typical energy bills are forecast to go up by £443 per year from January, pushing up the pace of price rises.

Separate economic data released on Friday showed the government borrowed slightly less than economists had expected in October.

Borrowing - the difference between public sector spending and income - was £17bn last month, the ONS said. , external

Although that was £0.8bn higher than October last year, it was below analysts' forecasts of about £18bn.

Interest repayments were £11.2bn - the highest October debt interest figure on record - and £2.8bn more than a year ago.

These repayments have been pushed up by higher inflation, as payments on index-linked government bonds are linked to the inflation rate.

Inflation rose to 3.6% in October, mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices. The rate has been rising in recent months as the Iran war has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
author: Mark Sweney
text:
State attorney says scandal ‘raises bright red flags’ and aims to find out if company misled investors

California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors.”

The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China .

Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”

Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back .

Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
author: Alice Nightingale-Smith for MetDesk
text:
Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recorded

Multiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.

Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. Already, record-breaking rainfall affected San Fransisco on Wednesday, with heavy rain also causing 32,000 customers to lose power in Sacramento. Into this weekend, a further area of low pressure will bring considerable amounts of moisture for southern Oregon and northern California. By Sunday night, more than 100mm (4in) of rain is expected in places, with further snowfall for areas such as Donner Pass across the northern Sierra Nevada mountains.

title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
author: Sarah Marsh
text:
Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019

T he name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning.

Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays.

“It was something quite different. Most people reacted really well to it,” said Steve Anderson, 57. “The only negative reaction I heard was to the ginger shot, which some found too strong … but that’s a preference thing. The pods themselves were very palatable.”

Global packaging waste is on course to hit a projected 434.5m tonnes in 2025, rising to 525m tonnes by 2030, a compound annual growth rate of 3.9%, according to research from Smithers . Plastic is at the heart of this: between 2000 and 2019, the volume of plastic waste doubled, with packaging responsible for about 40% of it. Yet plastic is among the least recycled materials, with a worldwide recycling rate of just 27.9% in 2024. The UK’s overall plastic packaging recycling reached 52.5% in 2023, up from 51.4% in 2022.

Edible packaging could be part of the answer to this problem, with the market size valued at $1.04bn (£790m) in 2024 and poised to grow to $1.84bn by 2033, driven by consumers’ environmental concerns.

But market research says challenges exist. One report said this was “due to the sensitivity of edible packaging to fluctuating environmental conditions, necessitating special handling during shipping and storage ”. It also said customers were reluctant to use edible utensils and the challenges hindered “widespread adoption”.

However, beyond the science of packaging, a wider debate remains about our consumption habits. Environmental campaigners argue that the ultimate solution to the plastic waste crisis is not finding better ways to wrap single-use items, but moving away from a throwaway culture altogether.

Even for those who do want to create better packaging, money remains a hurdle. Prof James Elliott at the University of Cambridge, who is working on plastic packaging alternatives, said manufacturers were not keen to pay more for biodegradable alternatives. “They are very cost driven,” he said, adding that the non-biodegradable plastic market was $265bn “so the $1bn proportion being edible is small”.

Andrew Wallis, packaging lead at Innocent Drinks, said 78% of consumers would consider buying ginger shots encased in seaweed, according to a survey. He said it could also be used in Innocent’s kids’ range, which currently uses paper straws in plastic packaging. “Could that wrap be exchanged for a seaweed wrapper?” he said.

Notpla created similar pods for the London Marathon. Other examples of innovation in this area include Xampla, which created a stock cube wrapped in edible film, and Cupffee, which made the world’s first edible cup.

At Notpla’s headquarters, in east London, seaweed is used to encase small amounts of olive oil as well as for sandwich packaging and to replace plastic film in cardboard packaging. The team has also made spoons out of seaweed, which are used in ice-cream parlours including Ice Cream Union in London.

Rodrigo García González, co-founder of Notpla, said seaweed was a good sustainable solution because it grew rapidly. “Some seaweed can grow up to 60cm a day,” he said. “It’s one of the fastest-growing plants on Earth, much faster than bamboo, and it doesn’t compete with anything on land.” He also said it biodegraded more quickly than a leaf.

At Notpla, a machine pushes out ginger shots into seaweed casing, like sausages on a factory conveyor belt. The company is still working out how a product such as this could work in a supermarket: it lasts only three days, but in an unopened bottle could be kept for weeks.

Elliott said one of the big problems with edible packaging was about scale: “About 30-40% of all plastics used worldwide are used in packaging … the scale is phenomenal. We use 2m tonnes of plastic in the UK per year.” He said it would be hard to “harvest that much seaweed without making huge changes”.

But González said seaweed “already operates at a scale most people don’t realise”. He added: “Around 40m tonnes are harvested every year, almost all of it farmed, and it’s already in everyday products from toothpaste to ice-cream. It’s also one of the fastest-growing organisms on the planet.”

Elliott has been working on developing a non-edible packaging made from cellulose. “It’s designed to be composted. Cellulose is abundant in every plant, so we take waste plant material and turn it into films.”

He pointed to Xampla, another company developing plastic alternatives, which makes film from pea protein. A big advantage, he said, is that the material was not just farmable but could be made in vats, like a biochemical process.

Lubomila Jordanova from Cupffee and a Berlin-based expert in sustainability solutions, said the hardest part “was that there was nowhere to turn for answers”. She said an edible cup “isn’t bread and it isn’t a wafer. It has to behave like a real cup: hold coffee at 85C, not leak, and not go soft in your hand while you drink.”

Cupffee is now producing millions of edible cups, and its recipe is patented in 14 European countries, she said. But it was very difficult to scale. “Because customers expect every cup to be identical, exactly like a plastic or paper cup. But we’re making food. Getting that consistency took heavy investment in automation, quality control and our own machines.”…

title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
text:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Evangeline Atkinson had a frustrating experience over her credit score.

"I was at university, paying rent, paying bills, as I had been doing for many years. I tried to get a £30-a-month phone contract, and they said no," she recalls.

"When I dug into it, it was because I was completely invisible to the system. No record could be found for me at any of the big three credit reference agencies."

That experience inspired her to try to change the system.

In 2021, Atkinson founded a credit reference agency with her best-friend from school, who had also experienced difficulties getting credit.

Their firm, Noggin HQ, was authorised by the FCA in June. Atkinson explains it was set up to help consumers access affordable credit by analysing their current account transactional data.

The platform helps lenders interpret thousands of individual data points about a person's spending habits.

Crucially, it does this without using AI, which Atkinson has also argued "carries the risk of inbuilt bias".

"You have to be very careful", she warns. "It's very sensitive data and it would be very easy for the models to be inferring various kind of protected characteristics."

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".…

title: UK government borrowing rises less than forecast in surprise boost for chancellor John Healey
author: Richard Partington Senior economics correspondent
text:
UK economy defies City predictions and Iran war fallout, with gap between spending and income about £1bn lower than expected in October, at £17bn

The UK government borrowed less than expected in October despite a rise in debt interest costs, in a boost for chancellor John Healey amid the pressure on Britain’s economy from the Middle East war.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said public sector net borrowing – the difference between government spending and income – was £17bn in October, about £800m higher than the same month a year ago. City economists had forecast borrowing would increase by more, to £18bn.

In the financial year so far, public sector net borrowing was £111.3bn, the ONS said – £7.3bn less than in the same period last year, helped by stronger tax receipts.

Grant Fitzner, the ONS chief economist, said: “Borrowing so far this financial year remained lower than in the same period last year with receipts growing faster than spending. Income-related taxes’ receipts grew particularly strongly.

“However, monthly borrowing was up on last October, partly down to higher debt interest.”

The latest figures showed rising borrowing costs on financial markets drove the UK’s debt interest payments to £11.2bn in October - £2.8bn more than in the same month last year, and the highest figure for any October since monthly records began in 1997.

Some government bonds are directly linked to the retail prices index measure of inflation, with payments rising in line with it. RPI has increased in recent months as the Iran war has pushed up energy costs.

Public sector net debt rose to £3.1tn, equivalent to 95.8% of GDP – 1.9 percentage points higher than last year and at levels last seen in the early 1960s.

Chief secretary to the Treasury, Emma Reynolds, said Britain was showing “standout resilience despite the global impact of the conflict in Iran.

“This year we’ve cut borrowing faster than any other G20 country. Now we’re going to cut waste and bureaucracy by reprioritising spending and making public services more efficient with AI,” Reynolds added.

Britain’s economy has continued to grow at the second-fastest rate in the G7 despite the fallout from the war in the Middle East, bolstered by AI investment and households continuing to spend.

In his budget last month, Healey raised taxes on banks to fund relief for households being squeezed by the energy shock from the Middle East war.

Against a highly uncertain global backdrop, Healey stuck to the government’s fiscal rules with £15bn of headroom – less than the £23.6bn buffer left by his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, as the conflict drove up the UK government’s borrowing costs.

After a low-key budget statement designed with febrile bond markets in mind, economists warned the chancellor had set himself up for a “brutal” spending review next year.

Avoiding a return to austerity for unprotected government departments could require a £17bn top-up to the spending plans for 2030-31, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies. That is before taking into account an additional £11bn needed to fund a commitment to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP.

Official figures on Wednesday showed inflation in the UK rose in October to 3.6% amid the global surge in energy prices triggered by the Iran war. Economic forecasters predict a further rise in inflation, with the Bank of England anticipating a peak of close to 5% next year.

Threadneedle Street raised interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month and warned further increases might be required to combat inflationary pressures unleashed by the Iran war. Financial markets predict three quarter-point rate increases before the end of next year.

Rob Wood, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Pantheon Macroeconomics, said: “The October budget did little to address the more serious challenges facing the public finances, so we continue to have doubts about the government’s ability to follow through on its fiscal plans, suggesting upside risks to borrowing in the coming years.”

title: Vape users hospitalised after losing consciousness, prompting public health warning in New South Wales
author: Catie McLeod
text:
Testing confirms presence of etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Three people who lost consciousness and were hospitalised in New South Wales after using certain vapes have tested positive for the unregulated anaesthetic agent etomidate, health officials said.

NSW health on Friday issued a public warning about vape liquids containing etomidate, a strong and fast-acting sedative used as a general anaesthetic overseas but not registered for medical use in Australia.

The three people who were hospitalised had used non-nicotine refillable vapes, the state health department said. Testing of their blood and urine confirmed the presence of etomidate.

The department would not confirm how old the three patients were, where they were hospitalised, or their condition on Friday.

The discovery of etomidate in vapes in NSW comes about four months after Victorian health officials announced they had found the powerful anaesthetic agent in an illicit vape sold in Melbourne.

On Friday, NSW health warned vapes sold as space pods, space oil, kpods, piu piu vapes, or zombie vapes may contain etomidate, or other substances, including ketamine, THC and potent opioids.

The medical director of the NSW poisons information centre, Dr Darren Roberts, said etomidate’s effects were unpredictable when used in a vape.

Roberts said etomidate could cause confusion, drowsiness, slow breathing, vomiting, muscle spasms or movements that were hard to control, and people who took it could become unresponsive.

These effects could be life threatening, especially if used with other drugs that could cause sedation, such as alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and GHB, Roberts said.

He said etomidate could also cause long-term harm when used regularly, including the disruption of hormones produced by the adrenal gland.

These hormones are important in regulating stress responses and need to be replaced if they aren’t produced naturally, he said.

“The contents found in non-nicotine vapes vary,” Roberts said. “You can’t assume what’s inside.”

He urged anyone considering using a vape to ask themselves what could be in it.

“You won’t get into trouble for seeking medical care,” he said. If you feel unwell, or if your friend feels unwell, after using a vape, do something about it.”

NSW health officials said it recommended people administer Naloxone to anyone who became responsive after using any drug, in case they had ingested opioids.

Naloxone is an opioid overdose treatment , which is free at pharmacies and does not require a prescription.

Naloxone won’t reverse the effects of etomidate, as the sedative does not belong to the opioid class of drugs, but it is still safe to give, health officials said.

The officials said anyone who witnessed someone experiencing unexpected symptoms after using drugs should call triple zero immediately or seek urgent medical attention.
